Microsoft Learn: Implement and manage storage in Azure
Microsoft Learn: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
Microsoft Learn: Configure and manage virtual networks for Azure administrators
Microsoft Learn: Monitor and back up Azure resources

flashcards.back: Creating and managing users, security groups, and Microsoft 365 groups. Dynamic group membership rules automatically add or remove members based on user or device attributes.
flashcards.detail: A dynamic group for every user whose department is "Sales" updates itself automatically as people move in and out.

flashcards.back: Assigning a license to a group instead of individual users, so every current and future member automatically receives (or loses) that license.
flashcards.detail: This is why new employees added to an "All Staff" group can get licensed automatically without a manual step.

flashcards.back: Inviting people from outside your organization as guests, who authenticate with their own existing identity rather than a new account you create for them.
flashcards.detail: External collaboration settings control who can invite guests and what guests can see once invited.

flashcards.back: Lets users reset their own forgotten password without contacting the help desk, after registering authentication methods like a phone number or authenticator app.
flashcards.detail: This is the direct answer whenever a scenario is about reducing help desk password-reset tickets.

flashcards.back: A role is assigned to a security principal at a scope — management group, subscription, resource group, or resource. Assignments are additive, and the most permissive applicable assignment wins.
flashcards.detail: If someone has Reader at the subscription and Contributor at one resource group, they have Contributor there and Reader everywhere else in that subscription.

flashcards.front: Owner vs. Contributor vs. Reader vs. User Access Administrator
flashcards.back: Owner: full access, plus can assign roles to others. Contributor: full access to manage resources, but cannot assign roles. Reader: view-only. User Access Administrator: manage others' access without managing the resources themselves.
flashcards.detail: The Owner-vs-Contributor distinction (can they grant access to others?) is one of the most commonly tested RBAC facts.

flashcards.back: A policy is a single rule, like requiring a specific region. An initiative groups multiple related policies together so they can be assigned as one bundle, useful for compliance standards.
flashcards.detail: Think of an initiative as a policy 'playlist' — several individual rules assigned together.

flashcards.back: As an administrator you directly create and move resources between resource groups, and troubleshoot conflicts between inherited policy and RBAC assignments from higher scopes.
flashcards.detail: AZ-104 expects you to reason about real conflicts, not just define the terms the way AZ-900 does.

flashcards.back: Set spending budgets with alert thresholds, and use Cost Analysis to break down spend by resource, tag, or service over time.
flashcards.detail: A budget alert doesn't stop spending by itself — it just notifies; stopping spend requires a separate automated action.

flashcards.front: Storage account types and performance tiers
flashcards.back: General-purpose v2 is the standard account type for most scenarios and uses Standard performance (HDD-backed, cost-effective). Premium performance (SSD-backed, for high-throughput, low-latency needs) comes from premium account types such as premium block blob, file share, and page blob accounts instead.
flashcards.detail: Premium is the answer whenever a scenario stresses low latency or high transaction rates.

flashcards.front: Access keys vs. Shared Access Signature (SAS)
flashcards.back: Access keys grant full, unrestricted access to the entire storage account. A SAS grants limited, time-boxed, scoped access to specific resources or operations, without exposing the account key.
flashcards.detail: Whenever a scenario wants to share limited, temporary access with a third party, the answer is SAS, not an access key.

flashcards.back: Restrict a storage account to specific virtual networks or IP address ranges, or allow trusted Microsoft services to bypass the firewall.
flashcards.detail: This is a network-level control, separate from identity-based access like RBAC or a SAS token.

flashcards.back: Rules that automatically transition blobs between access tiers, like Hot to Cool to Archive, or delete them after a set number of days, based on last-modified or last-accessed time.
flashcards.detail: This is the automation answer whenever a scenario wants aging data to move to cheaper storage without manual intervention.

flashcards.front: Blob versioning vs. soft delete vs. snapshots
flashcards.back: Versioning automatically keeps prior versions when a blob is overwritten. Soft delete lets you recover deleted blobs within a retention window and, when versioning is off, also keeps overwritten data as soft-deleted snapshots. A snapshot is a manual, read-only copy taken at a specific point in time.
flashcards.detail: Versioning is the fuller answer for getting back an overwritten blob's earlier content, since it keeps every prior version; soft delete alone only retains overwritten data as snapshots for its retention window.

flashcards.back: Azure Files provides SMB or NFS file shares that can be mounted like a network drive. Blob storage holds unstructured object data accessed through REST or an SDK, not mounted as a drive.
flashcards.detail: If a scenario needs multiple VMs to mount and share the same drive, that's Azure Files, not Blob storage.

flashcards.back: GRS replicates to a secondary region, but that data isn't readable during normal operation. RA-GRS (and RA-GZRS) additionally allow read access to the secondary region even before a failover.
flashcards.detail: If a scenario needs to actually read from the secondary region during normal operation, plain GRS isn't enough — it needs the read-access variant.

flashcards.back: A storage account can serve static website content, like HTML/CSS/JS, directly from Blob storage using a special $web container, without a separate web server.
flashcards.detail: This is the low-cost, serverless answer for hosting a purely static site.

flashcards.back: AzCopy, Azure Storage Explorer, and Azure Migrate/Data Box, first introduced at the AZ-900 level, remain the core tools an administrator configures and runs for moving data into storage accounts.
flashcards.detail: AZ-104 expects you to actually configure and troubleshoot these tools, not just recognize their names. Azure Storage Mover is Microsoft's managed service for migrating on-premises file shares into Azure Storage, and is the recommended route for large migrations rather than scripting AzCopy.

flashcards.back: VM size determines CPU, memory, and disk throughput. Series (like B, D, F) are optimized for different workloads: B for burstable/low-cost, D for general purpose, F for compute-optimized.
flashcards.detail: A burstable B-series VM is cheap but throttles sustained high CPU use — the wrong choice for a constantly busy server.

flashcards.back: Managed disks are Azure-managed storage for a VM's OS or data, offered as Standard HDD, Standard SSD, Premium SSD, and Ultra Disk, from lowest to highest performance.
flashcards.detail: Ultra Disk allows configuring throughput and IOPS independently of disk size, for the most demanding workloads.

flashcards.front: Availability sets vs. zones vs. Scale Sets
flashcards.back: Availability set: distributes VMs across fault and update domains within one datacenter. Availability zone: spreads VMs across physically separate datacenters in a region. Scale Set: automatically adds or removes VM instances based on demand.
flashcards.detail: Only availability zones protect against a whole-datacenter failure — availability sets only spread risk within one.

flashcards.front: VM extensions and Custom Script Extension
flashcards.back: Small agents installed on a VM to perform post-deployment configuration tasks, like the Custom Script Extension automatically running a script right after provisioning.
flashcards.detail: This is the answer whenever a scenario wants configuration to happen automatically without manually logging into the VM.

flashcards.back: An App Service plan defines the compute tier and region for one or more web apps. Scaling up changes the plan's tier or size; scaling out adds more instances of the same tier.
flashcards.detail: Scale up = bigger box. Scale out = more boxes. Both are configured on the App Service plan, not the individual app.

flashcards.back: Separate, swappable environments, like staging, for an App Service app, letting you validate a new version before swapping it into production with minimal downtime.
flashcards.detail: A swap exchanges the URLs/configuration between slots almost instantly, rather than redeploying code.

flashcards.front: Container Instances vs. Container Apps vs. AKS
flashcards.back: Container Instances run a single container quickly with no orchestration. Container Apps add serverless scaling and microservices features without managing a cluster. AKS gives full Kubernetes control.
flashcards.detail: Container Apps is called out in the skills outline alongside Container Instances, so it is tested content, not just AKS.

flashcards.back: ARM templates are Azure's native JSON Infrastructure as Code format. Bicep is a newer, more concise language that compiles down to ARM JSON — functionally equivalent, but easier to read and write.
flashcards.detail: The current skills outline expects you to be comfortable reading and modifying Bicep files, reflecting real-world administrator practice.

flashcards.back: Resizing a running VM to a size unavailable on its current hardware cluster typically requires deallocating (stopping) the VM first, then resizing.
flashcards.detail: This trips people up because 'stopped' in the portal isn't the same as 'deallocated' — only deallocated VMs release their hardware allocation. A move to another resource group or subscription never changes the region, and a region change is done with Azure Resource Mover or Site Recovery.

flashcards.front: VNets and subnets at admin depth
flashcards.back: As an administrator you create and size VNets and subnets, considering IP address space (CIDR) and the fact that Azure reserves 5 addresses in every subnet regardless of its size.
flashcards.detail: That reserved-address detail is a specific number the exam likes to test directly.

flashcards.back: Filter inbound and outbound traffic to subnets or network interfaces using security rules with a priority, source, destination, port, and protocol. Lower priority number wins and is evaluated first.
flashcards.detail: A lower-numbered rule that allows traffic can still be overridden by an even-lower-numbered rule that denies it. Azure Firewall works at a broader, whole-VNet scope for the same general goal.

flashcards.back: Connects two VNets directly, even across regions, with traffic staying on the Microsoft backbone. Peering is not transitive — peered VNets don't automatically reach each other's other peers.
flashcards.detail: If A is peered to B, and B is peered to C, A and C still cannot talk to each other without their own direct peering.

flashcards.back: Azure Load Balancer works at layer 4 (TCP/UDP), distributing traffic by IP and port only. Application Gateway works at layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS), and can route by URL path and terminate SSL centrally.
flashcards.detail: If a scenario needs to route by URL path, like /images vs /api, that's Application Gateway, not Load Balancer.

flashcards.back: A public Load Balancer distributes internet traffic to backend resources. An internal (private) Load Balancer only distributes traffic within a VNet, never from the public internet.
flashcards.detail: An internal Load Balancer is the answer when a scenario needs load balancing purely between internal tiers, like web servers talking to app servers. A NAT Gateway solves the opposite problem — stable outbound-only internet access, not inbound distribution. Basic Load Balancer was retired on September 30, 2025, so current scenarios assume the Standard SKU.

flashcards.front: Azure DNS and private DNS zones
flashcards.back: Azure DNS hosts public DNS zones, resolvable from the internet. Private DNS zones provide name resolution within one or more VNets, without exposing those records publicly.
flashcards.detail: Private DNS zones are the answer whenever internal name resolution shouldn't be visible outside the VNet — including resolving the normal hostname of a resource reached through a Private Endpoint.

flashcards.back: A suite of tools for monitoring and diagnosing network issues in Azure, including packet capture, IP flow verify (is a rule blocking traffic?), and connection troubleshoot.
flashcards.detail: IP flow verify specifically tells you whether an NSG rule is allowing or denying a particular flow of traffic.

flashcards.back: Provides secure RDP or SSH access to VMs directly through the Azure portal, without exposing the VM's public IP or needing a separate VPN connection.
flashcards.detail: This is the answer whenever a scenario wants secure remote access to a VM without giving that VM a public IP.

flashcards.front: VPN Gateway vs. ExpressRoute, admin depth
flashcards.back: VPN Gateway is encrypted and travels over the public internet. ExpressRoute is private but not encrypted by default. Administrators configure gateway SKUs and connection types, like site-to-site or point-to-site.
flashcards.detail: Point-to-site connects an individual device to a VNet; site-to-site connects two whole networks together.

flashcards.back: Metrics are lightweight numerical time-series data, like CPU percentage. Logs are detailed, queryable event and record data stored in a Log Analytics workspace.
flashcards.detail: Metrics answer 'how much' over time. Logs answer 'exactly what happened' with detail you can query.

flashcards.back: An alert rule triggers when a metric or log condition is met. An action group defines what happens next, like sending an email, an SMS, or running an Azure Function.
flashcards.detail: The alert rule is the trigger condition; the action group is the response — they're configured separately and linked together.

flashcards.front: Recovery Services vault and backup policies
flashcards.back: A Recovery Services vault stores backup data and manages backup policies, which define how often backups run and how long they're retained.
flashcards.detail: One vault can hold backup policies for multiple resource types, like VMs and file shares. Newer data sources such as Azure Disks and Azure Blobs use a Backup vault instead of a Recovery Services vault.

flashcards.back: Replicates VMs to a secondary region for disaster recovery, enabling a failover of an entire workload if the primary region becomes unavailable.
flashcards.detail: Backup restores a point-in-time copy. Site Recovery fails over a running workload to keep it operating elsewhere.

flashcards.back: A Log Analytics workspace collects log data from multiple resources. Kusto Query Language (KQL) is used to query that data for troubleshooting and reporting.
flashcards.detail: KQL is the specific query language name the exam expects you to recognize, even without writing complex queries yourself.

flashcards.front: Backup vs. Site Recovery, when to use each
flashcards.back: Backup protects against data loss, restoring a VM or file to a point in time. Site Recovery protects against a broader outage, failing over a whole workload to a secondary region.
flashcards.detail: A corrupted disk calls for Backup. A whole region going dark calls for Site Recovery.

flashcards.back: A CanNotDelete lock blocks deletion while still allowing reads and configuration changes. A ReadOnly lock blocks both deletion and any modification, treating authorized users like they only have Reader access.
flashcards.detail: Locks apply regardless of RBAC role — even an Owner cannot delete a CanNotDelete-locked resource until the lock is removed.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Entra roles vs. Azure RBAC roles
flashcards.back: Microsoft Entra roles (like Global Administrator) control the identity plane — users, groups, licenses, tenant settings. Azure RBAC roles (like Owner) control the resource plane — VMs, storage, networking. A Global Administrator has no Azure resource access by default.
flashcards.detail: The 'elevate access' setting in Microsoft Entra ID properties is what grants a Global Administrator the Azure RBAC User Access Administrator role at the root scope, if tenant-wide resource access is needed.

flashcards.back: Roles like Storage Blob Data Contributor, Reader, and Owner grant a user or managed identity direct access to blob data via Microsoft Entra ID authentication, without ever using an account key or a SAS token.
flashcards.detail: This is distinct from the control-plane Contributor role, which manages the storage account itself but does not automatically grant data access once key-based access is restricted.

flashcards.back: Time-based retention (once the policy is locked) and legal hold policies make blobs write-once-read-many: they cannot be modified or deleted by anyone, including the storage account Owner, until the retention period expires or the legal hold is removed.
flashcards.detail: This is the compliance answer whenever a scenario needs to prove data was never altered, not just backed up.

flashcards.back: A managed disk tier that, like Ultra Disk, lets you configure capacity, IOPS, and throughput independently — but with broader region/VM availability and typically lower cost than Ultra Disk.
flashcards.detail: Standard SSD and the original Premium SSD scale performance only as a side effect of the size tier chosen; v2 and Ultra Disk break that link.

flashcards.back: VMs that run on Azure's unused capacity at a steep discount, but can be evicted with little warning when that capacity is needed elsewhere.
flashcards.detail: The right fit for interruptible workloads like batch processing or dev/test — never for anything requiring guaranteed uptime.

flashcards.back: Group VM network interfaces by application role, like "WebTier," so an NSG rule can reference the group as a source or destination instead of hardcoded IP addresses that change over time.
flashcards.detail: This is the answer whenever a scenario wants an NSG rule to keep working automatically as VMs in a role are added or removed.

flashcards.back: The current, supported agent for collecting metrics and logs from VMs into Azure Monitor, configured through data collection rules. It replaced the legacy Log Analytics agent (MMA/OMS), retired in August 2024.
flashcards.detail: Any scenario describing a new deployment should use AMA — the old agent should be recognized as outdated, not chosen.

flashcards.back: A unified service for assessing OS patch compliance and scheduling recurring update installation windows across Windows and Linux VMs, including on-premises and multi-cloud machines connected via Arc.
flashcards.detail: This replaced the older, separate Update Management solution built on Log Analytics and Automation.

flashcards.back: Management groups sit above subscriptions in the scope hierarchy, letting you apply Azure Policy and RBAC assignments to many subscriptions at once instead of repeating them per subscription.
flashcards.detail: Because RBAC assignments inherit downward through the scope hierarchy, an assignment made at a management group flows down to every subscription and resource group underneath it.

flashcards.back: A managed, stateful network firewall for an entire VNet, filtering traffic by rules, FQDN tags, and threat intelligence feeds — broader in scope than a per-subnet NSG.
flashcards.detail: Where Network Security Groups (NSGs) filter traffic to a specific subnet or NIC, Azure Firewall centralizes filtering and logging for a whole hub VNet in a hub-and-spoke design.

flashcards.back: Gives a PaaS resource (like a storage account or SQL database) a private IP address inside your VNet, so traffic to it never traverses the public internet.
flashcards.detail: Making the resource's normal hostname resolve to that private IP is exactly the job of a private DNS zone linked to the VNet.

flashcards.back: Provides a stable, shared public IP for outbound-only internet connections from resources in a subnet, without exposing them to inbound internet traffic.
flashcards.detail: Unlike a public Load Balancer, which handles inbound traffic to backend resources, a NAT Gateway only handles the outbound direction.

flashcards.back: A JSON-defined role built from a specific set of allowed and denied actions, for when the built-in roles are either too broad or too narrow for what a team actually needs to do.
flashcards.detail: A custom role is assigned at a scope, and inherits downward from it, exactly the same way a built-in role does.

flashcards.back: Captures a VM's console output and a screenshot of its current screen state, letting an admin diagnose a VM that fails to boot or hangs during startup without needing an existing remote connection into it.
flashcards.detail: This is the first troubleshooting step for a VM that seems unreachable — it works even when RDP/SSH themselves are the thing that's broken, since it doesn't depend on the guest OS's network stack at all.

flashcards.back: A policy engine that evaluates signals at sign-in time — user, device, location, and risk — and applies a control in response, such as requiring MFA or blocking access outright, rather than every user getting the same static access rules.
flashcards.detail: This is layered on top of, not instead of, RBAC: Conditional Access decides whether a sign-in is allowed to happen at all, while RBAC decides what that signed-in identity can then do.

flashcards.front: ARM deployment modes: complete vs. incremental
flashcards.back: Incremental mode (the default) adds or updates resources in the template without touching anything else in the resource group. Complete mode deletes any resource in the resource group that isn't defined in the template being deployed.
flashcards.detail: Complete mode is the one that can silently delete resources someone else created by hand, which is a classic reason why ARM and Bicep deployments in Complete mode deserve a careful review, not a routine one.

flashcards.back: A point-in-time, read-only copy of a managed disk, usable to create a new disk or VM from that captured state. It is separate from blob snapshots, which protect blob data rather than disks.
flashcards.detail: Managed disks are protected by disk snapshots, or by a backup policy in a Recovery Services vault for a fuller backup solution; blob snapshots are a completely separate mechanism for a completely separate storage type.

flashcards.back: A managed identity lets an Azure resource, like a VM or an App Service app, authenticate to other Azure services without any credential stored in code or configuration. A system-assigned identity is created and tied to the lifecycle of one specific resource, and is deleted automatically when that resource is. A user-assigned identity is instead its own standalone resource that can be attached to several resources at once. Data-plane storage roles, like Storage Blob Data Contributor, are commonly assigned to a managed identity rather than to a human user.
flashcards.detail: This is the credential-free answer whenever a scenario wants one Azure resource to reach another without a stored secret or connection-string password sitting in application configuration.

flashcards.back: Analyzes your resource configurations and usage telemetry to produce personalized recommendations across cost, security, reliability, operational excellence, and performance. It is a proactive best-practices check, distinct from Azure Monitor metrics and logs, which report what is actually happening rather than what should be changed.
flashcards.detail: Advisor recommends configuration improvements before something breaks; it does not itself monitor live health or trigger alerts the way an alert rule paired with an action group does.

flashcards.back: An Azure Monitor feature purpose-built for application performance monitoring: request rates, response times, failure rates, and dependency tracing down to individual requests. It complements the infrastructure-level telemetry that a Log Analytics workspace collects from the underlying VMs and platform resources.
flashcards.detail: Whenever a scenario is specifically about an application's own performance, like slow page loads or failing dependencies, Application Insights is the targeted answer, not general infrastructure monitoring.

flashcards.back: Reports on Azure platform issues, outages, planned maintenance, and health advisories, filtered to the specific resources and regions your subscription actually uses — distinct from Azure Advisor, which recommends configuration improvements rather than reporting on ongoing platform incidents.
flashcards.detail: If a scenario is about whether an outage is Microsoft's problem or your own configuration, Service Health answers the first question and Advisor addresses the second.

flashcards.back: A policy definition's effect decides what happens to a non-compliant resource: Audit just flags it in reports, Deny blocks the request outright, Append/Modify quietly adds or changes specific fields in the request, and DeployIfNotExists automatically deploys a related resource, like a diagnostic setting, to bring it into compliance.
flashcards.detail: DeployIfNotExists is the one that actually fixes things going forward without blocking anyone — it's the automation answer whenever a scenario wants every new resource to come with some companion configuration already attached.

flashcards.back: A recurring, scheduled process where a designated reviewer explicitly confirms whether a user, often a guest or someone in a privileged role, still needs the access they have, with access automatically revoked if it isn't confirmed.
flashcards.detail: This is the recertification answer whenever a scenario describes access that was granted long ago and now needs periodic, human-confirmed justification rather than running forever unchecked.

flashcards.back: Scope a Microsoft Entra role, like Helpdesk Administrator, to only a defined subset of users, groups, or devices, such as one regional office or school, instead of that role applying across the whole tenant.
flashcards.detail: Think of it as the Microsoft Entra counterpart to scoping an Azure RBAC assignment to one resource group: an administrative unit narrows an Entra role's reach in the same way.

flashcards.back: Keeps an on-premises Windows Server file share synchronized with an Azure file share. Cloud tiering can replace infrequently-accessed local files with lightweight pointers that fetch the content on demand, freeing local disk space while frequently-used files stay fully cached nearby.
flashcards.detail: This is specifically the hybrid on-premises-to-cloud sync layer on top of an Azure file share; it is not a replacement for one, and Blob storage does not offer it.

flashcards.back: Manually promotes the secondary region of a GRS, RA-GRS, GZRS, or RA-GZRS account to primary during an outage. Because geo-replication to the secondary is asynchronous, the most recent writes made just before the outage may not have replicated yet and can be lost.
flashcards.detail: This is the operational other half of read-access redundancy: RA-GRS lets you read from the secondary region, while a customer-initiated failover is what actually cuts over to it.

flashcards.back: Asynchronously copies block blobs from a source storage account to a separate destination account, including across regions, for scenarios like serving a local read copy to users near the destination region or keeping an independently-managed secondary copy.
flashcards.detail: Unlike the Microsoft-managed secondary behind RA-GRS, which you can't address independently, object replication creates a real, separately-addressable destination account you control.

flashcards.back: Place a group of VMs as physically close together as possible within a datacenter, to minimize network latency between them. This is the opposite goal of availability sets and availability zones, which deliberately spread VMs apart for resiliency.
flashcards.detail: This is the answer whenever a scenario is about several VMs that talk to each other constantly and need the lowest possible latency between them, not protection from a shared failure.

flashcards.back: Controls how instances pick up a changed Scale Set model: Manual requires explicitly upgrading each instance, Automatic updates every instance right away, and Rolling updates instances in small batches with health checks between batches so a bad update can't take down the whole set at once.
flashcards.detail: Rolling is the answer whenever a scenario wants a model change to roll out safely in waves rather than all at once or one instance at a time by hand.

flashcards.front: Azure Disk Encryption vs. server-side encryption
flashcards.back: Every managed disk already gets server-side encryption at rest automatically, using a platform-managed key by default, with no setup required. Azure Disk Encryption is an optional additional layer that encrypts the guest OS/data volumes from inside the VM itself, using BitLocker or DM-Crypt.
flashcards.detail: A scenario asking what protects data at rest with zero configuration is describing the platform-managed default, not Azure Disk Encryption, which is the extra, opt-in layer. Microsoft has announced that Azure Disk Encryption retires on September 15, 2028, with encryption at host as the recommended replacement.

flashcards.back: Extends a subnet's identity onto the Microsoft backbone so traffic to a PaaS resource, like a storage account, takes an optimized route — but that resource keeps its normal public endpoint, reachable by other authorized callers too.
flashcards.detail: Contrast with Private Endpoint, which instead gives the PaaS resource an actual private IP address inside your VNet, changing how it's reached rather than just optimizing the route to its existing public one.

flashcards.back: Custom entries in a route table that override Azure's default system routes, letting traffic for a subnet be forced through a specific next hop, like a network virtual appliance or firewall, instead of its normal default path.
flashcards.detail: This is exactly how traffic gets forced through Azure Firewall or another inspection appliance in a hub-and-spoke design — the route table is what actually redirects it there.

flashcards.back: Basic (now called DDoS infrastructure protection) is automatically enabled for Azure public IPs at no cost and defends against common network-layer flood attacks. Standard (now offered as DDoS Network Protection, or per-public-IP DDoS IP Protection) adds tuned mitigation policies, attack analytics and alerting, and, with Network Protection, cost protection against scale-out charges incurred during a documented attack, for a paid plan.
flashcards.detail: If a scenario specifically wants attack-specific telemetry or billing protection during an attack, that's the paid tier; the free baseline is already running in the background either way.

flashcards.back: Define which resource logs and metrics a specific resource sends, and to where, like a Log Analytics workspace, a storage account, or an Event Hub. Without one configured, that resource's own logs aren't collected anywhere, even though basic platform metrics are already available in Azure Monitor automatically.
flashcards.detail: This is the missing piece whenever a scenario describes a resource whose detailed logs never show up in Log Analytics — platform metrics flow in automatically, but resource logs need a diagnostic setting routing them there explicitly.

flashcards.back: Define exactly what data the Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) collects from a VM, like a specific performance counter or event log channel, and which destination it's sent to — letting you include exactly what's needed and leave out noisier data you don't.
flashcards.detail: This is the configuration layer that sits behind Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) — the agent is the collector, but a DCR is what actually tells it what to collect and where to send it.

flashcards.back: A Kusto query starts with a table name and pipes (|) the data through operators in sequence, like where to filter rows, summarize to aggregate them, and project to choose which columns to keep — order matters, since each operator works on the output of the one before it.
flashcards.detail: Knowing the language is called KQL is only the start; this is the actual shape a query takes once you start writing one.

flashcards.back: Provides just-in-time, time-bound, approval-based activation of privileged roles. Users hold an eligible assignment and must activate it, often with MFA and a justification, for a limited window before it expires. It requires Microsoft Entra ID P2 or Microsoft Entra ID Governance licensing.
flashcards.detail: The answer when a scenario wants admins to have elevated rights only when needed instead of permanent standing access. It covers both Microsoft Entra roles and Azure RBAC roles.

flashcards.back: Requires a second proof of identity at sign-in, such as the Microsoft Authenticator app, a FIDO2 security key, or a one-time code, in addition to the password. It sharply reduces the risk from stolen or guessed passwords.
flashcards.detail: MFA is usually enforced through a Conditional Access policy or security defaults. A scenario that wants MFA only for admins, or only from untrusted locations, points to Conditional Access.

flashcards.back: A free, preconfigured set of identity protections in Microsoft Entra ID. It requires all users to register for MFA, requires MFA for administrators, and blocks legacy authentication protocols. It is turned on by default in newer tenants.
flashcards.detail: Choose Conditional Access instead when you need granular rules. The two are alternatives, so security defaults must be turned off before you can use Conditional Access policies.

flashcards.back: An app registration is the global definition of an application in its home Microsoft Entra tenant. A service principal is the local identity of that application in a tenant, and it is what receives permissions and Azure role assignments.
flashcards.detail: Use a service principal for automation such as a deployment pipeline. For an Azure resource calling another Azure service, a managed identity is preferred because there is no secret to store or rotate.

flashcards.back: Name-value pairs, like Environment=Prod or CostCenter=1234, attached to resources and resource groups to organize them for billing, ownership, and automation. Tags are not inherited from a resource group by default.
flashcards.detail: Cost Analysis can group spend by tag. Azure Policy can require a tag or copy it from the resource group, which is how teams enforce a tagging standard.

flashcards.back: The deployment and management layer for Azure. Every request from the portal, CLI, PowerShell, SDKs, or REST API goes through it, and it applies RBAC, Azure Policy, locks, and tags consistently before creating, updating, or deleting resources.
flashcards.detail: This is why one role assignment or policy behaves the same whether someone uses the portal or a script, and why a template can deploy many resources as a single operation.

flashcards.back: A logical container that holds related Azure resources so they can be deployed, secured, and deleted together. Every resource lives in exactly one resource group, and resource groups cannot be nested inside each other.
flashcards.detail: Deleting a resource group deletes everything inside it, and roles, policies, and locks applied to it are inherited by its resources. The group's location only stores its metadata.

flashcards.back: A deny assignment blocks specific actions at a scope and overrides any role assignment that would otherwise allow them, even Owner. Administrators cannot author them directly. Azure creates them for protected resources, such as those managed by deployment stacks or managed applications.
flashcards.detail: Deny is evaluated before allow, so an Owner who is still blocked from an action points to a deny assignment, not a missing role.

flashcards.back: A dedicated, trusted instance of Microsoft Entra ID that represents one organization and holds its users, groups, and app registrations. It has a unique tenant ID, and every Azure subscription trusts exactly one tenant for authentication.
flashcards.detail: One tenant can have many subscriptions, but a subscription belongs to only one tenant. Moving a subscription to a different tenant removes its existing Azure role assignments.

flashcards.back: A named set of constraints, such as start time, expiry time, and permissions, defined on a blob container, file share, queue, or table that a service SAS can reference. Changing or deleting the policy changes or revokes every SAS that uses it.
flashcards.detail: This is how you revoke an ad hoc SAS without rotating the account key. A container supports up to five stored access policies, and a user delegation SAS cannot use one.

flashcards.back: A shared access signature for Blob storage that is signed with a user delegation key obtained using Microsoft Entra credentials, rather than the storage account key. Its permissions are limited to what the signing identity is allowed to do.
flashcards.detail: Microsoft recommends it as the most secure type of SAS because no account key is involved. It is revoked by revoking the user delegation keys, not through a stored access policy.

flashcards.front: Blob access tiers (Hot, Cool, Cold, Archive)
flashcards.back: Hot suits frequently accessed data. Cool suits infrequent access kept at least 30 days, Cold suits rarely accessed data kept at least 90 days, and Archive suits offline long-term data kept at least 180 days. Colder tiers cost less to store but more to read.
flashcards.detail: Archive blobs cannot be read until rehydrated to an online tier, which can take hours. Moving or deleting a blob before its minimum period incurs an early deletion charge.

flashcards.back: ZRS keeps three synchronous copies across availability zones in one region, surviving a datacenter failure. GZRS adds an asynchronous copy to the paired region for both zone and regional protection, and RA-GZRS also allows reading from that secondary.
flashcards.detail: Pick ZRS when data must stay in one region but survive a zone failure. Pick GZRS when it must also survive the loss of the whole region.

flashcards.front: SFTP support for Azure Blob Storage
flashcards.back: Lets partners and legacy systems upload and download blobs using the SSH File Transfer Protocol, with no separate server to run. It requires a storage account with hierarchical namespace enabled and uses local users with permissions on specific containers.
flashcards.detail: A scenario about a vendor that can only use SFTP and must write into Azure storage points here. Remember the two prerequisites: hierarchical namespace and a local user.

flashcards.back: Automatically changes the instance count of a Virtual Machine Scale Set or App Service plan using rules based on metrics, such as CPU above 70 percent, or on a schedule. Each autoscale setting defines minimum, maximum, and default instance counts.
flashcards.detail: Use different thresholds for scale-out and scale-in, and a cooldown period after each action so metrics can settle. Without that gap, instances flap in and out.

flashcards.back: A repository for managing and sharing custom VM images, formerly called Shared Image Gallery. Images are organized as image definitions and versions, and versions can be replicated to other regions and shared across subscriptions or tenants.
flashcards.detail: Use it when many VMs or scale sets must deploy from the same golden image in several regions, since it adds versioning and replication that a standalone image lacks.

flashcards.back: The industry-standard way to configure a Linux VM on its first boot, using a script or configuration passed as custom data when the VM is created. It can create users, install packages, and write files before anyone signs in.
flashcards.detail: Contrast with the Custom Script Extension, which runs through the VM agent after provisioning and also works on Windows. Cloud-init is the Linux first-boot answer.

flashcards.front: Scale Set orchestration modes: Flexible vs. Uniform
flashcards.back: Flexible orchestration is the recommended mode. It spreads VMs across zones or fault domains, can mix VM sizes and Spot with on-demand instances, and uses standard VM APIs. Uniform orchestration runs identical instances from a single model for large-scale workloads.
flashcards.detail: Flexible is the default choice for new scale sets. Uniform instances are managed through Scale Set VM APIs and lack compatibility with standard features like Azure Backup and Site Recovery.

flashcards.back: A single-tenant deployment of Azure App Service that runs inside your own virtual network, with dedicated compute and Isolated v2 plans. It suits apps that need network isolation, very high scale, or private-only access.
flashcards.detail: Standard App Service plans share multitenant infrastructure. Choose an ASE when a scenario demands dedicated, VNet-injected hosting rather than just VNet integration.

flashcards.back: A managed private registry for storing and managing container images and related artifacts. It comes in Basic, Standard, and Premium tiers, and Premium adds geo-replication and Private Link support.
flashcards.detail: AKS, Container Apps, and Container Instances all pull images from it. A managed identity with the AcrPull role is the secure way to grant that pull access without stored credentials.

flashcards.back: An Azure resource that manages the set of resources deployed from a Bicep or ARM template as a single unit. Deny settings can block changes or deletion of managed resources, and when the stack is updated or deleted, unmanaged resources are either detached or deleted.
flashcards.detail: It is the successor to Azure Blueprints for lifecycle management and protection of deployed resources, and the usual source of deny assignments that cannot be created by hand.

flashcards.back: A licensing benefit that lets you apply eligible on-premises Windows Server, SQL Server, and some Linux subscriptions to Azure, so you pay only the base compute rate instead of a rate that includes the license.
flashcards.detail: It is a billing discount, not a different VM type. Look for it in cost-reduction scenarios where the company already owns Software Assurance or qualifying subscriptions.

flashcards.back: A DNS-based global traffic load balancer. It answers DNS queries with the endpoint chosen by a routing method: Priority, Weighted, Performance, Geographic, Multivalue, or Subnet. It checks endpoint health but does not proxy the traffic.
flashcards.detail: Because it works at the DNS layer, it is protocol-agnostic. Choose it for DNS-based regional failover, and Front Door when HTTP features like WAF or caching are needed.

flashcards.back: A global Layer 7 entry point that uses Microsoft's edge network to route HTTP and HTTPS requests to the fastest healthy backend. It offers SSL offload, URL path routing, caching, and Web Application Firewall integration.
flashcards.detail: Pick it over Application Gateway when the app runs in several regions and needs global acceleration and failover. Application Gateway is regional.

flashcards.back: A Layer 7 protection that inspects HTTP and HTTPS requests and blocks common web attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting, using managed rule sets based on OWASP guidance. It is available with Application Gateway and Front Door.
flashcards.detail: NSGs and Azure Firewall filter by address and port, while a WAF understands the web request itself. A scenario about SQL injection against a public web app is a WAF scenario.

flashcards.back: A named group of IP address prefixes for an Azure service, such as Storage, Sql, or AzureLoadBalancer, that Microsoft keeps up to date automatically. They are used in NSG and Azure Firewall rules instead of listing addresses by hand.
flashcards.detail: Using the Storage tag in an outbound NSG rule means you never maintain storage IP ranges. Regional variants like Storage.WestEurope narrow the rule further.

flashcards.back: Translates a VM's private IP address to a public IP address and port for outbound internet connections. Each public IP provides a limited pool of ports, and a busy workload can exhaust them, causing intermittent outbound connection failures.
flashcards.detail: A NAT Gateway, which supplies many more ports from dedicated public IPs, is the usual fix for SNAT port exhaustion. Adding more VMs behind the same IP makes it worse.

flashcards.back: A Network Watcher diagnostic that shows where Azure routes traffic from a VM to a given destination: the next hop type, such as VirtualAppliance, VirtualNetworkGateway, VnetLocal, Internet, or None, and which route decided it.
flashcards.detail: Use it to prove a user-defined route sends traffic to a firewall, or to find a route that sends it to None and drops it. IP flow verify checks NSG rules instead.

flashcards.back: A VNet peering setting that lets peered VNets share one VPN or ExpressRoute gateway. The hub that owns the gateway enables Allow gateway transit, and each spoke enables Use remote gateways, so spokes reach on-premises without deploying their own gateway.
flashcards.detail: Only one side owns the gateway, and a spoke that already has its own gateway cannot use remote gateways. It is a key piece of hub-and-spoke designs.

flashcards.back: A platform log that records subscription-level control-plane events, such as who created, changed, or deleted a resource, plus service health and autoscale events. Entries are kept for 90 days unless a diagnostic setting sends them elsewhere.
flashcards.detail: This is where you find out who deleted a VM. For retention beyond 90 days, route it to a Log Analytics workspace or storage account with a diagnostic setting.

flashcards.front: Metric alert rules and dynamic thresholds
flashcards.back: A metric alert fires when a platform metric crosses a threshold. A static threshold uses a value you set, like CPU above 80 percent. A dynamic threshold uses machine learning on the metric's history to detect anomalies and adapts to daily or weekly patterns.
flashcards.detail: Choose dynamic thresholds when normal load varies by time of day, so a fixed number would either miss real problems or alert constantly.

flashcards.back: Run a KQL query against a Log Analytics workspace or Application Insights on a schedule and fire when the results meet a condition, such as more than five failed sign-ins in ten minutes. They cover conditions a simple metric cannot express.
flashcards.detail: Use them when you must alert on log content rather than a numeric metric. Each rule still points to an action group for the response.

flashcards.back: An Azure Monitor feature that shows the performance and health of VMs and Scale Sets, with charts for CPU, memory, disk, and network, plus an optional Map view of processes and connections between machines. It uses Azure Monitor Agent configured by a data collection rule.
flashcards.detail: Enabling it is the quickest way to get guest-level detail from inside the operating system, such as per-process data and dependencies between servers.

flashcards.back: An agent installed on a Windows machine, on-premises or in Azure, that backs up files, folders, and system state directly to a Recovery Services vault without needing any backup server infrastructure.
flashcards.detail: Use it to protect an on-premises file server in Azure. It covers only files, folders, and system state, and runs only on Windows.

flashcards.back: A Recovery Services vault setting for vaults using geo-redundant storage that lets you restore backup data in the paired secondary region, either for a recovery drill or when the primary region is unavailable.
flashcards.detail: It must be enabled on a GRS vault, and after enabling it can take up to 48 hours for items to appear in the secondary region. Locally redundant vaults cannot use it.

flashcards.front: Interpreting access: Check access and Role assignments
flashcards.back: On the Access control (IAM) page of a scope, the Role assignments tab lists the assignments that apply there, and the Check access tab shows what a chosen user, group, service principal, or managed identity holds at that scope. Both views include assignments inherited from parent scopes, such as the subscription or a management group, but they do not list assignments made at child scopes. The Deny assignments tab lists any deny assignments.
flashcards.detail: To explain why a person can or cannot act on a resource, read the assignments at the resource and at every parent scope, plus the groups the person belongs to. An assignment on a child scope will not show up when you look at the parent.

flashcards.front: Managing user and group properties, bulk operations, and group types
flashcards.back: User properties such as job title, department, manager, and usage location are edited on the user's profile, and the Member or Guest user type can be changed. A usage location must be set before a license can be assigned. Bulk create, bulk invite, and bulk delete take a CSV template. Groups are Security or Microsoft 365; membership is Assigned, Dynamic User, or Dynamic Device. Dynamic membership needs Microsoft Entra ID P1.
flashcards.detail: A license assignment that fails for one user in a licensed group is very often a missing usage location. A group that can be assigned to a Microsoft Entra role must be created as role-assignable, and that setting cannot be changed later.

flashcards.front: Managing Azure subscriptions: rename, move, transfer, and cancel
flashcards.back: A subscription can be renamed, moved to another management group, have its billing ownership transferred, or be moved to a different Microsoft Entra directory. Changing the directory permanently deletes the subscription's Azure role assignments and custom roles, and managed identities have to be re-created in the target directory. Canceling a subscription stops billing and disables it, but you must delete all of its resources before it can be deleted manually.
flashcards.detail: Moving a subscription between management groups keeps role assignments and policy assignments flowing down from the new parent. Moving it between directories does not carry access over.

flashcards.front: Moving resources between resource groups and subscriptions
flashcards.back: A move changes only the resource group or subscription: the resource's region does not change and its resource ID does. Both the source and target groups are locked for create, delete, and update operations during the move, for up to four hours, but existing resources keep running. Only the parent resource is named in the request, because children move with it. A read-only lock on the source, the target, or the subscription blocks the move, and the subscriptions must be in the same tenant.
flashcards.detail: Not every resource type can be moved. Use the portal's validation step to see whether the selected resources can be moved. Moving to a different region is a separate task done with Azure Resource Mover or Azure Site Recovery.

flashcards.back: A budget is created at a management group, subscription, or resource group scope with a monthly, quarterly, or annual reset period. Alert conditions can be based on actual cost or forecasted cost, and notify by email or through an action group. A budget never stops spending or affects resources; to act on a breach, connect an action group that starts an Azure Automation runbook, a Logic App, or a Functions app.
flashcards.detail: Cost data typically arrives 8 to 24 hours late, so budget alerts lag real spending. The other cost alerts are credit alerts, department spending quota alerts, and cost anomaly alerts.

flashcards.front: Azure Policy compliance evaluation, remediation tasks, and exemptions
flashcards.back: Compliance is evaluated when a policy is assigned or updated, when a resource is created or updated in scope, when an exemption changes, and in a standard cycle once every 24 hours. Remediation tasks bring existing resources that are non-compliant with a deployIfNotExists or modify policy into compliance, using the managed identity of the assignment. An exemption, in the waiver or mitigated category, takes a resource or scope out of evaluation for a policy.
flashcards.detail: Deny and audit effects do not change existing resources: those only show as non-compliant. If a remediation task fails with an authorization error, check the roles granted to the assignment's managed identity.

flashcards.front: Storage account encryption: Microsoft-managed vs. customer-managed vs. customer-provided keys
flashcards.back: All data in a storage account is encrypted at rest with 256-bit AES and the encryption cannot be turned off. The default key is Microsoft-managed. A customer-managed key lives in Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM and applies to Blob Storage and Azure Files; the customer is then responsible for rotation. A customer-provided key is sent by the client on each Blob Storage request. Encryption scopes apply a different key to a single container or blob.
flashcards.detail: The vault holding a customer-managed key needs soft delete and purge protection, and the key must be RSA or RSA-HSM. The storage account reaches the vault through a managed identity.

flashcards.back: An optional second layer of 256-bit AES encryption at the storage infrastructure level, with a different algorithm and key from the service-level layer. Data is encrypted twice, which protects against the compromise of one algorithm or key. It always uses Microsoft-managed keys, and the setting has to be chosen when the storage account (or an encryption scope) is created: it cannot be enabled or disabled afterwards.
flashcards.detail: A scenario that asks to add a second layer to an existing account has no in-place answer: create a new account with infrastructure encryption and copy the data over.

flashcards.front: Identity-based access to Azure Files over SMB
flashcards.back: Azure Files authenticates over SMB with Kerberos against one identity source per storage account: on-premises Active Directory Domain Services, Microsoft Entra Domain Services, or Microsoft Entra Kerberos. Share-level access is granted with the Storage File Data SMB Share Reader, Contributor, or Elevated Contributor roles, and directory and file access is then controlled with Windows ACLs. NFS shares do not support identity-based authentication.
flashcards.detail: Entra Kerberos suits Entra-joined clients and clients with no line of sight to a domain controller. With on-premises AD DS, identities must be synced to Microsoft Entra ID so share-level permissions can be assigned.

flashcards.front: Azure Files share snapshots and soft delete
flashcards.back: A share snapshot is a read-only, point-in-time, incremental copy of a share; each share supports up to 200 snapshots, retained for up to 10 years, and users can restore individual files from them. Soft delete protects against deleting the whole share: it is on by default for new storage accounts, applies to every share in the account, and keeps a deleted share for 7 days by default, configurable from 1 to 365.
flashcards.detail: Snapshots protect against file-level changes. Soft delete protects against share deletion. Neither replaces a backup, and soft delete for blobs does not protect file shares.

flashcards.front: Soft delete for containers and blobs
flashcards.back: Blob soft delete keeps deleted or overwritten blobs and snapshots recoverable for a retention period; container soft delete does the same for a deleted container and the blobs in it. Retention can be set from 1 to 365 days. They are configured separately, in the Data protection settings of the storage account, and work alongside blob versioning and snapshots.
flashcards.detail: Soft delete answers 'someone deleted it'. Versioning answers 'someone overwrote it and I need the previous version'.

flashcards.back: A free standalone desktop app for Windows, macOS, and Linux for browsing and managing Blob, File, Queue, and Table data, plus managed disks. You connect by signing in to Azure or by attaching a single resource with a connection string, a SAS URL, an account key, or a Microsoft Entra sign-in. After an Azure sign-in it needs both control-plane (Resource Manager) and data-plane permissions.
flashcards.detail: If a user holds only a data role, such as Storage Blob Data Contributor, attach the resource and choose the Microsoft Entra ID option instead of signing in to the subscription.

flashcards.back: A command-line tool for moving data to, from, and between storage accounts. azcopy copy transfers data; azcopy sync is one-way, from a chosen source to a destination, and compares names and last-modified times by default (or MD5 hashes with --compare-hash). --delete-destination removes destination files that no longer exist in the source. You authorize with Microsoft Entra ID (azcopy login) or with a SAS token on the URL.
flashcards.detail: Being the Owner of the storage account does not give data access to AzCopy. Under Microsoft Entra ID the identity needs a data role such as Storage Blob Data Contributor. For large-scale migrations Microsoft points to Azure Storage Mover.

flashcards.front: Default access tier and per-blob tiers
flashcards.back: A storage account has a default access tier of Hot or Cool, inherited by blobs that do not set their own. Cold and Archive can be set only on individual blobs, either at upload, with a tier change, or through a lifecycle management rule. Tier changes between online tiers are immediate; leaving Archive requires rehydration. Moving a blob out early incurs an early deletion charge for Cool, Cold, and Archive.
flashcards.detail: If a scenario wants everything in the account to land in Archive by default, the answer is a lifecycle rule or per-blob tier, not the account default.

flashcards.back: An ARM template is JSON with a $schema and contentVersion, then optional parameters, variables, and functions sections, a required resources array, and an outputs section. Each resource declares its type, apiVersion, name, location, and properties, and can use dependsOn and copy loops. A template can deploy to a resource group, a subscription, a management group, or a tenant, chosen by the deployment command and the schema.
flashcards.detail: Interpreting a template means reading parameters for what the deployer supplies, variables for computed values, and resources for what is created. Complete mode, not the template contents, decides whether undeclared resources are removed.

flashcards.front: Reading a Bicep file and previewing with what-if
flashcards.back: A Bicep file declares param, var, resource, module, and output items. A resource has a symbolic name, a type with an API version, and properties, and referencing one resource's property from another creates an implicit dependency. A for expression loops over an array or range, and the existing keyword refers to a resource that is already deployed. Deploy with az deployment group create, and preview with the what-if operation, which reports Create, Modify, Delete, NoChange, Ignore, or Deploy for each resource.
flashcards.detail: Run what-if before any deployment in Complete mode: it shows the resources that would be deleted before anything changes.

flashcards.front: Exporting a deployment as a template, and ARM-to-Bicep conversion
flashcards.back: Export from a resource group or resource generates a snapshot of the current state, including manual changes, but it is autogenerated, mostly hard-coded, and might need cleaning; export is not guaranteed to succeed and is capped at 200 resources per group. Save from history returns the exact JSON template used for a deployment, with its parameters. az bicep decompile --file main.json converts JSON to Bicep on a best-effort basis, and az bicep build compiles Bicep back to JSON.
flashcards.detail: Choose export from the resource group to capture drift or resources that were not created from a template. Choose history for a clean, parameterized, reusable copy.

flashcards.back: A VM option that encrypts temporary disks and disk caches at rest, and encrypts data in flow to the Storage service, with the host server doing the work. It supports platform-managed or customer-managed keys, needs no agent in the guest, and cannot be combined with Azure Disk Encryption. Before use, the EncryptionAtHost feature must be registered for the subscription, and an existing VM must be deallocated to enable it.
flashcards.detail: Server-side encryption of managed disks does not cover the temp disk or cache unless encryption at host is on, though some newer VM sizes encrypt them by default.

flashcards.front: Moving a VM between resource groups, subscriptions, and regions
flashcards.back: Moving a VM to another resource group or subscription is a Resource Manager move that keeps the VM in its region and changes its resource ID. Moving it to another region is a different job: Azure Resource Mover validates dependencies such as the network, NICs, and disks, then prepares, initiates, and commits the move, and can discard or clean up afterward. Azure Site Recovery replication is another route for region moves.
flashcards.detail: A request to change the region through the Move blade is a trap: the Move blade changes only the container.

flashcards.front: Azure Container Apps environments, revisions, and scaling
flashcards.back: Container apps run in a managed environment, which is the secure boundary and can be placed in a virtual network. A revision is an immutable snapshot of an app version, and replicas are its running instances. Scaling is set by minimum and maximum replica counts and by rules: HTTP (concurrent requests), TCP (connections), or custom, such as CPU, memory, or event sources like Service Bus. The default minimum is 0, so an idle app scales to zero and incurs no usage charges.
flashcards.detail: Set the minimum replicas to 1 or more to avoid cold starts. Adding or editing a scale rule creates a new revision.

flashcards.front: Azure Container Instances sizing and restart policy
flashcards.back: CPU and memory are requested per container in a container group, and the group is billed by the second. There is no built-in autoscale: more capacity means more container groups. The restart policy is Always by default, OnFailure restarts only after a nonzero exit code, and Never does not restart after a successful exit. Run-to-completion tasks use OnFailure or Never so that the group stops and billing ends.
flashcards.detail: If a scenario needs built-in scale rules, revisions, or scale to zero on events, the answer is Container Apps rather than Container Instances.

flashcards.front: Azure Container Registry authentication and tasks
flashcards.back: Access to a registry uses Microsoft Entra identities: az acr login for a person, a service principal for pipelines, or a managed identity with the AcrPull role for services that pull images. The admin user is for testing only and is disabled by default. ACR Tasks builds and patches images in the cloud with az acr build, and can be triggered by source commits, base image updates, or a timer.
flashcards.detail: A base-image-update trigger is the answer when the question asks how to rebuild images automatically when the operating system image is patched.

flashcards.front: Mapping a custom domain to App Service
flashcards.back: A subdomain such as www.contoso.com maps with a CNAME record to the app's default hostname. A root domain maps with an A record to the app's IP address. A TXT record named asuid, holding the app's custom domain verification ID, proves ownership and is strongly recommended to prevent subdomain takeover. A certificate must then be bound to the domain to serve HTTPS.
flashcards.detail: A CNAME on a root domain is invalid DNS, so apex mappings use an A record.

flashcards.back: Certificates can be created free as an App Service managed certificate, bought as an App Service certificate, imported from Azure Key Vault, or uploaded as a password-protected PFX. The free managed certificate does not support wildcards, is not exportable, and renews automatically. TLS bindings use SNI SSL or IP-based SSL. Apps accept TLS 1.2 by default, HTTPS Only redirects HTTP requests to HTTPS, and certificates require a Basic, Standard, Premium, or Isolated plan.
flashcards.detail: Public certificates uploaded to an app are for calling remote services, not for securing a custom domain.

flashcards.back: Basic, Standard, Premium, and Isolated plans take automatic backups every hour, kept for 30 days, with no setup and no storage account; they cannot be downloaded. Custom backups are configured against a storage account, can run on demand or on a schedule, keep from 0 to 30 days or indefinitely, and can be downloaded. Restore overwrites an app or goes to a new app or a deployment slot.
flashcards.detail: Restoring stops the target app. To limit downtime, restore into a deployment slot and then swap.

flashcards.front: App Service networking: inbound and outbound features
flashcards.back: Inbound access is controlled with access restrictions (IP and service-endpoint allow or deny rules) or a private endpoint for private inbound access. Outbound access uses regional virtual network integration, which sends outbound calls through a delegated subnet and needs a Basic or higher plan. Virtual network integration never gives inbound access. App Service Environment places the whole environment inside your virtual network.
flashcards.detail: Private inbound and private outbound are separate requirements: a private endpoint and VNet integration are often used together.

flashcards.front: App Service plan tiers and what each unlocks
flashcards.back: Free and Shared run on shared infrastructure. Basic, Standard, and the Premium tiers run on dedicated VMs. Standard and higher add autoscale and deployment slots; Basic scales out only manually and has no slots. Backups, custom TLS, and virtual network integration need Basic or higher. Isolated v2 runs in an App Service Environment with network isolation. Scaling up changes the tier or size, and scaling out adds instances.
flashcards.detail: If a feature is missing in the portal, check the plan tier first and scale up, since every app in the plan shares it.

flashcards.front: Public IP addresses: Standard SKU, static, and secure by default
flashcards.back: Basic SKU public IP addresses were retired on September 30, 2025, so new work uses the Standard SKU. A Standard public IPv4 address uses static allocation, can be zone-redundant or zonal, and is secure by default: it is closed to inbound traffic until a network security group allows it. Addresses can be IPv4 or IPv6, and a public IP prefix reserves a contiguous range.
flashcards.detail: A VM with a new Standard public IP that cannot be reached over RDP or SSH usually has no NSG, or no inbound allow rule, on its NIC or subnet.

flashcards.front: Default outbound access and private subnets
flashcards.back: Where a VM has no explicit outbound method, Azure has historically given it an implicit default outbound IP address that Microsoft owns and can change. For virtual networks created with API versions released after March 31, 2026, subnets are private by default, so VMs there need an explicit outbound method such as a NAT gateway, a public IP, a load balancer outbound rule, or a route to a firewall. A subnet can be made private with its defaultOutboundAccess setting.
flashcards.detail: Prefer a NAT gateway for outbound traffic: it gives a stable, shared outbound address and avoids relying on the default IP.

flashcards.front: Effective security rules and NSG evaluation order
flashcards.back: The effective security rules of a network interface are the aggregate of the NSG on its subnet and the NSG on the NIC itself. For inbound traffic, the subnet NSG is evaluated first and then the NIC NSG; for outbound traffic the NIC NSG is evaluated first and then the subnet NSG. Traffic must be allowed by both. View the result on the NIC's Effective security rules page, or with the NSG diagnostics and IP flow verify tools in Network Watcher.
flashcards.detail: A deny at either layer blocks the traffic, so an allow rule on the NIC cannot rescue a flow that the subnet NSG denies.

flashcards.front: Network Watcher troubleshooting tools: which tool answers which question
flashcards.back: IP flow verify checks whether a packet to or from a VM is allowed or denied and names the NSG rule. Next hop reports the next hop type for traffic to a destination. Effective security rules aggregates the NSG rules on a NIC. Connection troubleshoot tests connectivity from a VM to a destination and reports latency and where the path fails. Packet capture records packets on a VM, and VPN troubleshoot diagnoses gateways and connections.
flashcards.detail: These are one-time diagnostics. For continuous measurement of latency and packet loss, the answer is Connection monitor.

flashcards.front: Virtual network flow logs and the retirement of NSG flow logs
flashcards.back: NSG flow logs retire on September 30, 2027, and new NSG flow logs can no longer be created. Their replacement, virtual network flow logs, records IP traffic for the workloads in a virtual network, so logging is enabled at the virtual network and not on each NSG. Logs are stored in a storage account and can be analyzed with Traffic Analytics in a Log Analytics workspace.
flashcards.detail: Any scenario that creates a new flow-logging configuration should name virtual network flow logs, not NSG flow logs.

flashcards.front: Troubleshooting Azure Load Balancer: probes and metrics
flashcards.back: Standard Load Balancer publishes the Data Path Availability and Health Probe Status metrics to Azure Monitor. A failing health probe is caused by an unhealthy backend, an application that is not listening on the probe port, or an NSG or guest firewall that blocks the probe. The probe source is 168.63.129.16, which the AzureLoadBalancer service tag represents, and a custom deny rule can override the default allow rule for it.
flashcards.detail: If instances show as unhealthy while the application is running, compare the probe port and protocol with what the application listens on, and then check NSG rules for the AzureLoadBalancer tag.

flashcards.front: Azure DNS alias records and zone delegation
flashcards.back: An alias record set points an A, AAAA, or CNAME record directly at an Azure resource, such as a public IP address, a Traffic Manager profile, or a Front Door endpoint, and updates automatically when that resource's address changes. Alias A records work at the zone apex, where a CNAME is not allowed. To make Azure DNS authoritative for a domain, delegate it by setting the registrar's NS records to the four name servers assigned to the zone.
flashcards.detail: A private DNS zone link with auto registration creates records for VMs automatically, and a virtual network can be linked to only one zone with auto registration enabled.

flashcards.back: Developer is a free shared-infrastructure SKU for development and test, for one VM at a time and in select regions, with no dedicated subnet. Basic, Standard, and Premium deploy into the virtual network with an AzureBastionSubnet of /26 or larger and a Standard public IP. Standard adds native client support, shareable links, custom ports, IP-based connections, host scaling, and file transfer. Premium adds session recording and private-only deployment.
flashcards.detail: A Basic host always has two instances. Anything about native SSH or RDP clients or scaling means Standard or higher.

flashcards.back: A Network Watcher feature for continuous connectivity monitoring of Azure and hybrid endpoints with TCP, ICMP, and HTTP checks. It measures latency and packet loss, shows the network path and hop performance, supports sources such as VMs and scale sets and Azure Arc-enabled servers, and sends metrics to Azure Monitor and logs to Log Analytics for alerting. Sources need the Network Watcher extension; destinations do not.
flashcards.detail: Connection monitor (classic) is retired. Connection troubleshoot is the one-time test, Connection monitor is the ongoing one.

flashcards.back: Alert processing rules change fired alerts rather than create them: they can add action groups to alerts, or suppress action groups, for a scope of resources, a resource group, or a subscription, with filters and an optional schedule. Typical uses are suppressing notifications during planned maintenance and attaching a standard action group to many alerts at once, including alerts from sources that have no action group setting, such as Azure Backup. They do not affect Service Health alerts.
flashcards.detail: Suppression stops the notification actions; the alert still fires and is recorded. Disabling the alert rule instead means nothing fires at all.

flashcards.front: Recovery Services vault vs. Backup vault
flashcards.back: A Recovery Services vault protects Azure VMs, SQL Server and SAP HANA in Azure VMs, Azure Files shares, and on-premises machines through the MARS agent, Azure Backup Server, or System Center DPM. A Backup vault protects newer data sources, including Azure Disks, Azure Blobs, and Azure Database for PostgreSQL servers. A vault stores backups within one region, and both types support Azure RBAC and managed identities.
flashcards.detail: A subscription that protects VMs and also disks and blobs needs both vault types, created in each region that holds the data.

flashcards.front: Monitoring Azure Backup: alerts, jobs, and reports
flashcards.back: Azure Backup raises built-in alerts through Azure Monitor, so notifications use alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules; classic Azure Backup alerts were deprecated on March 31, 2026. Backup jobs are tracked in the vault or in Resiliency (the new name of the Business Continuity Center). Backup reports are built on Azure Monitor logs and workbooks, which means a vault's diagnostic settings must send data to a Log Analytics workspace.
flashcards.detail: Long-range trends, usage, and audit questions point to Backup reports. A single failed job points to alerts.

flashcards.front: Site Recovery failover options and drills
flashcards.back: When you fail over, you choose a recovery point: Latest processed gives the lowest recovery time because it uses the latest point already processed, Latest processes all data received for the lowest data loss, Latest app-consistent uses the newest application-consistent point, and Custom picks a specific point for a single VM. After a failover you reprotect the VMs to replicate back to the original region. Run a test failover at least every 180 days.
flashcards.detail: A test failover goes to an isolated network and leaves production untouched. Keep recovery plans in order so that multi-tier apps start in the right sequence.

flashcards.front: Azure Monitor Insights for storage and networks
flashcards.back: Storage insights gives a unified view of capacity, availability, transactions, and latency across Blob, File, Table, and Queue services, for one account or across many from Azure Monitor. Network Insights shows topology, health and metrics for network resources without configuration, and links to Connection monitor, flow logs, Traffic Analytics, and the Network Watcher diagnostic tools. Both are curated experiences on top of Azure Monitor data.
flashcards.detail: Insights are the prebuilt dashboards; the underlying data still comes from metrics, resource logs, and diagnostic settings.

flashcards.front: Interpreting metrics: aggregation, dimensions, and retention
flashcards.back: Metrics explorer charts platform metrics with an aggregation (average, minimum, maximum, sum, or count), a time granularity, and optional splitting or filtering by dimension, such as instance or API name. Platform metrics are collected automatically and stored for 93 days, while the Activity log is kept for 90 days. Resource logs are not collected until a diagnostic setting routes them to a destination.
flashcards.detail: Choose maximum to catch spikes, average to see sustained load, and sum or count for totals such as transactions.

questions.question: You have a Microsoft Entra tenant with 5,000 users. A Conditional Access policy must apply to everyone in the Sales department, including people who transfer into Sales later. You need a group the policy can target. The solution must minimize administrative effort. What should you create?
options: A security group with dynamic user membership based on the department attribute
A Microsoft 365 group with assigned membership, populated by a scheduled PowerShell script
An administrative unit that contains the Sales department users
A security group with assigned membership and group-based licensing enabled
questions.explanation: A dynamic membership rule such as user.department -eq "Sales" is re-evaluated automatically whenever the attribute changes, and Conditional Access can target a security group directly. A script-populated assigned group reaches the same end state but is plumbing you must schedule, monitor, and fix. An administrative unit scopes Microsoft Entra role assignments to a subset of users; a Conditional Access policy cannot target an administrative unit. Group-based licensing hands licenses to whoever is already a member; it does nothing to decide who the members are.

questions.question: You assign Microsoft 365 E3 to Group1 through group-based licensing. User1, a member of Group1, also has E3 assigned directly from before the group existed. You need User1's license to be managed only through Group1, with no interruption to User1's mailbox or apps. What should you do?
options: Remove the direct E3 assignment from User1
Remove User1 from Group1, wait for the license to release, then add User1 back
Run Reprocess on Group1 to replace the direct assignment with the inherited one
Convert Group1 to a dynamic group so inherited licenses take precedence over direct ones
questions.explanation: A directly assigned license and a group-inherited license for the same product coexist on the user, so removing the direct one simply leaves the inherited one in force with no gap in service. Removing and re-adding the user from the group never touches the direct assignment and risks a brief interruption. Reprocess only re-evaluates the group's own assignments; it does not remove direct assignments. Dynamic membership changes how members are selected, not how direct and inherited licenses are reconciled.

questions.question: Contoso needs 40 consultants from Fabrikam to access a SharePoint site and one Azure resource group. The consultants must authenticate with their Fabrikam credentials, Contoso must not store or reset their passwords, and Fabrikam's IT department will not take part in the setup. What should you do?
