options: Invite each consultant as a guest user through Microsoft Entra External Identities
Configure cross-tenant synchronization between the Fabrikam and Contoso tenants
Create cloud-only member accounts for the consultants and require MFA at first sign-in
Create a Microsoft Entra External ID customer tenant and register the consultants in it
questions.explanation: A B2B invitation creates a guest object that the consultant redeems with their Fabrikam credentials, so Contoso never holds a password, and the guest can then be granted SharePoint and Azure RBAC access like any other identity. Cross-tenant synchronization also produces B2B users, but it must be configured in the source tenant by Fabrikam's administrators, which the scenario rules out. Member accounts mean Contoso owns and resets those passwords. An External ID customer tenant serves consumer-facing apps and does not grant access to Contoso's internal SharePoint or Azure resources.

questions.question: Your hybrid environment syncs on-premises Active Directory to Microsoft Entra ID. Self-service password reset is enabled and users complete resets successfully, but afterwards the new password only works for cloud apps; signing in to a domain-joined PC still requires the old password. What should you configure?
options: Password writeback in Microsoft Entra Connect
Password hash synchronization in Microsoft Entra Connect
Pass-through authentication with an additional authentication agent
Seamless single sign-on for the synchronized users
questions.explanation: SSPR changes the cloud password; password writeback is the component that pushes that change back into on-premises Active Directory so domain sign-in matches. Password hash synchronization flows the other direction, on-premises to cloud, and would never carry a cloud-initiated reset downward. Pass-through authentication validates sign-ins against on-premises AD, so without writeback it would make the new password fail everywhere rather than fix it. Seamless SSO suppresses sign-in prompts on domain-joined devices and does not synchronize credentials at all.

questions.question: A user is assigned Contributor at the subscription level and Owner at one specific resource group within it. What's their effective permission in that resource group?
options: Contributor
No access
Reader
Owner
questions.explanation: RBAC assignments are additive across scopes, and the more permissive assignment applies — Owner at that resource group wins there. Conflicting scopes don't cancel each other out into no access; the broader Contributor assignment from the subscription simply gets overridden by the more permissive Owner role at the narrower scope.
questions.whyTested: This question tests whether you actually understand 'additive across scopes' as a mechanism, not just as a phrase — the wrong options offer tempting shortcuts like 'no access' (as if conflicting scopes cancel out) or 'Reader' (as if the broader, less-permissive scope wins), both of which reverse how RBAC inheritance actually resolves.

questions.question: User1 must be able to grant colleagues access to resource group RG1, but must not be able to create, modify, or delete any resource in RG1. You need to assign a role to User1. The solution must follow the principle of least privilege. Which role assignment should you create?
options: User Access Administrator at the RG1 scope
Owner at the RG1 scope
Contributor at the RG1 scope plus Reader at the subscription scope
The Privileged Role Administrator Microsoft Entra role
questions.explanation: User Access Administrator grants Microsoft.Authorization/* for managing role assignments plus read access, and nothing that lets User1 change the resources themselves. Owner would satisfy the first requirement but hands over full resource management too. Contributor explicitly excludes Microsoft.Authorization/*/Write, so User1 could not grant access at all, and layering Reader on top changes nothing. Privileged Role Administrator is a directory role for managing Microsoft Entra role assignments; it carries no Azure RBAC permission on RG1.

questions.question: Your subscription has 200 resource groups. New resources must carry both a CostCenter and an Environment tag, and the compliance view must report one overall percentage for the tagging standard. You also want to add a third tag rule later without creating another assignment. What should you create?
options: An initiative containing a require-tag policy per tag, assigned once at the subscription
Two separate policy assignments at the subscription, one per tag
One policy assignment with the Modify effect that inherits both tags from the resource group
A tag on each resource group, applied through the Tags blade
questions.explanation: An initiative is the construct that gives you a single assignment and a single aggregated compliance score across several definitions, and adding a definition to the initiative later flows through the existing assignment. Two separate assignments report separately and would need a third assignment for the next tag. A Modify policy that inherits from the resource group copies tags rather than requiring them, so resources in untagged groups stay untagged, and it is still a single policy rather than a standard. Tagging each group by hand enforces nothing on the resources inside.

questions.question: User1 has Reader at management group MG1 and Contributor at subscription Sub1 beneath it. Sub1 contains RG1 and nine other resource groups. You must ensure User1 can only read RG1 while keeping Contributor access to the other nine resource groups. What should you do?
options: Remove Contributor at Sub1 and assign it at each of the other nine resource groups
Assign User1 the Reader role at the RG1 scope so the narrower scope applies
Create a deny assignment for User1 at the RG1 scope in Access control (IAM)
Apply a ReadOnly management lock at the RG1 scope
questions.explanation: RBAC is additive, so a narrower assignment can never subtract rights inherited from a wider one; the only way to carve RG1 out is to move Contributor down to the nine scopes where it is wanted, after which the inherited Reader from MG1 is all that applies in RG1. Assigning Reader at RG1 changes nothing because Contributor still flows down from Sub1. Deny assignments cannot be authored directly by administrators; they are created by Deployment Stacks (formerly Azure Blueprints) and managed applications. A ReadOnly lock would make RG1 read-only for every principal, not just User1.

questions.question: A company needs to grant a third-party app 24-hour, read-only access to a single blob container, without sharing the storage account key.
options: A Conditional Access policy
The storage account access key
A Shared Access Signature (SAS)
A Read-only resource lock
questions.explanation: A SAS grants limited, time-boxed, scoped access (read-only, one container, 24 hours) without exposing the account's full access key. Handing over the storage account key would give the app full, unrestricted, non-expiring access to the whole account, far more than needed. A Conditional Access policy governs sign-ins to Microsoft Entra-integrated apps, not access to storage data itself, and a read-only resource lock only prevents accidental deletion/modification of the storage account resource -- it doesn't grant a third party access in the first place.
questions.whyTested: This question packs in four options that each belong to a genuinely real Azure access-control concept — that's the trap. It's testing whether you can tell apart identity sign-in controls, data-level access grants, and resource-protection locks, three categories that get taught separately but blur together the moment a scenario just says 'access.'

questions.question: You create a lifecycle management rule on a general-purpose v2 account that moves block blobs to the Cool tier 30 days after they were last accessed. Forty-five days later, blobs that nobody has read since upload are still in the Hot tier. What should you do first?
options: Enable last access time tracking on the storage account
Change the rule to use days since last modification instead
Change the default access tier of the storage account to Cool
Upgrade the storage account to the Premium performance tier
questions.explanation: A daysAfterLastAccessTimeGreaterThan condition only works once access time tracking is enabled on the account; without it the policy has no last-access timestamp to evaluate and silently skips those blobs. Switching to last-modified would move the blobs but changes the business rule, since a frequently read but rarely modified blob would also be demoted. Changing the default tier affects only new uploads without an explicit tier. Premium block blob accounts do not support Cool or Archive tiers at all.

questions.question: A faulty script overwrote and deleted thousands of blobs in container data1 at 09:14 today. The storage account already has blob versioning, soft delete, change feed, and point-in-time restore enabled. You need to return the entire container to its 09:00 state with the least administrative effort. What should you do?
options: Perform a point-in-time restore of the container to 09:00
Undelete each affected blob and promote its previous version to current
Initiate a customer-managed failover to the secondary region
Copy the container from the most recent blob snapshots with AzCopy
questions.explanation: Point-in-time restore uses the change feed plus versions and soft-deleted data to roll a whole container, or a range of blobs, back to a chosen moment in one operation. Promoting versions blob by blob reaches the same end state but is thousands of manual actions. A geo-failover does not help because the asynchronous replica already received the destructive writes. Blob snapshots are only created when something explicitly takes them, and nothing in the scenario did.

questions.question: A storage account must stay writable if a single availability zone in its primary region fails, and an application must be able to read its data from the secondary region during a regional outage without waiting for a failover. The solution must minimize cost. Which redundancy option should you choose?
options: Read-access geo-zone-redundant storage (RA-GZRS)
Geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS)
Read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS)
Zone-redundant storage (ZRS) with three copies across zones
questions.explanation: Surviving a zone loss while staying writable needs synchronous zone redundancy in the primary region, and reading from the secondary before a failover needs the read-access variant, so RA-GZRS is the cheapest option that satisfies both. GZRS covers the zone requirement but the secondary is not readable until you fail over. RA-GRS keeps the secondary readable, but its primary is locally redundant, so a zone failure takes writes offline. ZRS has no secondary region at all.

questions.question: You migrate a departmental file server to Azure. Domain-joined Windows VMs must mount the share, and existing NTFS permissions must keep working so that each user sees only their own folders. The domain is on-premises Active Directory synced to Microsoft Entra ID. What should you deploy?
options: An Azure Files SMB share with on-premises AD DS authentication enabled
An Azure Files NFS share on a premium file storage account
An Azure Files SMB share mounted with the storage account key
A blob container with the SFTP endpoint enabled
questions.explanation: Identity-based authentication over SMB lets Azure Files honor Windows ACLs with the users' existing AD DS identities. Mounting with the account key is the near-miss: the share mounts fine, but every user connects as the same super-user identity, so per-user NTFS permissions are not enforced. NFS shares use POSIX permissions and have no Windows Kerberos integration. SFTP on Blob Storage is file transfer, not a mountable share with NTFS semantics.

questions.question: A storage account must accept requests only from two corporate office public IP ranges and from subnet App1 in VNet1. Requests from anywhere else, even with a valid key or SAS, must be refused. What should you configure?
options: Storage firewall IP rules for the offices plus a virtual network rule for App1
A private endpoint for the storage account in subnet App1 of VNet1
A network security group on the storage account that permits those sources
A SAS token whose allowed IP range is limited to the office addresses
questions.explanation: The storage firewall is the account-level network control that blocks everything not explicitly allowed, regardless of what credential a caller presents. A private endpoint gives App1 a private path, but on its own it leaves the public endpoint open, and the offices arrive over the internet anyway. NSGs attach to subnets and NICs, not to storage accounts. An IP-restricted SAS only constrains callers using that particular token; the account key and other tokens still work from anywhere.

questions.question: An administrator wants to change a running VM's managed disk from Standard HDD to Premium SSD to improve performance. What has to happen first?
options: The VM must be deallocated before the disk tier can be changed
Nothing — the tier can be changed while the VM keeps running
The disk must be deleted and recreated from a snapshot
The VM must be moved to a different region
questions.explanation: Changing a managed disk's performance tier requires the VM to be stopped (deallocated) first — it isn't a live, no-downtime operation. Deleting and recreating the disk, or moving regions, are unnecessary and far more disruptive than the actual requirement.
questions.whyTested: AZ-104 likes testing small operational prerequisites like this one because they're exactly what trips up someone who understands the concept (disk tiers) but hasn't internalized the mechanical step required to actually change one — the distractors escalate to more drastic, wrong actions to see if you overcorrect instead of picking the minimal real requirement.

questions.question: A stateless web tier must meet a 99.99% availability SLA, and the number of identical VMs must grow and shrink automatically with CPU load. The region supports availability zones. What should you deploy?
options: A VM Scale Set spread across three availability zones with an autoscale rule
A VM Scale Set in a single zone configured with five fault domains and an autoscale rule
An availability set with two update domains and three fault domains
Three VMs in separate proximity placement groups behind a load balancer
questions.explanation: The 99.99% VM SLA applies only when instances are spread across two or more availability zones, and a Scale Set is what adds and removes instances automatically. A single-zone Scale Set with fault domains tops out at 99.95%, the same as an availability set, and the availability set cannot autoscale at all. Proximity placement groups pull VMs physically closer together for latency, which is the opposite of spreading risk and carries no SLA uplift.

questions.question: You must run a PowerShell script once on 200 existing Windows VMs to change a registry value. The VMs have no public IP addresses, you must not sign in to any of them, and the change must not be re-applied automatically afterwards. What should you use?
options: The Custom Script Extension, deployed to each VM
cloud-init configuration added to each VM
Azure Machine Configuration with a configuration package
Scripted Azure Bastion sessions to each VM
questions.explanation: The Custom Script Extension is delivered through the VM agent, so it runs on existing VMs with no inbound connectivity, executes once, and is done. cloud-init only runs during first boot of a Linux VM, so it cannot touch VMs that already exist. Machine Configuration continuously audits and re-applies desired state, which violates the one-time requirement. Bastion still means an interactive session into each machine.

questions.question: A production App Service app runs in a Standard-tier plan. Each release must be validated against production settings, warmed up, switched to users with no cold start, and reverted within seconds if a problem appears. The solution must minimize cost. What should you do?
options: Add a staging deployment slot, deploy there, then swap it with production
Create a second App Service plan and shift traffic with weighted Traffic Manager routing
Scale the plan out to two instances and deploy the release to one of them
Move the app to an App Service Environment with a separate staging app
questions.explanation: Slots run inside the same plan, so there is no extra compute to pay for; the swap warms the staging instance first, then exchanges routing almost instantly, and swapping back is the rollback. A second plan doubles compute cost and DNS-based traffic shifting reverts only as fast as TTLs expire. Instances of one plan all serve the same code, so you cannot deploy to only one of them. An App Service Environment is the most expensive option and solves an isolation problem nobody asked about.

questions.question: A nightly job runs for about 20 minutes inside a Linux container, started by a Logic App. It needs no inbound HTTP endpoint and no scaling to multiple replicas, and you must pay only while it runs. You want to deploy the fewest Azure resources. What should you use?
options: A container group in Azure Container Instances
An Azure Container Apps app in a new Container Apps environment
Web App for Containers on a Basic App Service plan
An Azure Kubernetes Service cluster with a CronJob
questions.explanation: A container group is a single resource, bills per second only while the container runs, and the Logic App connector can start and stop it directly. Container Apps is the near-miss: it can also run on-demand work, but it requires a Container Apps environment first and is built around HTTP ingress, revisions, and replica scaling that this job never uses. An App Service plan bills continuously whether or not anything runs. An AKS cluster means node pools and upgrades for a 20-minute job.

questions.question: A company wants microservices-style container scaling with built-in HTTP-based autoscaling, without managing a Kubernetes cluster directly.
options: Azure Container Apps
An App Service plan alone
Azure Container Instances
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
questions.explanation: Container Apps adds serverless scaling and microservices features on top of containers, without exposing the underlying cluster.

questions.question: A developer deploys a Bicep file to resource group RG1 using az deployment group create with --mode Complete. Afterwards, a storage account an administrator had created manually in RG1 is gone. Future deployments of the file must update the templated resources without touching anything that is not in the file. What should you do?
options: Deploy with the Incremental mode instead
Apply a CanNotDelete lock to the manually created resources in RG1
Run the what-if operation before each deployment
Declare the storage account in the Bicep file so Complete mode keeps it
questions.explanation: Complete mode deletes any resource in the group that the template does not declare; Incremental, the default, leaves undeclared resources alone and still updates the ones that are declared. A lock would make the Complete-mode deployment fail when it tries to delete the locked resource rather than make the deployment safe. What-if previews the deletions but does nothing to prevent them. Adding the storage account to the file works for that one resource, but it means every hand-made resource must be maintained in the template forever.

questions.question: VM1, VM2, and VM3 are in availability set AS1. You deallocate VM1 and try to resize it to Standard_E8s_v5, but that size is not offered for VM1 even though other VMs in the region can use it. You need to complete the resize with the least disruption. What should you do?
options: Deallocate all three VMs in AS1, resize VM1, then start them
Remove VM1 from AS1, resize it, then add it back to AS1
Delete VM1 and recreate it from its disks in a new availability set
Move VM1 to a different resource group and resize it there
questions.explanation: VMs in an availability set are pinned to a shared hardware cluster, so a size that cluster lacks only becomes available once every VM in the set is deallocated and the set can be placed on a cluster that offers it. A VM cannot be moved into or out of an availability set after creation, so removing VM1 from AS1 and adding it back is not possible. Recreating the VM is far more disruptive than a coordinated stop. Resource group membership has no effect on which hardware cluster hosts the VM.

questions.question: A SQL Server VM needs a 512 GiB data disk that delivers 20,000 IOPS, and you must be able to raise or lower the IOPS later without resizing the disk or redeploying the VM. The VM size and region support every disk type. The solution must minimize cost. Which disk type should you use?
options: Premium SSD v2
Ultra Disk
Premium SSD (P20) with on-demand bursting enabled
Standard SSD (E20)
questions.explanation: Premium SSD v2 decouples IOPS and throughput from capacity, so 20,000 IOPS can be provisioned on 512 GiB and adjusted later, at a lower price than Ultra Disk. Ultra Disk meets every technical requirement but costs more for the same numbers. A P20 delivers 2,300 baseline IOPS, and on-demand bursting is only offered on disks larger than 512 GiB, so it cannot be enabled here. Standard SSD E20 provides 500 IOPS.

questions.question: Two NSG rules apply to the same NIC: one at priority 100 allowing inbound port 443, another at priority 200 denying all inbound traffic. What happens to inbound HTTPS traffic?
options: Both rules apply, and the NIC merges them into a partial allow
It's denied, since a Deny rule takes precedence over an Allow rule whenever both target the same traffic
It's allowed, since the lower priority number is processed first
It's denied, since NSG rules are evaluated from the highest priority number down to the lowest
questions.explanation: Lower priority numbers are evaluated first and win — priority 100 (allow) is processed before priority 200 (deny), so the traffic is allowed. Deny doesn't have some inherent precedence over Allow, evaluation order runs from the lowest priority number up (not the other way around), and NSG rules aren't merged or blended — whichever rule is evaluated first decides the outcome outright.
questions.whyTested: This is one of the most heavily tested single facts on AZ-104 because the intuitive-but-wrong answer, 'Deny always wins over Allow,' feels like reasonable security instinct even though it's simply false for NSGs — exams keep testing it precisely because real admins carry that instinct in from other systems and misapply it here.

questions.question: Hub-VNet contains an Azure Firewall. Spoke1 and Spoke2 are each peered with Hub-VNet. Traffic between Spoke1 and Spoke2 must pass through the firewall for inspection, and you must not create any additional peerings. What should you configure?
options: Route tables on the spoke subnets sending the other spoke's prefix to the firewall's private IP as next hop
Use remote gateways on the spoke peerings and Allow gateway transit on the hub side of each peering
Allow forwarded traffic on the existing hub and spoke peerings, with no other changes
A direct peering between Spoke1 and Spoke2 with the hub firewall configured as its gateway
questions.explanation: Peering is not transitive, so spoke-to-spoke traffic only flows if a user-defined route sends it to the firewall as a virtual appliance next hop. Gateway transit is the near-miss: it shares a VPN or ExpressRoute gateway through the hub, not a firewall or NVA. Allow forwarded traffic is required for the firewall's forwarded packets to be accepted, but on its own nothing routes to the firewall in the first place. A direct spoke-to-spoke peering violates the constraint and bypasses inspection.

questions.question: A web application runs in App Service in East US and West Europe. Users worldwide must be routed to the nearest healthy region, requests to /api and /images must go to different backend pools, a web application firewall must inspect traffic, and TLS must terminate at the edge. Which service should you deploy?
options: Azure Front Door Premium
Application Gateway v2 with the WAF SKU
Traffic Manager with the Performance routing method
A cross-region Azure Load Balancer
questions.explanation: Front Door is the global layer-7 entry point: it chooses the closest healthy origin, routes by URL path, includes WAF, and terminates TLS at Microsoft's edge. Application Gateway offers the same path routing and WAF but is regional, so it would need a global service in front of it to steer users between regions. Traffic Manager steers by DNS and never sees the HTTP request, so no path routing, WAF, or TLS termination. Cross-region Load Balancer works at layer 4.

questions.question: Two network virtual appliances in an active-active pair must receive every TCP and UDP flow from the spoke subnets, on any port, through a single internal load balancer frontend. What should you create?
options: A Standard internal load balancer with an HA ports load-balancing rule
A Basic internal load balancer with one load-balancing rule per protocol and port
An Application Gateway v2 with both appliances in its backend pool
A Standard public load balancer with an outbound rule for the spoke subnets
questions.explanation: An HA ports rule (port 0, protocol All) on a Standard internal load balancer forwards every port and protocol to the backend pool, which is exactly the pattern for highly available NVAs. The Basic SKU has no HA ports feature, and one rule per port cannot cover every port anyway. Application Gateway only handles HTTP and HTTPS. An outbound rule provides SNAT for egress; it does not distribute inbound flows to the appliances. The Basic SKU was also retired on September 30, 2025.

questions.question: VMs in VNet1 must resolve each other by name under corp.internal, with records created and removed automatically as VMs are deployed and deleted. VMs in VNet2 must resolve those same names, but VNet2's own VMs must not register records. What should you do?
options: A private DNS zone corp.internal linked to VNet1 with auto-registration on and to VNet2 with auto-registration off
A private DNS zone corp.internal linked to both VNets with auto-registration enabled on both links
A public Azure DNS zone corp.internal with name servers delegated from both virtual networks
Custom DNS servers on VNet2 set to the private IP addresses of two VMs in VNet1
questions.explanation: Auto-registration is a per-link setting on a private DNS zone, so you can register from VNet1 while VNet2 gets resolution only. Enabling it on both links would make VNet2's VMs register records too. A public zone would expose the names on the internet and cannot auto-register VMs. Pointing VNet2 at VMs in VNet1 presumes those VMs run a DNS service and recreates by hand what a private zone link does natively.

questions.question: Azure Bastion (Basic SKU) is deployed in VNet1. Administrators must connect to VMs in VNet1 using the native ssh client and key files on their workstations rather than the browser, and the VMs must still have no public IP addresses. What should you do?
options: Upgrade the Bastion host to the Standard SKU and enable native client support
Deploy an additional Bastion host in each subnet that contains VMs
Assign a public IP to each VM and allow TCP 22 from the administrators' addresses in the NSG
Enable just-in-time VM access in Microsoft Defender for Cloud
questions.explanation: Native client connectivity through az network bastion ssh or tunnel is a Standard-SKU feature; the Basic SKU is browser-only. One Bastion host serves a whole VNet, and even peered VNets, so more hosts add cost without adding the feature. Public IPs break the stated constraint. Just-in-time access narrows when an NSG rule is open, but it still needs the VM to be reachable through a public IP or a VPN.

questions.question: VM1 in subnet A cannot reach VM2 in subnet B on TCP 1433. Both subnets are in the same VNet, and a route table is associated with subnet A. You suspect the traffic is being sent to a network virtual appliance that is offline. Which Network Watcher tool shows where VM1's packets to VM2 are being sent?
options: Next hop
IP flow verify
Effective security rules
NSG flow logs
questions.explanation: Next hop evaluates the effective routes for a source VM and destination address and reports the next hop type and IP, which exposes a user-defined route pointing at a dead appliance. IP flow verify is the near-miss: it answers only whether an NSG rule allows or denies the flow, and says nothing about routing. Effective security rules lists the NSG rules applied to a NIC, and flow logs record what the NSGs allowed or denied after the fact.

questions.question: You are adding a subnet to VNet1 (10.10.0.0/16) that must host 60 virtual machines, each with a single network interface, and you want to consume as little address space as possible. Which subnet prefix should you use?
questions.explanation: Azure reserves five addresses in every subnet (network, broadcast, and three for the platform), so a /26 provides 64 minus 5, or 59 usable addresses, one short of the 60 NICs. A /25 yields 123 usable and is the smallest prefix that fits. A /27 leaves 27. A /24 works but wastes space, and 10.10.0.0/24 may collide with an existing subnet at the start of the range.

questions.question: Application-tier VMs in VNet1 are spread across three availability zones and listen on TCP 8443 and a custom UDP port. Web-tier VMs in peered VNet2 must reach them through one private IP address that keeps working if a zone fails. Nothing may be exposed to the internet. What should you deploy?
options: A Standard internal load balancer with a zone-redundant frontend
A Basic internal load balancer with a frontend in the application subnet
A Standard public load balancer with an NSG that denies the Internet service tag
An Application Gateway v2 with a private frontend IP address
questions.explanation: Only the Standard SKU supports availability zones, and a zone-redundant frontend is served from every zone so the single private IP survives a zone outage. The Basic SKU is the near-miss: it is internal and private, but it has no zone awareness and goes down with its zone. A public load balancer wrapped in an NSG still has an internet-facing IP. Application Gateway proxies HTTP and HTTPS only, so the UDP port rules it out. The Basic SKU was also retired on September 30, 2025.

questions.question: You must receive an email within minutes whenever any virtual machine in resource group RG1 is deleted, including deletions performed through the CLI or a template. What should you create?
options: An activity log alert for the Delete Virtual Machine operation at RG1 scope, with an action group
A metric alert rule on Percentage CPU with a threshold of 0 for the VMs in RG1
A log search alert rule on the Heartbeat table that fires when a VM in RG1 stops reporting
A Service Health alert rule for virtual machines in the region that contains RG1
questions.explanation: Deleting a VM is a control-plane operation recorded in the activity log, and an activity log alert on that operation fires on every delete regardless of the tool used. The heartbeat query is the near-miss: a deleted VM does stop sending heartbeats, but so does a stopped, deallocated, or disconnected one, and the alert only fires after the missing-heartbeat window elapses. A deleted VM emits no metrics at all, so a CPU threshold never evaluates. Service Health reports Microsoft platform incidents, not actions taken in your subscription.

questions.question: Fifty Windows VMs send their Security event log to a Log Analytics workspace through the Azure Monitor Agent. You must be alerted when event ID 4625 occurs more than 20 times in any 15-minute period on any single VM. Which type of alert rule should you create?
options: A log search alert rule that queries the Event table, split by computer
A metric alert rule on the VMs with a dynamic threshold
An activity log alert rule filtered to the Security category
A Service Health alert rule with the Incident event type
questions.explanation: Event IDs live in log data, so only a log search alert can count a specific ID per computer over a window and fire per VM using a dimension split. Metric alerts evaluate numeric time series such as CPU or disk; there is no metric for a Windows event ID. The activity log's Security category covers Defender for Cloud alerts about Azure resources, not events from inside a guest OS. Service Health alerts cover Azure platform incidents.

questions.question: A company wants to be able to fail over an entire application's VMs to a secondary region if the primary region goes down entirely.
options: A resource lock
Azure Advisor
Azure Backup alone
Azure Site Recovery
questions.explanation: Site Recovery replicates and fails over whole workloads to a secondary region, unlike Backup, which restores point-in-time copies.
questions.whyTested: Backup and Site Recovery get tested against each other constantly because both answer 'what if something goes wrong,' and the exam wants you to key in on scope, one restores a point-in-time copy, the other fails over a whole running workload, rather than treating the two as interchangeable disaster-protection tools.

questions.question: A user deleted a 2 GB folder from the data disk of VM1 yesterday. VM1 is protected by Azure Backup in a Recovery Services vault and must keep running. You need to recover only that folder with the least administrative effort. What should you do?
options: Use File Recovery on the recovery point to mount the disk and copy the folder back
Restore the recovery point to a new VM, then copy the folder across the network
Restore the recovery point as disks, attach them to VM1, and copy the folder
Use Azure Site Recovery to fail VM1 over to yesterday's recovery point
questions.explanation: File Recovery generates a script that mounts the recovery point's disks over iSCSI directly on VM1 or another machine, so you browse to the folder and copy it, then unmount. Restoring a whole VM or restoring disks and attaching them both work, but they create extra resources, cost, and cleanup for 2 GB of data. Site Recovery replicates VMs to another region for disaster recovery; it is not a backup product and VM1 has no replica to fail over to.

questions.question: Assigning the Reader role at a resource group to a user who already holds Contributor at the parent subscription restricts that user to read-only access inside the resource group.
questions.explanation: Role assignments are additive across scopes and the most permissive applicable assignment wins, so the inherited Contributor still applies in that resource group and the extra Reader assignment is redundant. Narrowing someone's access means removing or moving the broader assignment, not stacking a smaller one beneath it.

questions.question: A user who holds the Contributor role at the subscription scope can assign the Reader role to a colleague on any resource group in that subscription.
questions.explanation: Contributor's NotActions exclude Microsoft.Authorization/*/Write and /Delete, which is exactly what creating a role assignment requires, so a Contributor can manage every resource yet cannot grant anyone access. Only Owner, User Access Administrator, or a custom role that includes the role-assignment write action can do that.

questions.question: When a policy with the Deny effect is assigned at a management group, existing resources beneath it that violate the policy are automatically removed or brought into compliance.
questions.explanation: Deny only blocks new create or update requests that would violate the rule. Existing resources are evaluated and reported as non-compliant, but nothing is changed or deleted. Fixing what already exists requires a DeployIfNotExists or Modify policy together with a remediation task.

questions.question: When you create a storage account with geo-redundant storage (GRS), you choose which secondary region the data replicates to.
questions.explanation: GRS and GZRS always replicate to the fixed Azure paired region of the primary; the administrator cannot pick a different secondary. If data must be copied to a region of your choosing, that calls for object replication to a second storage account, not a redundancy setting.

questions.question: Enabling soft delete for blobs on a storage account also protects the Azure file shares in that account from accidental deletion.
questions.explanation: Blob soft delete and file share soft delete are separate settings configured in different places (Data protection for blobs, the File shares settings for shares) with their own retention periods. Turning on one does nothing for the other, which is a common gap discovered only after a share is deleted.

questions.question: A shared access signature that was signed with storage account key1 keeps working after key1 is regenerated, because the token carries its own expiry time.
questions.explanation: A SAS is validated by recomputing its signature with the key that signed it, so regenerating that key immediately invalidates every SAS it signed, whatever their expiry. That is also why rotating keys is the emergency way to revoke an ad hoc SAS, and why a stored access policy is the gentler option for revoking a service SAS without rotating keys.

questions.question: An autoscale rule on a VM Scale Set can use a metric from a different resource, such as the active message count of a Service Bus queue, instead of a metric emitted by the scale set itself.
questions.explanation: Autoscale rules let you pick a different metric source resource, so a worker tier can scale on queue depth, storage queue length, or any other Azure Monitor metric rather than only on its own CPU or memory. The common misconception is that scale sets can only react to host metrics from their own instances.

questions.question: Deploying the same Bicep file a second time to the same resource group fails because the resources it declares already exist.
questions.explanation: Resource Manager deployments are idempotent: a resource that already matches the template is left as is, and one whose properties differ is updated in place. Repeating a deployment is the normal way to roll out changes. The only time a redeploy removes anything is Complete mode, which deletes resources that are missing from the file.

questions.question: An Azure Container Instances container group can run several containers that share the same host, lifecycle, local network, and mounted volumes.
questions.explanation: A container group is scheduled as a unit, much like a Kubernetes pod: its containers start and stop together, reach each other on localhost, and can mount the same Azure Files volume. What Container Instances lacks is orchestration across many groups, such as replica scaling and rolling updates, which is where Container Apps or AKS come in.

questions.question: Two virtual networks whose address spaces overlap can be peered as long as the overlapping ranges are not assigned to any subnet.
questions.explanation: Peering is refused whenever the address spaces overlap at all, used or not, because Azure routes between peered networks by address space, not by subnet. Fixing it means removing the overlapping prefix from one VNet's address space before the peering can be created.

questions.question: A network security group associated with a subnet also filters traffic between two virtual machines that are both inside that same subnet.
questions.explanation: A subnet-level NSG is enforced on every flow to and from the NICs in that subnet, including VM-to-VM traffic that never leaves it. The default AllowVnetInBound rule is why that traffic normally works, and a custom deny rule with a lower priority number will block it, which surprises people who assume the NSG only guards the subnet boundary.

questions.question: You plan to deploy Azure Bastion (Standard SKU) into VNet1 (10.1.0.0/16) so administrators can reach VMs that have no public IP addresses. Which subnet should you create for the Bastion host?
options: AzureBastionSubnet with prefix 10.1.1.0/26
AzureBastionSubnet with prefix 10.1.1.0/27
BastionSubnet with prefix 10.1.1.0/26
GatewaySubnet with prefix 10.1.1.0/26
questions.explanation: The subnet name must be exactly AzureBastionSubnet, and it must be /26 or larger so the service can scale its instances. A /27 is rejected at deployment time. A differently named subnet is simply not recognized by Bastion. GatewaySubnet is the reserved name for VPN and ExpressRoute gateways, which cannot be shared with Bastion.

questions.question: A Global Administrator in Microsoft Entra ID tries to edit a resource group in the Azure portal and gets an access-denied error, despite being a Global Administrator. What lets them manage Azure resources across every subscription in the tenant?
options: Turning on the "elevate access" setting for Global Administrators in Microsoft Entra ID properties
Assigning themselves the Reader role manually at the tenant root management group scope
Waiting 24 hours for the new Global Administrator role to finish synchronizing to Azure
Creating a brand new subscription under their own account and moving the resource group into it
questions.explanation: Microsoft Entra roles like Global Administrator control the identity plane, not Azure resources, by default. The "elevate access" setting grants Global Administrators the Azure RBAC User Access Administrator role at the root management group scope, letting them manage resources tenant-wide. Self-assigning just Reader would only grant read access, not the ability to edit; nothing about this permission gap resolves on a timer; and creating a new subscription does nothing for access to resources in existing ones.

questions.question: A finance team's storage account keeps getting accidentally deleted by administrators who legitimately have Contributor access. Which safeguard specifically blocks deletion while still letting their authorized configuration changes continue?
options: A CanNotDelete resource lock
A ReadOnly resource lock
Revoking Contributor from the whole team
An audit-effect Azure Policy
questions.explanation: A CanNotDelete lock blocks deletion but still allows reads and writes. A ReadOnly lock would also block the configuration changes the team needs; removing Contributor access would block those too, and an audit-only policy effect just flags noncompliance without preventing the delete.

questions.question: An application's managed identity needs to read and write blobs in a container, without ever handling a SAS token or the storage account key.
options: Assign the managed identity the Storage Blob Data Contributor role on the container or storage account
Generate a long-lived SAS token and embed it in the application's configuration for the managed identity to use
Share the storage account's access key with the application so it can authenticate directly
Add the application to a dynamic group whose membership rule grants storage access automatically
questions.explanation: Data-plane RBAC roles like Storage Blob Data Contributor let an identity authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID and access blob data directly, with no key or token to manage at all. A SAS token or the account key both reintroduce exactly the credential-handling this scenario wants to avoid, and dynamic groups manage user/group membership rules, not resource-level data permissions.

questions.question: A batch rendering job can tolerate being interrupted and restarted, and the team wants to run it on Azure VMs at a steep discount versus pay-as-you-go pricing.
options: Azure Spot Virtual Machines
Reserved Instances
A VM Scale Set with manual scaling
Azure Dedicated Host
questions.explanation: Spot VMs use Azure's unused capacity at a steep discount but can be evicted with little notice when that capacity is needed back — a good fit for interruptible workloads. Reserved Instances are a billing commitment for guaranteed capacity, not an eviction-prone discount.

questions.question: An administrator wants one NSG rule that allows traffic to every VM tagged as 'WebTier,' regardless of each VM's individual IP address, which changes as instances are added or removed.
options: Group the VMs’ network interfaces into an Application Security Group and reference it in the rule
Write a separate NSG rule for every VM's current IP address, updating it manually each time an instance changes
Replace the NSG with a public Load Balancer configured with the same allow rule
Move all the VMs into one dedicated subnet and apply the rule to that subnet as a whole
questions.explanation: An Application Security Group (ASG) groups VM network interfaces logically, like 'WebTier,' so an NSG rule can reference the group as a source or destination instead of hardcoding IP addresses that change over time. Per-IP rules break the moment an instance is replaced, a Load Balancer distributes traffic but doesn't filter it the way an NSG rule does, and a subnet-wide rule would also catch any other VM later placed in that same subnet.

questions.question: An administrator is deploying monitoring to a fleet of new VMs and wants Microsoft's current, supported agent for collecting metrics and logs into Azure Monitor.
options: The Azure Monitor Agent with a data collection rule
The legacy Log Analytics agent (MMA) with a workspace key
The Azure Diagnostics extension (WAD) sending to a storage account
The Dependency agent on its own
questions.explanation: The Azure Monitor Agent, configured through data collection rules, is the supported agent for new deployments. The Log Analytics agent was retired in August 2024 and should not be used for anything new. The Azure Diagnostics extension is an older collector aimed at storage accounts and Event Hubs, not Log Analytics. The Dependency agent only adds process and connection mapping for VM insights and depends on the Azure Monitor Agent being present.

questions.question: A company needs a VM's resource logs both queryable right away in Log Analytics and archived cheaply for 7 years to satisfy a compliance requirement.
options: One diagnostic setting that sends the logs to both a Log Analytics workspace and a storage account
Two diagnostic settings on the VM, because a diagnostic setting supports a single destination
Azure Backup of the VM with a seven-year retention rule in the vault policy
Continuous export from Microsoft Defender for Cloud to a storage account
questions.explanation: A single diagnostic setting can fan the same logs out to several destinations at once, so one setting covers the workspace for querying and the storage account for cheap long-term archive. A second setting is unnecessary because the one-destination limit does not exist. Azure Backup protects disks, not the log stream. Continuous export from Defender for Cloud ships security alerts and recommendations, not a resource's own diagnostic logs.

questions.question: An administrator needs to schedule recurring patch installation windows across dozens of Windows and Linux Azure VMs, and track patch compliance centrally.
options: Azure Update Manager with a maintenance configuration
Azure Automation Update Management
Automatic VM guest patching enabled on each VM
An Azure Policy assignment with the DeployIfNotExists effect
questions.explanation: Update Manager is the current service for assessing compliance across a fleet and installing updates in maintenance configurations you schedule. Automation Update Management is the near-miss: it did the same job, but it was retired in August 2024 along with the Log Analytics agent it depended on. Automatic guest patching installs updates during off-peak hours Azure chooses, with no administrator-defined window across the fleet. Policy can enforce that patch settings exist, but it does not orchestrate installations.

questions.question: An immutable blob storage policy with a legal hold in effect can be bypassed by the storage account's Owner role to delete data early if needed.
questions.explanation: Immutability policies, including legal holds, block deletion and modification for everyone, including the account owner, until the hold is removed or the retention period expires — that is what makes them valid for regulatory retention requirements.

questions.question: Virtual network flow logs, viewed through Traffic Analytics, can show which allowed and denied flows are hitting resources in a virtual network without manually correlating raw log files. They replace NSG flow logs, which retire on September 30, 2027.
questions.explanation: Network Watcher flow logs record IP traffic, and Traffic Analytics processes them in a Log Analytics workspace into visual, queryable insights instead of raw JSON. NSG flow logs retire on September 30, 2027 and can no longer be created, so virtual network flow logs, enabled at the virtual network, are the current feature.

questions.question: Soft delete for Azure Backup keeps deleted backup data recoverable for a retention window, even if someone deletes the backup item or disables backup entirely.
questions.explanation: This protection is distinct from blob soft delete and is designed to guard against accidental or malicious deletion of backup data itself, such as during a ransomware attack that disables backups.

questions.question: User1 is assigned the Contributor role at the scope of subscription Sub1 and holds no other role assignments. Which two actions can User1 perform? (Choose two.)
options: Create a new resource group in Sub1
Deploy a virtual machine into an existing resource group in Sub1
Assign the Reader role to User2 on a resource group in Sub1
Apply a CanNotDelete lock to a resource group in Sub1
questions.explanation: Contributor grants every action except those under Microsoft.Authorization (role assignments, deny assignments, locks, elevate access) and Blueprints (now being retired in favor of Deployment Stacks), so creating resource groups and deploying resources are both allowed. Assigning a role needs Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write, which Contributor excludes. The lock is the near-miss: management locks also live under Microsoft.Authorization/locks, so a Contributor can neither create nor remove them, even though it can otherwise fully manage the resource group.

questions.question: You plan to attach Premium SSD v2 disks to a new virtual machine. Which two statements about Premium SSD v2 are true? (Choose two.)
options: It cannot be used as the operating system disk of the VM
Its IOPS and throughput can be adjusted without changing the disk size
It supports ReadOnly host caching on the VM
It requires the VM to be deployed in a proximity placement group
questions.explanation: Premium SSD v2 is a data-disk-only type, and its headline feature is performance provisioned independently of capacity, the same decoupling Ultra Disk offers at a lower price. Host caching is the near-miss: the original Premium SSD supports ReadOnly and ReadWrite caching, but Premium SSD v2 does not, which matters when migrating a disk that relied on it. Proximity placement groups are unrelated to disk type.

questions.question: An alert rule fires when a VM's CPU exceeds 90%. Which two of the following can the alert's action group do directly? (Choose two.)
options: Start an Azure Automation runbook
Send a push notification to the Azure mobile app
Increase the instance count of a VM Scale Set
Restart the virtual machine without any additional resource
questions.explanation: Action groups deliver notifications (email, SMS, voice, push) and invoke automation targets such as runbooks, Functions, Logic Apps, and webhooks. Changing a Scale Set's instance count is the job of autoscale rules, not alert actions; an alert can only reach a runbook that then calls the scale API. Likewise, restarting a VM is not a built-in action type, so it requires a runbook or Function to perform the restart.

questions.question: Your tenant has 2,000 users. You must block sign-ins that use legacy authentication protocols such as IMAP and SMTP AUTH, but one on-premises scanner account must keep using SMTP AUTH, and users must not be forced to register for MFA as part of this change. What should you configure?
options: A Conditional Access policy that blocks the Other clients client-app condition, excluding the scanner account
Security defaults enabled at the tenant level in Microsoft Entra ID properties
Per-user multifactor authentication set to Enforced for the user accounts, excluding the scanner
A sign-in risk policy in Microsoft Entra ID Protection that blocks medium and high risk sign-ins
questions.explanation: Conditional Access exposes legacy protocols as a client-app condition and supports per-user exclusions, so the scanner can be carved out. Security defaults block legacy authentication too, but tenant-wide with no exclusions, and they also require every user to register for MFA. Per-user MFA does not block legacy protocols directly; legacy clients simply fail MFA inconsistently, and it forces registration. A sign-in risk policy reacts to risk signals, not to the protocol a client uses.

questions.question: An organization wants administrators to normally hold no standing Global Administrator access, activating that role with approval and only for a limited, time-boxed window when actually needed. Which feature enables this?
options: Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM) with eligible assignments
A quarterly access review of the Global Administrator role
A Conditional Access policy with a one-hour sign-in frequency for administrators
An administrative unit that contains the administrator accounts
questions.explanation: PIM makes the role assignment eligible rather than active, so the administrator must activate it, optionally with approval and justification, and it expires after the configured duration. An access review is the near-miss: it periodically confirms whether someone should keep a role, but between reviews the assignment is still standing access. A sign-in frequency control forces re-authentication; it does not remove the role between uses. An administrative unit narrows which users a role applies to, not when the role is held.

questions.question: A storage account should be reachable from resources inside a specific subnet using the subnet's private IP address space, with traffic never traversing the public internet, and the storage account itself getting an address inside that VNet. Which feature specifically provides this?
options: A Shared Access Signature
A service endpoint
A storage account firewall IP rule alone
A private endpoint
questions.explanation: A private endpoint gives the storage account an actual private IP address inside the VNet, so traffic from the subnet stays fully off the public internet. A service endpoint instead extends the subnet's identity over the Microsoft backbone to reach the storage account's still-public endpoint, optimizing the route without the storage account ever getting an address inside the VNet. A SAS only grants a scoped credential, and a firewall IP rule alone still means the storage account is reachable at its public endpoint from allowed IPs, not an address inside your VNet.

questions.question: An administrator deploys three VMs into the same availability zone within a region for a critical app. What risk does this configuration still leave unaddressed, compared to spreading them across three separate zones?
options: A failure affecting that one physical datacenter
A single VM crashing due to an application bug
A DDoS attack against the application
An expired SSL certificate on the app
questions.explanation: Placing all three VMs in the same availability zone means they all still depend on that one physical datacenter — a power or cooling failure there could take out all three simultaneously, which is exactly the risk spreading them across zones addresses. The other three risks, an application bug, a DDoS attack, and an expired certificate, are not related to physical datacenter placement at all, so zone distribution would not change any of them.

questions.question: An organization wants to build one standardized, versioned custom VM image and make it available for deployment across multiple subscriptions and regions in their tenant. Which service fits?
options: Azure Compute Gallery with an image definition and versions replicated to each region
A managed disk snapshot copied to a storage account in each target region
The Custom Script Extension with the configuration applied at first boot
A managed image created in each region from a generalized copy of the VM
questions.explanation: Azure Compute Gallery is built for publishing versioned images, replicating them to chosen regions, and sharing them across subscriptions or the whole tenant. A snapshot is a point-in-time copy of one disk with no versioning or sharing model. The Custom Script Extension configures a VM after it is already running rather than producing an image. A managed image is the near-miss: it is a real image, but it is regional, unversioned, and lives in one subscription, so you would end up maintaining many copies by hand.

questions.question: An administrator wants traffic from a subnet destined for the internet to be forced through a network virtual appliance for inspection first, instead of going directly out. Which feature enables this custom routing?
options: A user-defined route in a route table with the appliance as the next hop
A network security group rule that redirects outbound traffic to the appliance
VNet peering between the subnet's VNet and the appliance's VNet with gateway transit
A NAT gateway associated with the subnet in front of the appliance
questions.explanation: A user-defined route for 0.0.0.0/0 with next hop type Virtual appliance overrides the default internet system route, so the subnet's egress is steered through the appliance. NSG rules allow or deny traffic; they have no concept of redirecting it. Peering with gateway transit shares a VPN or ExpressRoute gateway, not an inspection appliance, and establishes connectivity rather than a forced path. A NAT gateway performs outbound SNAT for the subnet and would send traffic straight to the internet, bypassing the appliance.

questions.question: A subnet with several VMs needs reliable outbound-only internet connectivity that does not consume a public IP on each individual VM, and avoids SNAT port exhaustion under heavy outbound load. Which service fits best?
options: A public Load Balancer
Azure Bastion
A NAT gateway
A private endpoint
questions.explanation: A NAT gateway provides scalable, outbound-only internet connectivity for an entire subnet through a small pool of shared public IPs, specifically designed to avoid the SNAT port exhaustion a Load Balancer's outbound rules can run into under heavy load. Azure Bastion is for inbound RDP or SSH management access, not outbound internet traffic, and a private endpoint is for inbound access to a specific PaaS resource, not outbound internet connectivity at all.

questions.question: A team wants to track end-to-end response times, failure rates, and dependency calls for a live web application, down to individual requests, not just VM-level metrics. Which Azure Monitor feature fits?
options: Azure Service Health
Application Insights
Azure Advisor
Network Watcher
questions.explanation: Application Insights is the Azure Monitor feature purpose-built for application performance monitoring — request rates, response times, failure rates, and dependency tracking down to individual requests. Service Health reports on Azure platform outages, Advisor gives configuration recommendations, and Network Watcher diagnoses network connectivity, none of which provide application-level performance telemetry.

questions.question: A custom role that grants only Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/restart/action, with no read action, lets the assignee restart virtual machines from the Azure portal.
questions.explanation: The portal has to list and open the VM before it can offer a Restart button, and that requires Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/read. Without a read action the VM is invisible in the portal, even though a CLI call that targets the resource ID directly could still succeed. Real least-privilege custom roles pair the specific action with the matching read permission.

questions.question: Applying Azure Hybrid Benefit to a Windows Server VM eliminates the compute charge for that VM entirely, leaving only a licensing fee.
questions.explanation: Azure Hybrid Benefit only offsets the licensing portion of the cost by letting you reuse an eligible on-premises license — it does not eliminate the underlying compute charge for the VM's CPU, memory, and disk, which is billed separately regardless of licensing.

questions.question: Azure Backup's cross-region restore feature lets an administrator restore a VM into the paired secondary region, even while the primary region is fully available, provided the vault uses geo-redundant storage.
questions.explanation: Cross-region restore is specifically designed to let you restore into the secondary paired region on demand, for testing or migration purposes, not only during an actual regional outage, as long as the Recovery Services vault's storage redundancy is geo-redundant (GRS or RA-GRS) or geo-zone-redundant.

questions.question: You create a private endpoint for storage account st1 in VNet1. A VM in VNet1 still resolves st1.blob.core.windows.net to a public IP address, and st1 remains reachable from the internet. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)
options: Link a privatelink.blob.core.windows.net private DNS zone that holds the endpoint A record to VNet1
Set Public network access on st1 to Disabled
Add a service endpoint for Microsoft.Storage to the VM subnet
Add an NSG rule on the VM subnet that allows outbound TCP 443 to the storage service tag
questions.explanation: The private endpoint only creates a NIC with a private IP; name resolution to that IP depends on a private DNS zone linked to the VNet, and the public endpoint stays open until public network access is disabled or restricted. A service endpoint is the near-miss: it optimizes the route to the public endpoint and does not change DNS or close public access. An NSG rule permitting 443 was never the problem, since traffic to the public endpoint already works.

questions.question: An application in two regions sits behind an Azure Traffic Manager profile. Which two statements describe how Traffic Manager behaves? (Choose two.)
options: It returns a DNS response pointing the client at one endpoint rather than proxying the traffic itself
Its Performance routing method directs each client to the endpoint with the lowest network latency
It can send requests for different URL paths to different endpoints
An existing TCP connection moves to a healthy endpoint immediately when the current endpoint fails a health check
questions.explanation: Traffic Manager works purely at the DNS layer, resolving the profile name to the best endpoint and then stepping out of the path; Performance routing picks the lowest-latency endpoint for the client's source network. Because it never sees the HTTP request it cannot route by URL path, which is a layer-7 job for Application Gateway or Front Door. And since clients hold a cached DNS answer, failover only takes effect when the TTL expires and the client re-resolves; established connections are not redirected.

questions.question: This real Access control (IAM) role assignments list shows several assignments scoped as 'Subscription (Inherited)'. What does that scope label mean?
options: The role was assigned directly on this resource group and cannot be changed
The role was assigned at the subscription level and applies down to this resource group automatically
The role only applies to resources created before this resource group existed
The role is a deprecated legacy assignment that Azure will remove automatically
questions.explanation: Azure RBAC is inherited down the hierarchy — a role assigned at the subscription scope automatically applies to every resource group and resource beneath it. The Scope column shows exactly where in that hierarchy each assignment was actually made, which matters because removing an inherited assignment here requires going up to where it was actually granted, not editing it at this resource group.

questions.question: You're partway through Create a storage account and see this real tab row: Basics, Advanced, Networking, Data protection, Security, Encryption, Tags. Which tab would you use to restrict the account to a specific virtual network?
options: Advanced
Networking
Security
Data protection
questions.explanation: Networking is where you configure things like virtual network integration, private endpoints, and firewall rules — restricting access to specific VNets is a networking concern, separate from the account-level defaults on Advanced or the threat-protection settings on Security.

questions.question: In this real Instance details section for a new VM, Availability options is set to 'No infrastructure redundancy required.' What's the practical effect of that choice?
options: The VM won't be protected against a single hardware failure or planned maintenance taking down its host
The VM will automatically be placed in an Availability Zone chosen by Azure at deployment time
Azure will refuse to create the VM until an explicit redundancy option is selected in this section
The VM will be replicated to a secondary paired region automatically at no extra cost
questions.explanation: "No infrastructure redundancy required" is a valid, selectable option — Azure won't block VM creation over it — but it means skipping Availability Zones or an Availability Set, so a single host failure or planned maintenance event on that host can take the VM down with no built-in protection.

questions.question: User2 is assigned the Owner role at subscription Sub1. User2 must also be able to reset the passwords of standard, non-administrator users in the Microsoft Entra tenant, and currently receives an access-denied error when trying. The solution must follow the principle of least privilege. What should you do?
options: Assign User2 the Password Administrator Microsoft Entra role
Assign User2 the Owner role at the Tenant Root Group management group
Assign User2 the User Access Administrator role at the Tenant Root Group
Assign User2 the Global Administrator Microsoft Entra role
questions.explanation: Password resets are a directory operation, and no Azure RBAC assignment at any scope, even the Tenant Root Group, grants directory permissions; Owner and User Access Administrator there only widen control over Azure resources. Password Administrator is the narrowest Microsoft Entra role that covers resetting passwords for non-administrators. Global Administrator would work but is far broader than the requirement.

questions.question: An organization creates an emergency access ('break-glass') account that's excluded from every Conditional Access policy, in case a misconfigured policy locks out all admins at once. Which additional practice is recommended to keep that account secure?
options: Give the account a long, complex credential that isn't stored with any one person, plus alerting on any sign-in
Enroll the account in the same Conditional Access policies it was created to bypass, for consistency
Assign the account the Reader role only, so it can never make changes even in a real emergency
Rotate the account's password automatically every 24 hours through a Conditional Access policy
questions.explanation: A break-glass account needs to stay usable if Conditional Access itself is misconfigured, so it's deliberately excluded from those policies — but it still needs strong secrecy (a long, closely-held credential) and monitoring (alerting on any sign-in, since real use should be rare and noteworthy). Enrolling it back into Conditional Access defeats its purpose, Reader access wouldn't let it actually fix anything during an emergency, and Conditional Access has no role in password rotation.

questions.question: An IoT platform writes about 2 TB of sensor files per day. Files are read often during the first week, rarely afterwards, and must be retained for one year. You need to choose storage that minimizes cost over the retention period. What should you use?
options: Block blobs in a standard GPv2 account with a lifecycle management policy
Block blobs in a premium block blob storage account for low-latency reads
A standard Azure Files share with daily share snapshots for retention
Azure Table storage with one entity per sensor file and a timestamp property
questions.explanation: Standard GPv2 blob storage offers Hot, Cool, Cold, and Archive tiers, so a lifecycle rule can push each file to cheaper tiers as it ages. Premium block blob accounts give low latency for hot, high-transaction data but offer no cooler tiers, so a year of rarely read files stays at the highest price. Azure Files is priced for file-share semantics and does not tier individual files. Table storage holds structured entities, not multi-megabyte files.

questions.question: A company needs its nightly database export files, currently written to Azure Blob Storage in the Hot tier, to automatically move to the Cool tier after 30 days of no access, and then to the Archive tier after 90 days, without anyone doing it manually. Which feature accomplishes this?
options: A blob lifecycle management policy with time-based tier transition rules
Changing the storage account's default access tier to Cool
A SAS token scoped to expire after 90 days
Azure Backup configured with a 90-day retention policy
questions.explanation: Lifecycle management policies automatically transition or delete blobs based on rules like 'no access for N days,' handling exactly this tiering without manual intervention. Changing the account's default tier only affects new blobs uploaded without an explicit tier, a SAS token controls access duration rather than storage tier, and Backup protects against data loss — it doesn't move blobs between access tiers.

questions.question: You migrate a line-of-business application to Azure. Its installer registers a Windows service, writes under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE, and loads a third-party kernel-mode driver. You want the lowest operational overhead that still supports the application. Where should you host it?
options: An Azure virtual machine
Azure App Service on a Windows plan
Azure Container Apps with a Windows container image
Azure Functions on a Premium plan
questions.explanation: Installing services and kernel drivers requires full control of the guest operating system, which only a VM provides. The App Service sandbox blocks Windows services, kernel drivers, and HKLM writes. Container Apps runs Linux containers only, and a kernel driver cannot be packaged into a container in any case. Functions hosts event-driven code, not an installer-based desktop application.

questions.question: A team runs a VM Scale Set where new instances need a configuration script to run automatically the moment they're provisioned, with no one logging in manually. They also want existing instances to keep running with their current configuration even after the script is updated later. Which approach fits both requirements?
options: Add the Custom Script Extension to the Scale Set model, so it runs on each new instance without touching existing ones
Run the script manually on each new instance as it appears, using the Run Command feature in the portal
Add the script to a scheduled task on each instance that re-runs whenever the Scale Set model is updated
Use Azure Machine Configuration to apply the script to the existing and new instances nightly
questions.explanation: Adding the Custom Script Extension to the Scale Set model makes it part of every new instance's provisioning, but with a Manual upgrade policy an updated model is not pushed to instances that already exist, which matches both requirements. Run Command on each new instance reintroduces the human step the team wants removed. A scheduled task keyed to model updates and Machine Configuration both force the change onto existing instances, which is exactly what the team wants to avoid.

questions.question: A company's on-premises network connects to Azure over an ExpressRoute circuit. During a rare ExpressRoute outage, they want traffic to automatically fail over to a site-to-site VPN connection instead of losing connectivity entirely. What should you do?
options: Deploy a VPN gateway connection to the same virtual network, coexisting with the ExpressRoute connection
Nothing further, because an ExpressRoute circuit includes an automatic VPN fallback path
Migrate the circuit to Azure Virtual WAN, which fails over to the internet on its own
Enable zone-redundant gateways and ExpressRoute Direct for the circuit
questions.explanation: ExpressRoute and site-to-site VPN connections can coexist on the same virtual network, and with both routes advertised the VPN path takes over when the circuit's routes disappear; this has to be deliberately configured, since nothing is created automatically. Virtual WAN also needs an explicit VPN connection before it can fail over to one. Zone-redundant gateways protect the gateway instances within a region, and ExpressRoute Direct is higher-bandwidth connectivity; neither provides an alternate path when the circuit itself is down.

questions.question: A company already filters subnet traffic with NSGs but wants centralized, tenant-wide outbound filtering — for example, blocking outbound traffic to a specific list of known-malicious FQDNs — enforced consistently across many VNets from a single place to manage the rule set. Which is the better fit, and why doesn't relying on more NSGs solve this well?
options: Azure Firewall, since it supports centralized FQDN-based filtering across multiple VNets from one managed instance
NSGs alone, since an NSG rule can already reference an FQDN directly as a destination
Azure Firewall, since NSGs are being fully retired and no longer supported on new subnets
NSGs alone, since adding one NSG per VNet is functionally identical to a centralized firewall
questions.explanation: Azure Firewall supports FQDN-based filtering rules and is deployed once to centrally enforce policy across many VNets, matching the centralized, tenant-wide requirement here. NSGs filter by IP, port, and protocol — they don't support FQDN-based rules the way Azure Firewall does, and NSGs remain fully supported, not being retired. Reproducing the same rule set across many separate NSGs also isn't equivalent to one centrally managed policy — it means maintaining consistency across every one of them by hand.

questions.question: An administrator wants an email sent automatically whenever a VM's CPU usage stays above 90% for more than 10 minutes, without having to check the portal manually. Which Azure Monitor component should they configure?
options: A metric alert rule with an action group that sends an email notification
Log Analytics, since it emails a daily summary of all metrics automatically
Azure Advisor, since it emails cost and performance recommendations weekly
Application Insights, configured to alert on high CPU for the application's App Service plan
questions.explanation: A metric alert rule watches a specific metric like CPU percentage against a threshold and duration, and an action group defines what happens when it fires — including sending an email. Log Analytics stores and queries data but doesn't send scheduled summary emails on its own, Advisor gives periodic recommendations rather than real-time threshold alerts, and Application Insights is scoped to application-level telemetry, like an App Service plan's own metrics, not the CPU of an arbitrary VM.

questions.question: A compliance team wants every new storage account created in a subscription to automatically get a specific diagnostic setting applied at creation time, without anyone remembering to configure it by hand. Which Azure Policy effect fits this?
options: DeployIfNotExists
Audit
Deny
Append
questions.explanation: DeployIfNotExists evaluates new or updated resources against a condition and, if it isn't met, automatically deploys a related resource, like a diagnostic setting, to bring the resource into compliance. Audit only flags noncompliant resources in reports without changing them, Deny blocks the resource from being created in the first place rather than fixing it, and Append only adds or overwrites specific fields in the request itself — it doesn't deploy a separate related resource the way this scenario needs.

questions.question: A company has had the same set of guest users with access to a sensitive SharePoint site for two years and wants a recurring, scheduled process where a manager has to explicitly confirm each guest still needs access, or it gets automatically revoked. Which Microsoft Entra feature fits?
options: An access review of the guest users, recurring quarterly, with results applied automatically
A Conditional Access policy that limits guest sign-in frequency to 24 hours
Privileged Identity Management eligible assignments for the guest users
The guest user access restrictions setting in External collaboration settings
questions.explanation: Access reviews are the recertification feature: a designated reviewer approves or denies each guest on a schedule and denied users lose access automatically. A sign-in frequency control forces guests to re-authenticate but never asks anyone whether they should still have access. PIM provides time-boxed activation of privileged roles, which does not fit ongoing access to a site. Guest access restrictions limit what guests can see in the directory; they do not review or remove existing site access.

questions.question: A branch office runs a local Windows file server that's running low on disk space, but needs to keep offering fast local access to files that are actually opened often. Which Azure service lets infrequently-used files get replaced locally with lightweight pointers to a cloud copy, while frequently-used files stay fully cached on-premises?
options: Azure File Sync with cloud tiering enabled
AzCopy run on a nightly schedule
A storage account lifecycle management policy
Azure Site Recovery, configured for the file server
questions.explanation: Azure File Sync keeps an Azure file share and the on-premises file server in sync, and cloud tiering can replace cold, infrequently-accessed files locally with small pointer stubs that fetch the content from Azure on demand, freeing local disk space while keeping hot files cached nearby. AzCopy only performs one-off or scheduled copy jobs, not continuous sync with tiering; a lifecycle policy only moves blobs between access tiers in the cloud, not files on a local server; and Site Recovery replicates whole VMs for disaster recovery, unrelated to local disk space.
