questions.question: A media company wants newly uploaded blobs in its primary storage account to be automatically and asynchronously copied to a separate storage account in another region, so read requests from users near that region can be served from a local copy. Which feature fits?
options: Object replication
Blob lifecycle management
RA-GRS
A storage account access key
questions.explanation: Object replication asynchronously copies block blobs from a source account to a destination account, including across regions, which is exactly this scenario of serving a local copy to users near the second region. Lifecycle management only moves blobs between access tiers within the same account, RA-GRS makes a Microsoft-managed secondary readable but doesn't create an independently addressable second storage account, and an access key is a credential, not a replication mechanism.

questions.question: A latency-sensitive trading application splits its workload across three VMs that constantly exchange data with each other, and the team wants Azure to place them as physically close together as possible within a datacenter to minimize network latency between them. Which feature fits?
options: A proximity placement group
An availability set
An availability zone
A VM Scale Set
questions.explanation: A proximity placement group is specifically for colocating VMs physically close together to minimize inter-VM network latency. An availability set and availability zones do the opposite, deliberately spreading VMs apart across hardware or datacenters for resiliency, and a Scale Set manages a group of identical instances but doesn't by itself guarantee physical proximity between them.

questions.question: A team updates their VM Scale Set's model with a new image version and wants Azure to update instances automatically in small batches, pausing to confirm each batch is healthy before moving to the next, rather than updating everything at once or requiring someone to upgrade each instance by hand. Which upgrade policy fits?
options: Rolling
Manual
Automatic
Spot
questions.explanation: A Rolling upgrade policy updates instances in batches with health checks between batches, limiting the damage if a bad update slips through. Manual requires explicitly triggering the upgrade on each instance, Automatic updates every instance right away with no batching or health gating, and Spot isn't an upgrade policy at all — it's a VM pricing and eviction model.

questions.question: An administrator wants to capture a configured VM as a reusable image that deploys new VMs with fresh, unique identities, not clones carrying the original VM's exact hostname and security identifiers. What must happen to the source VM immediately before capturing the image?
options: Generalize it with Sysprep on Windows or waagent -deprovision on Linux
Deallocate it and take an incremental snapshot of the OS disk first
Enable boot diagnostics and reset the local administrator password
Add it to a proximity placement group and resize it to the smallest size
questions.explanation: Generalizing strips machine-specific state such as the hostname, security identifiers, and cached credentials, so an image built from it produces clean, unique VMs on each deployment. A snapshot is the near-miss: it captures the disk faithfully, but a VM created from a specialized snapshot is an exact clone with the same SID and name. Boot diagnostics, password resets, placement groups, and resizing change nothing about the identity baked into the disk.

questions.question: An app team wants traffic from their subnet to a storage account to take an optimized path over the Microsoft backbone instead of the public internet, but the storage account itself can stay reachable at its existing public endpoint for other authorized callers. Which feature fits best?
options: A service endpoint
A private endpoint
VNet peering
Azure Bastion
questions.explanation: A service endpoint extends a subnet's identity onto the Microsoft backbone so traffic to the storage account takes an optimized route, while the storage account keeps its normal public endpoint reachable by other authorized callers. A private endpoint instead gives the storage account an actual private IP inside the VNet, changing how it's reached entirely rather than just optimizing the route. Peering connects two VNets to each other, not a VNet to a PaaS service, and Bastion is for RDP/SSH access to VMs, unrelated to storage connectivity.

questions.question: A team enables a new Azure SQL Database and expects its detailed resource logs, like query performance insights, to start flowing into their existing Log Analytics workspace automatically. A week later, the workspace still shows nothing for that database. What's the most likely cause?
options: No diagnostic setting was configured on the database to route its resource logs anywhere
Log Analytics workspaces only accept data from virtual machines, not platform services like Azure SQL Database
The workspace has reached its maximum data retention limit and is rejecting new data
Resource logs take a minimum of 30 days to begin appearing after a resource is created
questions.explanation: Resource logs aren't sent anywhere by default — a diagnostic setting has to be explicitly configured on the resource to route its logs to a destination like a Log Analytics workspace, a storage account, or an event hub. Log Analytics accepts data from many platform services, not just VMs; a workspace hitting its retention limit affects how long old data is kept, not whether new data is rejected; and there's no 30-day delay built into resource logging.

questions.question: A team needs the Azure Monitor Agent to collect one specific custom Windows event log channel from a fleet of VMs and send it to their Log Analytics workspace, leaving out the noisier default channels they don't need. Which component defines exactly what gets collected and where it goes?
options: A data collection rule associated with the VMs
A diagnostic setting on each VM
The Azure Diagnostics extension (WAD) with a storage account sink
VM insights enabled on the VMs
questions.explanation: A data collection rule tells the Azure Monitor Agent which data sources to collect, down to an XPath filter for one event channel, and which workspace to send them to. A diagnostic setting is the near-miss: it routes a resource's platform logs and metrics, but it has no view into the guest operating system's event logs. The Azure Diagnostics extension is the legacy collector aimed at storage accounts. VM insights deploys its own rule for performance counters and dependency maps, not custom event channels.

questions.question: If the User Administrator role is assigned to User1 with its scope set to administrative unit AU1, User1 can reset passwords for every non-administrator in the tenant except members of other administrative units.
questions.explanation: An administrative-unit-scoped assignment applies only to the users, groups, and devices that are members of that unit. Users who belong to no administrative unit at all are still out of reach. Tenant-wide scope requires assigning the role at the tenant level rather than at AU1.

questions.question: Customer-initiated storage account failover promotes the secondary region to primary for a GRS account, but data written to the primary just before the outage may not have replicated yet and can be lost.
questions.explanation: Because GRS replication to the secondary region is asynchronous, a customer-initiated failover can lose the most recent writes that had not yet replicated — a real tradeoff administrators need to plan around, not a lossless operation.

questions.question: Enabling encryption at host for a virtual machine requires installing the Azure Disk Encryption extension inside the guest operating system.
questions.explanation: Encryption at host is a platform setting on the VM that encrypts temp disks and disk caches on the host itself, with no agent or extension in the guest. Azure Disk Encryption is the separate in-guest option that uses BitLocker or DM-Crypt, and the two cannot be enabled on the same VM, so confusing them leads to a failed configuration rather than extra protection.

questions.question: If a route table on subnet A contains a 0.0.0.0/0 route whose next hop is a network virtual appliance, traffic between two VMs that are both in subnet A is also sent through the appliance.
questions.explanation: Routes are selected by longest prefix match, and the system route for the VNet's own address space is far more specific than 0.0.0.0/0, so intra-subnet and intra-VNet traffic keeps going direct. Forcing that traffic through an appliance requires an explicit user-defined route for the VNet or subnet prefix with the appliance as next hop.

questions.question: Which two of the following are true about Azure RBAC deny assignments? (Choose two.)
options: A deny assignment blocks specified actions regardless of any role assignment that would otherwise allow them
Deny assignments are created and managed directly by subscription administrators the same way role assignments are
Deny assignments are most commonly created automatically by Deployment Stacks (formerly Azure Blueprints) or managed apps to protect their own resources
A deny assignment can be overridden by assigning the affected user the Owner role
questions.explanation: A deny assignment blocks specified actions no matter what role assignments would otherwise allow, and in practice they're usually created automatically by system features like Deployment Stacks (formerly Azure Blueprints) and managed applications to protect resources they manage, not hand-authored by administrators the way ordinary role assignments are. Owner access doesn't override a deny assignment — deny always takes precedence over any allow, including Owner.

questions.question: Which two of the following are benefits that DDoS Protection Standard adds on top of the Basic protection every Azure resource already gets automatically? (Choose two.)
options: Attack analytics, metrics, and alerting tuned to the specific protected resource
Protection against common network-layer flood attacks
Cost protection credits for resource scale-out charges incurred during a documented attack
Automatic enrollment with no configuration or cost
questions.explanation: DDoS Protection Standard (now DDoS Network Protection) adds resource-tuned attack analytics, metrics, and alerting, plus cost protection credits for scale-out charges incurred while defending against a documented attack — both are paid, Standard-only capabilities. Basic protection already covers common network-layer flood attacks for every resource at no cost, which is also why automatic, no-configuration, no-cost enrollment describes Basic, not something Standard adds on top of it.

questions.question: You need a KQL query against the SigninLogs table that returns, for the last 24 hours, the number of failed sign-ins per user and nothing else. Which two operators does the query require? (Choose two.)
options: where
summarize
join
union
questions.explanation: where narrows the rows to TimeGenerated > ago(24h) and ResultType != 0, and summarize count() by UserPrincipalName produces the per-user totals, which is the complete query. join and union both combine rows from more than one table or query, and only SigninLogs is involved here, so adding either would be unnecessary work at best.

questions.question: On resource group RG1 you open Access control (IAM) and run Check access for User1. User1 holds Reader on the subscription that contains RG1, Contributor directly on RG1, and Owner on VM1, which is a resource inside RG1. Which assignments does Check access list for User1 at the RG1 scope?
options: Owner on VM1 only, because Check access reports the single most privileged assignment held anywhere below the scope
Reader, Contributor, and Owner, because Check access always includes assignments made on child scopes below the one you opened
Contributor on RG1 only, because assignments inherited from the subscription are listed only on the subscription's own page
Reader inherited from the subscription, and Contributor on RG1
questions.explanation: Check access shows the assignments made at the scope and those inherited to it from parents such as the subscription. An assignment made on VM1 is at a child scope, so it is not listed when you look at RG1; open VM1's own IAM page to see it. Inherited assignments are included, which rules out Contributor alone, and the view lists assignments rather than picking the highest-privilege one.
questions.whyTested: Interpreting access assignments is an explicit skill: you must know which direction inheritance flows and which scope a view covers.

questions.question: Your team has a monthly $5,000 budget on subscription Sub1. When actual cost reaches 100 percent, a Logic App must run that deallocates all VMs tagged Environment=Dev. Which configuration meets the requirement?
options: An Azure Policy assignment with the Deny effect that blocks VM start operations once spend exceeds $5,000
A budget on Sub1 with a 100 percent actual-cost alert that calls an action group running the Logic App
An Azure Advisor cost recommendation configured to run the Logic App when spending passes the threshold
A budget on Sub1 configured with the option to automatically stop and deallocate resources once the amount is reached
questions.explanation: Budget alerts can call an action group, and an action group can start a Logic App, Automation runbook, or Function, so that is the supported way to react to a breach. A budget by itself only notifies; it has no setting that stops resources. Advisor produces recommendations and does not run actions on cost thresholds. Azure Policy evaluates resource properties and has no visibility of spending.

questions.question: You move VM1, along with its NIC and managed disk, from resource group rg-dev in West Europe to resource group rg-prod, which was created in North Europe. Both are in the same subscription. Which statement describes the result?
options: The VM stays in West Europe and its resource ID now references rg-prod
The VM is migrated to North Europe and keeps its original resource ID
The VM is stopped and redeployed in North Europe, and gets a new resource ID
The VM keeps its resource ID because only tags and locks are updated
questions.explanation: Moving a resource changes only its resource group or subscription. The location of the resource does not change, even if the destination group's own location differs, and the resource ID changes because it contains the resource group name. The VM remains operational during the move. Changing the region is a different operation, performed with Azure Resource Mover or Site Recovery.
questions.whyTested: Scenario questions on moving resources test whether you separate the management container from the physical region.

questions.question: Contoso is changing the Microsoft Entra directory that Sub1 trusts, from the old tenant to a new tenant. After the transfer, an application that runs on a VM in Sub1 with a system-assigned managed identity cannot read secrets, and administrators find that nobody has any Azure role on the subscription. What should you do?
options: Restore the role assignments by running a reprocess on the subscription in the old directory
Wait for role assignments to replicate from the old directory, which takes up to 24 hours
Re-create the role assignments, custom roles, and managed identities in the target directory
Assign the Global Administrator role in the new tenant, which restores all Azure role assignments
questions.explanation: When a subscription moves to a different directory, Azure role assignments and custom roles are permanently deleted rather than carried over, and managed identities must be re-created and re-authorized. Nothing replicates later, and the old directory no longer holds the subscription. Global Administrator is a Microsoft Entra role, and it does not recreate Azure RBAC assignments; elevating access is only a way to regain control to make new ones.

questions.question: A policy definition with the deployIfNotExists effect that enables diagnostic settings was assigned to a subscription last year. Forty existing storage accounts are reported non-compliant. Which two statements about fixing them are true? (Choose two.)
options: A remediation task can deploy the required settings to the existing non-compliant resources
The remediation task uses the managed identity of the policy assignment, which needs sufficient roles on the resources
The standard evaluation cycle remediates existing resources automatically within 24 hours
Changing the effect to Deny remediates existing resources without a task
questions.explanation: Remediation tasks are how deployIfNotExists and modify policies reach resources that existed before the policy, and the task deploys with the assignment's managed identity, so the identity must hold roles that allow the deployment. The evaluation cycle only recalculates compliance; it does not change existing resources. Deny blocks new or updated resources that violate a rule and never alters existing ones.
questions.whyTested: Remediation tasks and their managed-identity permissions are the usual cause of 'the policy is assigned but nothing happened' scenarios.

questions.question: A group with dynamic user membership assigns Microsoft 365 licenses. A newly created user is a member of the group, but the license shows an error and the user cannot be licensed. The tenant has enough licenses. What is the most likely cause?
options: The dynamic rule has not been re-evaluated for 24 hours
The user type is Guest, which blocks all licensing
The group is a Microsoft 365 group rather than a security group
The user has no usage location set
questions.explanation: A license cannot be assigned to a user until a usage location is set, because some services are not available in every country or region. Group-based licensing can use security groups and Microsoft 365 groups, so the group type is not the cause. Guest accounts can be licensed when the product allows it, and the question states that the user is already in the group, so the rule has evaluated.

questions.question: An engineer tries to move VM1 from RG1 to RG2 in the same subscription and the operation fails with an error saying the scope is locked. The VM is running and healthy. Which of the following should you check first?
options: Whether the VM size supports accelerated networking on its network interface
Whether a read-only lock exists on RG1, RG2, or the subscription
Whether the VM's network security group has an inbound rule allowing port 3389
Whether the VM's operating system disk uses a Premium SSD rather than a Standard SSD
questions.explanation: A move cannot proceed when a read-only lock exists on the source resource group, the target resource group, or the subscription, because the move writes to those scopes. Running VMs can be moved without being stopped, and NSG rules, disk SKU, and VM size features have no bearing on a scope-locked error.

questions.question: A budget with an alert at 100 percent of actual cost deallocates virtual machines automatically when the amount is reached.
questions.explanation: Budgets only generate notifications. To take an action such as deallocating VMs, you attach an action group that triggers automation, such as an Azure Automation runbook or a Logic App. Resources are not affected and spending is not stopped by the budget itself.

questions.question: Assigning a policy with the Deny effect to a subscription removes existing resources that violate the rule.
questions.explanation: Deny blocks new and updated resource requests that violate the rule. Resources that already exist are not deleted or changed; they are reported as non-compliant. Bringing them into compliance needs a remediation task for a deployIfNotExists or modify policy, or manual correction.

questions.question: Regulations require that data in storage account st1 is encrypted with a key that your security team controls and rotates, and that the key is held in Azure Key Vault. The account is a general-purpose v2 account that stores blobs and Azure files. Which configuration meets the requirement with the least effort?
options: Turn on Azure Disk Encryption for the storage account from the Encryption blade in the portal
Enable infrastructure encryption on st1 so that a second layer is applied with a separate key
Have the client application provide its own encryption key on each Blob Storage request
Enable customer-managed keys using a key in a vault with soft delete and purge protection
questions.explanation: Customer-managed keys are stored in Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM, rotated by the customer, and apply to Blob Storage and Azure Files. The vault must have soft delete and purge protection. Infrastructure encryption adds a second layer but uses Microsoft-managed keys. Customer-provided keys are sent per request and cover only Blob Storage, not files, and they are not held in Key Vault. Azure Disk Encryption is a feature for VM disks, not storage accounts.
questions.whyTested: Encryption options questions hinge on who holds the key, which services are covered, and whether the choice can be changed later.

questions.question: A storage account was created last month without infrastructure encryption. A new compliance rule demands double encryption for the data it stores. What must you do?
options: Enable customer-managed keys, which switches on infrastructure encryption as a second layer automatically
Create a new account with infrastructure encryption enabled and copy the data into it
Enable blob versioning, which applies a second encryption layer to every previous version of a blob
Enable infrastructure encryption on the existing account from the Encryption blade in the portal
questions.explanation: Infrastructure encryption has to be configured when the storage account is created and cannot be enabled afterward, so the data must move to a new account. Customer-managed keys change who controls the service-level key; they do not add a layer. Versioning is a data-protection feature unrelated to encryption layers.

questions.question: Several applications store customer files in one storage account, and the security team wants Customer A's blobs encrypted with a different key from Customer B's blobs, so that Customer A's key can be disabled independently. All files stay in the same account. Which feature should you use?
options: Immutable storage with a legal hold
Infrastructure encryption
Stored access policies
Encryption scopes
questions.explanation: An encryption scope applies a separate key, Microsoft-managed or customer-managed, to a container or an individual blob, creating a cryptographic boundary between the customers inside one account. Infrastructure encryption is account-wide and always uses Microsoft-managed keys. Stored access policies control SAS parameters, and legal holds block deletion and changes; neither separates keys.

questions.question: Cloud-only users on Microsoft Entra-joined Windows 11 devices must open an Azure Files SMB share with their Entra credentials. The devices cannot reach any domain controller and the company has no Active Directory. Which identity source should you enable on the storage account?
options: A shared access signature on the file share
Shared key authentication through the storage account key
Microsoft Entra Kerberos
On-premises Active Directory Domain Services
questions.explanation: Microsoft Entra Kerberos lets Entra ID issue Kerberos tickets for cloud-only or hybrid identities, with no need for connectivity to a domain controller. AD DS authentication requires an on-premises domain and clients that can reach its controllers. Account keys and SAS tokens are not identity-based, and they give broad or token-based access instead of per-user permissions.
questions.whyTested: The three Azure Files identity sources are distinguished by what the clients and the directory look like.

questions.question: Users of an Azure Files share report that a folder was deleted this morning. The share has daily share snapshots enabled. What is the fastest way to bring the folder back with the least effect on other files?
options: Open the latest snapshot taken before the deletion and restore the folder from it
Fail over the storage account to its secondary region and copy the folder back from there
Restore the whole storage account from a recovery point held in a Recovery Services vault
Undelete the file share from the list of soft-deleted shares in the storage account
questions.explanation: Share snapshots are point-in-time copies from which a folder or single file can be restored, so only the deleted content is affected. Soft delete applies when the whole file share is deleted, not a folder inside it. Account failover and a vault restore are heavy tools; the storage account has not failed, and nothing in the question says it is backed up to a vault.

questions.question: Which two statements about Azure Files soft delete and share snapshots are correct? (Choose two.)
options: A share can hold up to 200 snapshots
Share snapshots are full independent copies that are billed for the whole size of the share each time
Soft delete is enabled at the storage account level and covers every share in the account
Soft delete restores a single file that was deleted from within a share
questions.explanation: Soft delete settings apply per storage account to all shares, and a share supports up to 200 snapshots. Soft delete only protects a deleted share, not individual files inside it; snapshots are for that. Snapshots are incremental, so only changes since the previous snapshot are stored and billed.

questions.question: An administrator holds the Storage Blob Data Contributor role on container c1 only, with no other role on the subscription or storage account. When she signs in to Azure from Storage Explorer, she cannot see the account's containers. What should she do?
options: Ask for the Owner role on the storage account so that the data role takes effect in the explorer
Attach the container as a single resource and use the Microsoft Entra ID sign-in option
Switch to the storage account key for all future access from her desktop machine
Turn off the storage firewall so that the containers become visible to Storage Explorer
questions.explanation: After an Azure sign-in, Storage Explorer needs both management-plane and data-plane permissions to enumerate accounts. A person with only a data role can attach to the specific resource using Microsoft Entra ID instead. Owner on the account would grant management access but is far broader than needed. Turning off the firewall and using the account key remove protections and ignore least privilege.

questions.question: You are the Owner of storage account st1 and run azcopy login to copy files into a container. The command fails with an authorization error, although you can see the container in the portal. What is the cause?
options: AzCopy authenticates only with an account key and cannot use Microsoft Entra ID at all
AzCopy copies only to file shares and does not support blob containers as a destination
The Owner role must be assigned at the subscription scope before AzCopy can use it
Owner does not grant data access; you need a data role such as Storage Blob Data Contributor
questions.explanation: Control-plane roles such as Owner do not automatically grant data-plane access. With Microsoft Entra authorization, AzCopy needs an identity with a data role like Storage Blob Data Contributor or Storage Blob Data Owner. Alternatively use a SAS token. AzCopy supports Microsoft Entra sign-in, and it works with both blobs and files.

questions.question: You must keep an on-premises folder and a blob container synchronized, so that the container always reflects the folder, including files removed locally. Nothing in the container should ever flow back to the folder. Which command fits?
options: azcopy copy with --recursive, using the container as the source and the local folder as the destination
azcopy sync from the folder to the container with --delete-destination=true
azcopy login with the --tenant-id switch, which mirrors the folder into the container
azcopy sync with the container as the source and --delete-destination=true set on the command
questions.explanation: azcopy sync is one-way from the source to the destination, and --delete-destination removes destination files that no longer exist in the source, which gives an exact mirror of the folder. azcopy copy only copies and never removes anything at the destination. Reversing the source and destination would overwrite the local folder from the container. azcopy login only authenticates.

questions.question: The default access tier of a storage account can be set to Archive so that every new blob is stored in the cheapest tier.
questions.explanation: The account-level default access tier can only be Hot or Cool. Cold and Archive are set on individual blobs, either directly or through a lifecycle management rule, and an Archive blob is offline until it is rehydrated.

questions.question: A container with 3 million blobs was deleted by mistake yesterday. Blob versioning is enabled and blob soft delete is on, but container soft delete was never configured. Which statement is correct?
options: Blob soft delete recovers the container together with all of the blobs inside it
It cannot be recovered, because container soft delete is a separate setting that was off
Blob versioning restores the deleted container automatically from the previous version
Share snapshots recover the container, because they were enabled on the account
questions.explanation: Container soft delete and blob soft delete are configured separately. Blob soft delete protects deleted blobs and snapshots; it does not recover a deleted container, and versions inside a deleted container go with it. Share snapshots are an Azure Files feature and do not apply to blob containers.

questions.question: You have an ARM template and must deploy it to resource group RG1 in Complete mode. Before the deployment, the change approver must see exactly which existing resources would be deleted and which would be modified, without changing anything. What should you run?
options: az group export, which lists resources that are not in the template
az deployment group validate, which lists every resource it would delete
az bicep build, which compares the template with the live resources
az deployment group what-if with the template and Complete mode
questions.explanation: The what-if operation compares the template with the current state and reports Create, Modify, Delete, and other change types without deploying, and it respects the deployment mode. Validate only checks that the template and parameters are valid and the deployment could start; it does not list changes. Bicep build compiles Bicep to JSON and has no live comparison. Export generates a new template from live resources rather than a diff.
questions.whyTested: The exam asks you to deploy and interpret templates, and preview-before-deploy is the safe-change habit.

questions.question: Two years ago an engineer deployed a template that created RG-Web. Since then, administrators have changed several settings by hand in the portal. You need a template that reflects the resources exactly as they are today, and you also need to select only some of the resources. What should you do?
options: Run az bicep decompile against the original template file
Export the template from the resource group, selecting the required resources
Save the template from the deployment history of the original deployment
Deploy the original template in Incremental mode to read its current values
questions.explanation: Exporting from a resource group or resource produces a snapshot of the current state, includes manual changes, and lets you choose which resources to include. Saving from history returns the exact original template, so later manual changes are missing and you cannot pick a subset. Decompile only converts a template's syntax and has no knowledge of the live environment. A deployment changes the environment instead of reading it.

questions.question: A team has a library of ARM JSON templates and wants to adopt Bicep. You need to convert main.json to a Bicep file, accepting that the result may need manual cleanup. Which command should you use?
options: az bicep decompile --file main.json
az bicep build --file main.json
az deployment group export --name main
az bicep upgrade --file main.json
questions.explanation: az bicep decompile turns an ARM template into main.bicep, on a best-effort basis that can produce warnings to fix by hand. az bicep build goes the other way, compiling Bicep into JSON. Exporting a deployment retrieves a template and does not convert it, and az bicep upgrade updates the Bicep tooling to the latest version rather than converting any file.

questions.question: A template exported from a resource group is guaranteed to deploy unchanged in another subscription, because the export includes every parameter and all dependencies.
questions.explanation: Export is not guaranteed to succeed, and the generated template is a snapshot with mostly hard-coded values and often missing parameters, such as some password parameters. It usually needs cleanup before reuse. A template saved from deployment history is the cleaner, parameterized copy.

questions.question: A Bicep file contains the following resource declaration: resource st 'Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts@2023-05-01' = [for i in range(0, 3): { name: 'st${i}${uniqueString(resourceGroup().id)}', location: resourceGroup().location, sku: { name: 'Standard_LRS' }, kind: 'StorageV2' }]. What does a successful deployment of this file to RG1 create?
options: Three storage accounts, with names starting st0, st1, and st2
No storage accounts, because the loop only defines a variable
Three storage accounts, with names starting st1, st2, and st3
One storage account whose name contains a list of three suffixes
questions.explanation: range(0, 3) yields 0, 1, and 2, so the for expression creates three resources, and the index is part of each name. Names that start at 1 confuse range with a one-based count. A for expression around a resource declaration deploys one resource per element rather than a single one, and it is a resource loop, not a variable declaration.
questions.whyTested: Interpreting a snippet of Bicep or ARM JSON is a typical exam task; read loops, parameters, and dependencies before the properties.

questions.question: VM security policy requires that temporary disks and disk caches on new VMs are encrypted at rest and that data flows to storage encrypted, using customer-managed keys. No agent may be installed in the guest operating system. Which solution meets the requirement?
options: Server-side encryption with platform-managed keys, which is on by default
Azure Disk Encryption with BitLocker for Windows and DM-Crypt for Linux
Storage account infrastructure encryption on the account holding the disks
Encryption at host with a disk encryption set that uses customer-managed keys
questions.explanation: Encryption at host is performed by the host, covers temp disks and caches, encrypts data flowing to storage, supports customer-managed keys through a disk encryption set, and needs nothing inside the guest. Azure Disk Encryption works inside the guest with BitLocker or DM-Crypt, so it needs a VM extension, and it cannot be combined with encryption at host. Default platform-managed server-side encryption leaves the temp disk and cache uncovered. Infrastructure encryption is a storage account feature, and managed disks are not governed by it.

questions.question: You registered the EncryptionAtHost feature for the subscription. VM1 is running and has data on a managed disk. You must turn on encryption at host for VM1. What should you do?
options: Detach all data disks, enable the setting, and then reattach them
Deallocate VM1, enable encryption at host, and start VM1 again
Install the Azure Disk Encryption extension first, then enable the setting
Enable the setting while VM1 is running; it applies at the next hourly sync
questions.explanation: Encryption at host is enabled on an existing VM only when the VM is deallocated, then it takes effect when the VM starts again. It is not applied to a running VM, it cannot coexist with Azure Disk Encryption, and the data disks do not need to be detached.

questions.question: VM1, its virtual network, NIC, and managed disks are in West Europe. You must move them to North Europe. You want dependencies validated automatically, an option to test the move and discard it, and cleanup of the source after the move. Which service should you use?
options: Azure Backup with a restore to a new VM in the same vault region
The Move resources option to another resource group
A resource lock on VM1 followed by a subscription transfer
Azure Resource Mover
questions.explanation: Azure Resource Mover moves VMs and associated resources between regions, resolves dependencies, lets you commit or discard, and can delete the source afterward. Moving to another resource group or subscription changes only the container and leaves the region as it was. A restore into the same vault region does not relocate the workload, and locks and subscription transfers have nothing to do with regions.

questions.question: A container app processes web requests. It must scale out when an average of more than 50 concurrent HTTP requests per replica occur, and it must use no compute charges when it receives no traffic for a while. Which configuration meets the requirement?
options: A custom CPU rule set to 50 percent and a minimum of 2 replicas
A manual replica count of 50 on the container app environment
An HTTP scale rule with a concurrent request threshold of 50 and a minimum of 0 replicas
A TCP scale rule set to 50 connections and a minimum of 1 replica
questions.explanation: An HTTP scale rule scales on concurrent requests, and a minimum of zero lets the app scale to zero so that no usage charges accrue when idle. A TCP rule counts connections, not requests, and holding one replica always running keeps charges flowing. A CPU rule measures utilization and a minimum of two keeps instances warm all the time. A fixed manual count has no rule and never scales in.

questions.question: Users of a container app complain about a long delay on the first request after a quiet night. The app uses an HTTP scale rule and the default replica limits. You must remove the delay while keeping autoscaling. What should you change?
options: Increase the maximum number of replicas to 1,000
Move the app to Azure Container Instances
Replace the HTTP rule with a TCP rule
Set the minimum number of replicas to 1
questions.explanation: The default minimum is 0, so the app scales to zero when idle and the first request waits for a replica to start. Setting a minimum of 1 or higher keeps a replica running while the rules continue to add more. A higher maximum only changes the ceiling. A TCP rule scales to zero in the same way, and Container Instances has no autoscaling at all.

questions.question: A container runs a data conversion once, then exits with code 0 when finished. If the process fails, it should be retried automatically. You do not want the container group to be started again after a successful run, so that billing stops. Which restart policy should you set for the Azure Container Instances group?
options: Always, with an Automation runbook to stop it
OnFailure
Always
Never, because Never retries failures
questions.explanation: OnFailure restarts the containers only if the process ends with a nonzero exit code and lets a successful run stop for good, which ends billing. Always restarts even after a successful exit, which means the group runs forever. Never does not restart after a successful exit, but it is not designed as the retry-on-failure policy the question needs. A runbook to stop an Always group is unnecessary complexity.

questions.question: Operations wants the container images in a private Azure Container Registry rebuilt automatically whenever the Microsoft-published base image they use is updated, without a separate build server. Which should you use?
options: A GitHub Actions secret that stores the admin password
A webhook that deletes old tags nightly
Geo-replication on a Premium registry
ACR Tasks with a base image update trigger
questions.explanation: ACR Tasks builds images in the cloud and can be triggered by a base image update, a source commit, or a timer, so images are rebuilt and patched automatically. Geo-replication copies registries across regions and does not build anything. Storing the admin password is an authentication choice and not a trigger. Deleting old tags tidies the registry rather than rebuilding images.

questions.question: You must map the root domain contoso.com, not a subdomain, to an App Service app and verify domain ownership. Which DNS records should you create?
options: An MX record pointing to the app's default hostname and an NS record delegating the zone
Two CNAME records, one for contoso.com and one for www.contoso.com, both pointing to the app
An A record to the app's IP address and a TXT record named asuid with the verification ID
A CNAME record to the app's default hostname, plus a TXT record named asuid for verification
questions.explanation: A root (apex) domain maps with an A record to the app's IP address, and the asuid TXT record carries the custom domain verification ID that proves ownership and prevents subdomain takeover. A CNAME cannot be used at the root of a domain, and MX and NS records have nothing to do with directing web traffic to an app.

questions.question: An app at www.contoso.com and its sibling apps need HTTPS for *.contoso.com with a single wildcard certificate that already exists in Azure Key Vault. The apps run in a Standard App Service plan. Which approach should you use?
options: Import the certificate from Key Vault into App Service and create SNI SSL bindings
Upload the certificate as a public certificate and bind it to the domain
Scale the plan down to Shared so wildcard certificates are supported
Create a free App Service managed certificate for the wildcard name
questions.explanation: An existing private certificate, including a wildcard, can be imported from Key Vault and bound with SNI SSL. The free managed certificate does not support wildcards. Public certificates are not used to secure custom domains. Certificates require a Basic or higher plan, so the Shared tier would remove support instead of adding it.

questions.question: A web app runs in the Shared (D1) pricing tier of an App Service plan. You attempt to add a custom domain TLS binding with a purchased certificate and the option is unavailable. What should you do?
options: Create a deployment slot and bind the certificate there
Enable HTTPS Only in the app's settings
Scale the App Service plan up to the Basic tier or higher
Scale the plan out to two instances
questions.explanation: Certificates and TLS bindings need a Basic, Standard, Premium, or Isolated plan, so the plan must be scaled up. Adding instances does not change the tier, slots also depend on higher tiers, and HTTPS Only only redirects traffic and does not provide a certificate.

questions.question: Policy requires App Service app backups kept for 90 days that can be downloaded and archived by the security team. The app is in a Standard plan. Which approach meets the requirement?
options: Swap the production slot with a staging slot each week to act as a point-in-time backup
Configure custom backups to a storage account with long retention and download them
Rely on automatic backups, which keep 90 days of history when the plan is Standard
Configure automatic backups in the portal with a 90-day retention period
questions.explanation: Custom backups write to a storage account you choose, can be kept from 0 to 30 days or indefinitely, and can be downloaded as blobs. Automatic backups are fixed at 30 days of retention, cannot be configured, and cannot be downloaded. A slot swap exchanges content between slots and is not a backup.

questions.question: An engineer restores a backup over the production app during business hours and users see an outage while it runs. For future restores, what should you recommend to minimize downtime?
options: Scale the plan out before restoring so that other instances keep serving users
Restore only the content, because the configuration restore causes the outage
Stop the app, restore, then start it, because that is faster
Restore the backup to a deployment slot, validate it, and swap it into production
questions.explanation: App Service stops the target app while a restore is running. Restoring into a staging slot and swapping avoids any downtime for the production slot. Extra instances do not help because the target app is stopped as a whole, and stopping the app manually does not shorten the work.

questions.question: An App Service app must call an Azure SQL Managed Instance by its private IP address inside VNet1, and it must be reachable by clients only through the private network. Which two features should you configure? (Choose two.)
options: Regional virtual network integration for outbound calls
Hybrid connections for traffic to the managed instance
A private endpoint on the web app for inbound access
A service tag on the app's public hostname
questions.explanation: Virtual network integration provides the outbound path from the app into the VNet, and a private endpoint provides private inbound access, because integration alone never makes an app reachable privately. A service tag is a label used in network rules and does not grant connectivity. Hybrid connections relay traffic to specific endpoints, usually on-premises, and are not needed for a managed instance reachable inside the VNet.

questions.question: Enabling regional virtual network integration for an App Service app lets clients in the virtual network reach the app on a private IP address.
questions.explanation: Virtual network integration is for outbound calls from the app into the virtual network only. Private inbound access needs a private endpoint, or an App Service Environment for the entire environment.

questions.question: An app must accept requests only from the subnet that holds an Application Gateway, and all other callers must be rejected at the App Service front end. Which feature meets the requirement?
options: A deployment slot configured with the public IP address of the Application Gateway
An access restriction that allows the gateway subnet using a service endpoint
An NSG on the Application Gateway subnet that denies all outbound traffic to the internet
Virtual network integration into the Application Gateway subnet for the web app
questions.explanation: Access restrictions are inbound allow and deny rules enforced by the App Service front ends, and they can match a subnet through a service endpoint. An NSG on the gateway subnet does not govern what the app accepts, virtual network integration is outbound only, and a slot is a deployment construct rather than a filter.

questions.question: A production web app is in a Basic-tier App Service plan. The team wants traffic-driven autoscale rules and a staging slot with swap. What is the minimum change that enables both?
options: Move the app to the Free tier and enable preview features
Scale out the plan to three instances
Create a second App Service plan in Basic and use Traffic Manager
Scale up the plan to the Standard tier
questions.explanation: Autoscale and deployment slots begin at the Standard tier, while Basic supports only manual scale-out and has no slots. Adding instances changes the instance count and not the feature set. Free has fewer features than Basic. A second Basic plan with Traffic Manager adds cost and does not provide slots or autoscale.

questions.question: You create a Standard SKU public IP address and associate it with the NIC of VM1, which runs Windows. The VM's subnet and NIC have no network security group. An administrator cannot connect over RDP from the internet. What should you do?
options: Add a user-defined route with the next hop type Internet to the subnet
Create an NSG that allows inbound TCP 3389 and associate it with the NIC or subnet
Change the public IP address allocation from static to dynamic
Convert the public IP address to the Basic SKU
questions.explanation: Standard SKU public IPs are secure by default, so inbound traffic is blocked until an NSG explicitly allows it; with no NSG, nothing is allowed. Standard addresses are static only, and the Basic SKU was retired on September 30, 2025. A route to the Internet is already the default for outbound and does not open inbound ports.

questions.question: Several new subnets are created with the private subnet setting (defaultOutboundAccess disabled). VMs in them must reach the internet to download packages, and the team does not want a public IP on each VM. Which statement is correct, and what should you configure?
options: The VMs have no implicit outbound path, so attach a NAT gateway to the subnets
Outbound access works once an NSG rule allows outbound traffic to the Internet service tag
The VMs use the default outbound IP, so no change is required
Outbound access works only if each VM is given a Basic SKU public IP
questions.explanation: In a private subnet, Azure does not provide default outbound access, so VMs need an explicit method, and a NAT gateway shared by the subnet needs no public IP on the VMs. Relying on the default outbound IP is what the private subnet setting removes. The Basic SKU public IP is retired, and an NSG rule filters traffic but does not supply an outbound path.

questions.question: VM1 has an NSG on its NIC with an inbound rule allowing TCP 443 from the internet. Clients still cannot connect on 443. The Effective security rules page for the NIC also shows a rule from the subnet's NSG at priority 200 that denies inbound TCP 443 from the internet. Why does the NIC-level allow have no effect?
options: Allow rules in an NSG apply only to outbound traffic
A NIC NSG is ignored whenever a subnet NSG exists
Inbound traffic is evaluated by the subnet NSG first, and the deny stops it before the NIC NSG is reached
The NIC NSG is evaluated first, and its allow is overridden by the higher-priority subnet NSG
questions.explanation: For inbound traffic Azure applies the NSG on the subnet first, then the NSG on the NIC, and traffic must pass both. A deny in the subnet NSG ends the flow. The rules of the two NSGs are not merged by priority, a NIC NSG is never ignored, and allow rules apply to inbound traffic as well.

questions.question: You need a one-time test from VM1 to a SQL endpoint on TCP 1433 that reports whether the connection works, the latency, and the hop where it fails. You do not need continuous monitoring. Which Network Watcher capability should you use?
options: Connection troubleshoot
Packet capture
Connection monitor
Next hop
questions.explanation: Connection troubleshoot runs a one-time connectivity check from a VM to a destination and reports reachability, latency, and the hop that fails. Connection monitor is the continuous, alert-capable service. Packet capture records packets for deeper analysis but does not test the path, and next hop only returns the routing decision for a destination.

questions.question: You need to measure latency and packet loss every minute between web VMs in Azure and a database server in an on-premises datacenter that has Azure Arc enabled, and to be alerted when latency exceeds 100 ms. Which solution fits?
options: A Service Health alert for the region that hosts the datacenter
Packet capture running continuously on each of the web VMs
IP flow verify on each web VM, scheduled with an Automation runbook
Connection monitor with an alert on its latency metric
questions.explanation: Connection monitor provides continuous connectivity monitoring across Azure and hybrid endpoints, supports Arc-enabled servers as sources, measures latency and packet loss, and publishes metrics that can drive alert rules. IP flow verify only evaluates NSG rules for one flow. Packet capture is a short diagnostic recording. Service Health reports Microsoft platform incidents and says nothing about your path latency.

questions.question: You must start logging allowed and denied IP traffic for every workload in VNet1 and analyze it with Traffic Analytics. A colleague proposes creating NSG flow logs, but the portal will not allow it. What should you use instead?
options: Azure Advisor network recommendations
Virtual network flow logs enabled on VNet1
A packet capture on every VM in the virtual network
Activity log diagnostic settings on the subscription
questions.explanation: NSG flow logs are retiring on September 30, 2027 and can no longer be created, and virtual network flow logs are the replacement, enabled at the virtual network and covering its workloads. The activity log records control-plane operations, not traffic. Packet captures are short, per-VM diagnostics, and Advisor gives recommendations, not traffic logs.

questions.question: A Standard internal load balancer has a TCP health probe on port 443. The application on the backend VMs listens on port 8443 only, and the Health Probe Status metric shows 0 percent for all instances although the VMs are running. What should you change?
options: Increase the idle timeout of the load-balancing rule to ten minutes
Convert the Standard load balancer to the Basic SKU to relax probes
Add a public IP address to each of the backend VMs for probing
Change the health probe port to 8443 and align the backend port
questions.explanation: A probe fails when nothing listens on the probed port, so the load balancer marks every instance unhealthy and stops sending traffic. Aligning the probe and backend port with the port the application uses fixes it. The Basic SKU is not a fix, backend VMs do not need public IPs for probes, and the idle timeout affects established flows, not health checks.

questions.question: After a security review, an administrator adds an NSG rule at priority 4000 that denies all inbound traffic to the backend subnet, except 443 from the internet. Backend VMs for a Standard load balancer are now marked unhealthy even though the application is running and listening. What should you do?
options: Change the load-balancing rule to use floating IP on the backend port
Disable the health probe so that all backend instances stay in rotation
Add an inbound allow rule for the AzureLoadBalancer tag below priority 4000
Delete the default AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound rule from the NSG so it is recreated
questions.explanation: The default rule allowing the AzureLoadBalancer tag has priority 65001, so a custom deny at 4000 is processed first and blocks the probe source 168.63.129.16. An explicit allow with a lower priority number restores probing. Default rules cannot be deleted, floating IP does not affect probes, and disabling probes removes failover protection.

questions.question: The root domain contoso.com must resolve to a Standard public IP address, and the address might change if the resource is recreated. A CNAME cannot be used at the zone apex. Which Azure DNS configuration meets the requirement?
options: A CNAME record at the apex that targets the public IP's DNS label
An A record at the apex holding today's IP address, updated by hand
An NS record at the apex that points to the public IP address
An alias A record set at the apex that targets the public IP resource
questions.explanation: An alias record set references the Azure resource itself and follows its address changes automatically, and alias A records are allowed at the apex. A CNAME at the apex is not valid DNS, a hand-maintained A record breaks whenever the address changes, and NS records delegate a zone and cannot point to an IP address.

questions.question: A virtual network can be linked to several private DNS zones with auto registration enabled, so VMs register their records in all of them.
questions.explanation: A virtual network can be linked to only one private DNS zone with auto registration enabled. It can be linked to additional zones with registration disabled, where it can resolve records but does not register VMs automatically.

questions.question: A compliance team requires that all RDP and SSH sessions made through Azure Bastion are recorded for later review, and that the host has no public IP address. Which Bastion SKU supports this?
options: Standard
Developer
Basic
Premium
questions.explanation: Session recording and private-only deployment are Premium features. Standard adds native client, shareable links, and scaling, but not recording. Basic offers browser access with two instances, and Developer is a free shared offering for one VM at a time.

questions.question: Maintenance on all VMs in rg-app happens every Sunday from 02:00 to 04:00. Dozens of alert rules cover those VMs, and the on-call team must not be paged during that window, but the alerts should still be recorded. What should you create?
options: A Service Health alert that fires during the maintenance window
A new, empty action group that replaces the existing groups on every rule
An alert processing rule on rg-app that suppresses notifications weekly
A change to each alert rule so that it disables itself on Sunday nights
questions.explanation: An alert processing rule can suppress action groups for a scope on a schedule, so alerts still fire and are recorded but notifications are not sent, and one rule covers all alert rules. Disabling rules one by one is slow and means nothing fires or is recorded. Replacing action groups changes every rule's behavior permanently, and a Service Health alert tells you about Azure incidents, not your maintenance.

questions.question: Azure Backup alerts for all vaults in a subscription must trigger a single action group that opens an incident in the team's ITSM tool. Backup alerts do not offer an action group setting of their own. What should you configure?
options: An alert processing rule that adds the action group in this subscription
Classic Azure Backup alert email settings configured on each vault
A new metric alert rule created on each of the Recovery Services vaults
A budget alert on the subscription that notifies the same action group
questions.explanation: Alert processing rules can add an action group to alert types that have no action group setting of their own, such as Azure Backup alerts. A metric alert rule creates different alerts instead of routing the built-in ones, budget alerts track cost, and classic Azure Backup alerts were deprecated on March 31, 2026.

questions.question: An alert processing rule that suppresses notifications prevents the alert from being created, so the alert does not appear in the alerts list.
questions.explanation: Alert processing rules modify alerts as they fire. Suppression removes the action groups, so no notification is sent, but the alert still fires and is recorded and visible in the alerts view. Disabling the alert rule is what prevents alerts from being generated.

questions.question: Your company must protect Azure VMs, an Azure Files share, several Azure managed disks, and blobs in a storage account using Azure Backup in the same region. How many vault types do you need?
options: A Backup vault for VMs and files, and a Recovery Services vault for disks and blobs
A Recovery Services vault for VMs and files, and a Backup vault for disks and blobs
A single Backup vault that holds the backups for all four data sources
A single Recovery Services vault that holds the backups for all four data sources
questions.explanation: Recovery Services vaults hold VMs, Azure Files, and on-premises workloads, while Backup vaults hold newer data sources such as Azure Disks and Azure Blobs, so both types are needed. No single vault type covers all four, and the pairing that puts VMs and files in a Backup vault reverses which vault holds what.
questions.whyTested: Choosing the right vault for the data source is a core step in implementing backup.

questions.question: A backup administrator needs reports that show backup usage trends, job success, and storage consumed across 12 Recovery Services vaults in 3 subscriptions over the last 6 months. What must be configured to get them?
options: A Cost analysis view filtered to the vaults and grouped by resource group
An Azure Advisor recommendation enabled on each of the vaults with weekly emails
A resource lock on each vault, combined with an activity log alert on it
Diagnostic settings sending vault data to a Log Analytics workspace, then Backup reports
questions.explanation: Backup reports use Azure Monitor logs and workbooks, so each vault's diagnostic settings must send data to a Log Analytics workspace, which can collect from vaults across subscriptions. Advisor gives recommendations, Cost analysis reports spending rather than job success, and a lock protects the vault but does not collect data.

questions.question: VMs in the primary region failed over to the secondary region using Azure Site Recovery. The primary region is available again, and you want the VMs in the secondary region to start replicating back to the primary region so you can fail back later. What should you do?
options: Run a failover using the Custom recovery point
Reprotect the failed-over VMs
Delete the replicated items and enable replication again from scratch
Run a test failover on the failed-over VMs
questions.explanation: After a failover, reprotecting the VMs makes them replicate from the secondary region back toward the original region, which prepares a failback. A test failover creates a copy in an isolated network and starts nothing in reverse. Deleting items loses the replication relationship, and another failover is the wrong direction.

questions.question: An application tier is replicated with Azure Site Recovery. During a drill, the business says it can accept no more than a few seconds of data loss, even if recovery takes several minutes longer. Which recovery point should you choose when failing over?
options: Latest
Latest app-consistent
Latest processed
Custom
questions.explanation: Latest processes all data already sent to Site Recovery before creating the VM, so it gives the lowest recovery point objective at the price of more time. Latest processed fails over immediately using the newest processed point, giving the lowest recovery time but possibly more data loss. App-consistent points are taken less often, and Custom is a manual choice for one VM.

questions.question: Azure Site Recovery raises a health issue when no successful test failover has been run for a protected VM in the last 180 days.
questions.explanation: Site Recovery expects a successful test failover at least once every 180 days and raises a failover-readiness health issue if none exists or the latest one is older. Regular drills confirm that failover will work before an outage.

questions.question: You need one view that shows capacity, transactions, availability, and latency across 30 storage accounts in several resource groups, with the ability to drill into a hotspot. Which tool should you use?
options: VM insights in Azure Monitor
Azure Service Health
Network Insights in Azure Monitor
Storage insights in Azure Monitor
questions.explanation: Storage insights gives a unified at-scale view of Azure Storage accounts, including capacity, availability, transactions, and latency, with drill-down. Network Insights covers network resources, VM insights covers the performance and dependencies of VMs, and Service Health reports on Azure platform incidents.

questions.question: Which two statements about retention of Azure Monitor data are correct? (Choose two.)
options: The Activity log is kept for 90 days
Platform metrics are stored for 93 days with no configuration needed
Resource logs are collected automatically and kept for 93 days
Platform metrics are kept for 30 days unless a workspace is attached
questions.explanation: Platform metrics are collected automatically and stored for 93 days, and the Activity log is retained for 90 days. Resource logs are not collected until a diagnostic setting sends them to a destination, and metrics do not depend on a workspace for their standard retention.

questions.question: The following KQL query is run against a Log Analytics workspace: Heartbeat | where TimeGenerated > ago(15m) | summarize count() by Computer. What does it return?
options: Each computer that sent a heartbeat in the last 15 minutes, with its heartbeat count
A time chart showing heartbeat counts per computer in 15-minute bins
Every computer that has ever sent a heartbeat, with the total count since onboarding
Only the computers that missed every heartbeat in the last 15 minutes
questions.explanation: where filters the rows to the last 15 minutes, and summarize count() by Computer returns one row per computer with the number of heartbeats in that window. It does not look at older data, it cannot list computers with no rows because they do not appear in the table, and without bin() or render it does not produce time bins or a chart.

lessons.title: Identities & Access
lessons.summary: Users, groups, licensing, external users, and self-service password reset.
lessons.reading:
As an administrator, you'll create and manage the users and groups that make up an organization's identity. Security groups hold manually-managed membership, while dynamic groups automatically add or remove members based on rules matching attributes like department or job title — useful for keeping large, frequently-changing teams in sync without manual upkeep.

Licensing follows the same logic: rather than assigning a Microsoft 365 license to each person individually, group-based licensing lets you assign it once to a group, and every current and future member picks it up automatically.

For people outside your organization, like contractors or partners, external B2B users let them sign in with their own existing identity rather than you creating them a new internal account. And for your own users, self-service password reset removes the help desk from the equation entirely for the most common request there is.

User and group administration is mostly properties and membership rules. A user's profile holds job title, department, manager, and usage location, and the usage location must be set before any license can be assigned. Users can be created, invited, or deleted in bulk with a CSV template. Groups are either Security or Microsoft 365 groups, and membership is Assigned, Dynamic User, or Dynamic Device; dynamic membership needs Microsoft Entra ID P1. A group that will hold Microsoft Entra role assignments must be created as role-assignable, and that cannot be changed later.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to identity administration? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: A dynamic group is like an email distribution list that updates itself based on someone's job title, instead of someone manually adding and removing names every time staff changes. Group-based licensing is like a company handing out badges by department rather than issuing one individually to every new hire — join the department, get the badge automatically.
commonTraps: A dynamic group updates its membership automatically — a security group requires manual changes.
Group-based licensing still requires someone to be a group member; adding the license alone doesn't add them.
External B2B users authenticate with their own identity — you don't create them a normal internal account.
A license that fails to assign to a group member is most often a missing usage location, not a group type or tenant problem.
lessons.scenario: A hospital's radiology department grows from 8 to 30 staff over a year. Rather than manually adding each new hire to a group and assigning a license individually, an administrator sets up a dynamic group based on department, with a license attached to that group — every new radiology hire is automatically added and licensed the moment their account is created, with zero manual steps.
lessons.onTheJob: In a real tenant, dynamic groups and group-based licensing are what save an admin from a Friday afternoon of manually re-provisioning accounts every time a reorg happens, but they also mean a misconfigured rule can silently strip a whole department's license overnight with no one noticing until support tickets pile up. SSPR is usually the single biggest reduction in help-desk ticket volume an admin can point to when justifying their own workload to management, since password resets are consistently the most common ticket type any service desk handles. A dynamic group's membership rule also takes a few minutes to fully evaluate after a bulk attribute change, like an HR import updating hundreds of department fields at once, so an admin who expects instant membership updates right after a mass edit is usually just watching normal processing lag, not a broken rule.

lessons.title: Governance & Cost
lessons.summary: RBAC scope and roles, Azure Policy initiatives, and cost management.
lessons.reading:
As an administrator, RBAC role assignments are additive across scopes — if someone has Reader at a subscription and Contributor at one resource group within it, they effectively have Contributor there and Reader everywhere else in that subscription. The built-in roles worth knowing well: Owner can manage resources and grant access to others; Contributor can manage resources but cannot grant access; Reader is view-only; and User Access Administrator can manage who has access without touching the resources themselves.

Azure Policy enforces configuration rules, and when several related policies need to be assigned together, like a full tagging standard, they can be bundled into a single initiative rather than assigned one by one.

Day to day, this ties back to cost: budgets with alert thresholds, and Cost Analysis, let you see where spending is actually going, broken down by resource, tag, or service.

To interpret access, open Access control (IAM) at the scope in question: the Role assignments tab lists what applies there, including inherited assignments, and Check access shows what a chosen user, group, or identity holds. An assignment made on a child scope will not appear at the parent. For subscriptions, you can rename them, move them between management groups, transfer billing ownership, or change their directory; a directory change deletes role assignments and custom roles, so they must be re-created. Moving resources between resource groups or subscriptions locks both groups for writes while it runs, changes the resource ID, and leaves the region alone.

Cost control starts with budgets at a management group, subscription, or resource group scope. Alerts can use actual or forecasted cost, and an action group can start automation, because the budget itself never stops anything. Azure Policy is evaluated when an assignment changes, when resources are created or updated, and once every 24 hours; existing resources that fail a deployIfNotExists or modify policy are corrected with a remediation task that runs under the assignment's managed identity, and an exemption removes a resource or scope from a policy.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to RBAC in practice? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of RBAC assignments like keys handed out at different levels of a building. A master key at the building level, plus an extra key to one specific supply closet, means you effectively have full access to that closet even if your master key alone wouldn't normally reach it — the more specific, more permissive key wins in that one room.
commonTraps: Contributor can manage all resources but CANNOT assign roles to others — only Owner and User Access Administrator can.
RBAC is additive: the most permissive assignment across all applicable scopes wins, not the most restrictive.
An initiative is a bundle of policies assigned together — it isn't a single rule by itself.
Check access and Role assignments show assignments at the scope and inherited from parents, never from child scopes.
A budget never stops spending; to react to a breach an action group must start automation.
Moving a resource changes its resource group or subscription and its resource ID, not its region.
lessons.scenario: A company wants a lead engineer to manage all resources in a specific resource group AND decide which teammates can access it, without giving them company-wide Owner rights. Assigning Owner at just that one resource group achieves this — Owner both manages resources and grants access, but scoped to that resource group alone, leaving the rest of the subscription untouched.
lessons.onTheJob: RBAC assignments in a real subscription accumulate the way old keys accumulate in a junk drawer — a 'temporary' Contributor grant from a project two years ago that nobody remembers to revoke, discovered only during a security audit or an incident investigation. Budgets and cost alerts matter less as an exam fact and more as the thing that actually gets an admin paged when a forgotten VM Scale Set runs all weekend, since nobody reviews the bill in real time otherwise.

lessons.title: Storage Management
lessons.summary: Access keys and SAS, firewalls, lifecycle policies, and protecting blob data.
lessons.reading:
Managing storage at the administrator level means configuring the account itself, not just knowing what it holds. General-purpose v2 is the standard account type and uses Standard (HDD-backed) performance, while Premium (SSD-backed) performance comes from premium account types (block blob, file share, page blob), chosen by how demanding the workload is.

For access, a storage account access key grants full, unrestricted control over the whole account — risky to hand out. A Shared Access Signature (SAS) instead grants limited, time-boxed access to specific resources, without ever exposing that key. A storage firewall adds a network-level layer on top, restricting access to specific VNets or IP ranges regardless of what credentials someone has.

Ongoing management includes lifecycle policies, which automatically move aging blobs to cheaper tiers or delete them outright, and choosing the right protection for accidental changes: blob versioning keeps every prior version automatically, while soft delete keeps deleted (and, with versioning off, overwritten) data recoverable for a retention window.

Storage encryption is always on and uses Microsoft-managed keys by default. To control the key yourself, use a customer-managed key held in Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM, which needs soft delete and purge protection; encryption scopes apply a different key to a container or blob, and infrastructure encryption adds a second layer but has to be chosen when the account is created. Azure Files can authenticate users over SMB with Kerberos against on-premises AD DS, Microsoft Entra Domain Services, or Microsoft Entra Kerberos, with Azure roles for share-level access and Windows ACLs below that. Share snapshots recover files and folders, while soft delete recovers a deleted share.

For moving data, Azure Storage Explorer is a desktop app for browsing and managing storage, and AzCopy is the command-line tool for copying and one-way syncing. Both authorize with Microsoft Entra ID or a SAS; owning the account does not give data access, so an identity needs a data role such as Storage Blob Data Contributor. The default access tier of an account is Hot or Cool, and Cold or Archive are set per blob or by a lifecycle rule.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to storage account administration? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: An access key is like a master key to an entire building — powerful, and dangerous to hand out casually. A SAS is like a visitor badge that only opens one door, only works for a limited window of time, and can be revoked without changing the master key at all.
commonTraps: An access key grants full account access — always prefer a scoped, time-limited SAS when sharing access externally.
Soft delete is about retention windows; versioning is the fuller answer for keeping every prior version of an overwritten blob.
A storage firewall is a network-level control — separate from, and in addition to, who has valid credentials.
Infrastructure encryption cannot be turned on after the storage account exists.
Owner on a storage account does not give data access to AzCopy or Storage Explorer; a data role or a SAS is needed.
Container soft delete and blob soft delete are separate settings, and soft delete for blobs does not protect Azure file shares.
lessons.scenario: A marketing agency needs to let an external contractor upload files to one specific container for 48 hours, then lose access automatically. Issuing a SAS scoped to that container, valid for 48 hours, does exactly this — no account key changes hands, and access expires on its own without anyone having to remember to revoke it.
lessons.onTheJob: SAS tokens are the day-to-day answer to the constant stream of 'can you just send me the storage key' requests from a vendor or contractor, and part of an admin's actual job is pushing back on that request every time instead of taking the shortcut, because a leaked account key means rotating credentials across every application that uses it. Lifecycle management policies are also one of the few cost levers that quietly pay for themselves for years once configured, which is exactly why they're the first thing to check when a storage bill looks unexpectedly high.

lessons.title: Virtual Machines & Compute
lessons.summary: VM sizing, managed disks, availability options, extensions, and resizing.
lessons.reading:
Choosing a VM means balancing size against workload: the size determines CPU, memory, and disk throughput, while the series, B, D, F, and others, is tuned for different needs — B-series is cheap and burstable, D-series is general purpose, F-series is compute-optimized. Underneath, managed disks come in four performance tiers, Standard HDD, Standard SSD, Premium SSD, and Ultra Disk, from cheapest to fastest.

For resilience, availability sets spread VMs across separate hardware within one datacenter, availability zones go further by using physically separate datacenters within a region, and VM Scale Sets automatically add or remove instances based on demand or a schedule.

Day-to-day operations include extensions, small agents that run post-deployment tasks like the Custom Script Extension, and resizing, which may require deallocating a running VM first if the target size isn't available on its current hardware.

Encryption at host extends server-side disk encryption to temporary disks and caches and encrypts data as it flows to storage, with no agent in the guest. It needs the EncryptionAtHost feature registered on the subscription, and an existing VM must be deallocated to turn it on. Moving a VM is two different tasks: a move to another resource group or subscription keeps the region and changes the resource ID, while a move to another region uses Azure Resource Mover, which validates dependencies and lets you commit or discard the move.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to VM sizing and resilience? See the everyday analogy
