lessons.fundamentals: Choosing a VM series is like choosing a vehicle for a job: a compact car (B-series) is cheap and fine for occasional errands, a pickup truck (D-series) handles general hauling, and a race car (F-series) is built for one specific kind of performance. Availability sets and zones are about not parking every vehicle in the same garage — spreading them out so one disaster doesn't take out the whole fleet at once.
commonTraps: A B-series VM is burstable and cheap, but throttles under sustained heavy CPU load — the wrong pick for a constantly busy server.
Resizing a running VM may require deallocating it first if the new size isn't available on its current hardware.
Ultra Disk lets you configure performance independently of size — the highest, most consistent tier available.
Encryption at host covers temp disks and caches and cannot be combined with Azure Disk Encryption.
lessons.scenario: A team runs a database VM that needs consistent, high IOPS around the clock, plus a batch of short-lived web front-ends that spike unpredictably during business hours. The database gets a larger D-series or F-series VM with a Premium SSD or Ultra Disk. The front-ends go into a VM Scale Set, which adds instances automatically during the spikes and scales back down overnight, rather than running a fixed, oversized fleet all day.
lessons.onTheJob: Picking a VM series in practice is often less about the workload spec sheet and more about what the team is already comfortable operating and who's on call for it — a burstable B-series VM under sustained production load is a classic middle-of-the-night page that traces back to a sizing decision nobody revisited after the workload grew. The requirement to deallocate before resizing or changing a disk tier is also the kind of detail that turns a routine maintenance window into an unplanned outage when a change gets scheduled without accounting for the downtime it actually requires. A Scale Set's autoscale rule is its own common source of a 3am page: a threshold tuned during initial testing against a quiet dataset can flap instances in and out under real production traffic, so the rule itself needs revisiting as usage patterns mature rather than being set once and forgotten.

lessons.title: App Hosting & Infrastructure as Code
lessons.summary: App Service plans, deployment slots, container options, and ARM/Bicep.
lessons.reading:
An App Service plan defines the compute tier and region for one or more web apps — scaling up changes the plan's size, scaling out adds more instances of it. Deployment slots give you a separate, swappable environment, like staging, to validate a new version before swapping it into production with minimal downtime.

For containers, the right choice depends on how much orchestration you need: Container Instances run a single container with none, Container Apps add serverless, HTTP-based autoscaling without managing a cluster, and AKS gives full Kubernetes control when you need it.

For repeatable deployments, ARM templates are Azure's native JSON Infrastructure as Code format, and Bicep is a newer, more concise language that compiles down to the same ARM JSON — functionally identical, just easier to write and read.

Infrastructure as code questions ask you to read, change, and deploy templates. An ARM template has parameters, variables, resources, and outputs; a Bicep file declares param, var, resource, module, and output items, and a reference to another resource creates a dependency. The what-if operation previews creates, modifications, and deletions before a deployment, which matters most in Complete mode. A deployment can be exported from the resource group as a snapshot of current state, or saved from history as the exact original template, and az bicep decompile converts ARM JSON into Bicep.

Containers split by need. Container Apps runs revisions and replicas that scale on HTTP, TCP, or custom rules and can scale to zero, while Container Instances runs container groups with a restart policy and no autoscale. Azure Container Registry holds the images, authenticates with Microsoft Entra identities, and can rebuild them with ACR Tasks. For App Service, map a root domain with an A record and a subdomain with a CNAME, add a TXT record with the verification ID, and secure the domain with a managed, imported, or uploaded certificate. Backups are automatic and hourly on Basic and higher plans, or custom to a storage account; networking splits into access restrictions and private endpoints for inbound, and virtual network integration for outbound.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to app hosting and IaC? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: A deployment slot is like a dress rehearsal before opening night — you run the full show in a separate space first, then swap it into the real venue once it's ready, instead of testing changes directly in front of the audience. Infrastructure as Code is like a recipe instead of a memory of how you cooked something once: written down, repeatable, and shareable, rather than trusting yourself to click through the same steps identically every time.
commonTraps: Scaling up changes the App Service plan's tier or size; scaling out adds more instances of the same tier.
Container Instances run a single container with no orchestration — that's what AKS is for.
Bicep is not a different deployment mechanism — it compiles down to the same ARM JSON underneath.
Export from a resource group is a snapshot that needs cleanup, and Save from history is the exact original template.
A CNAME cannot be used at the root of a domain; map the root with an A record.
Virtual network integration is for outbound traffic only; private inbound access needs a private endpoint.
lessons.scenario: A team wants to test a major update to their web app without any risk to the live site, then cut over quickly once it checks out. They deploy the new version to a staging slot, run their validation there against production-like settings, and swap it into the production slot in seconds once satisfied — with the previous version now sitting in the staging slot in case a fast rollback is ever needed.
lessons.onTheJob: Deployment slots are the thing that actually lets a team sleep at night before a release, since a bad swap can be reversed in seconds by swapping back — teams that skip slots and deploy straight to production are usually the ones with the worst on-call stories. Bicep versus raw ARM JSON is mostly a team-preference and readability argument in practice, not a functional one, so a manager standardizing on one over the other is usually optimizing for how fast a new hire can read the templates, not for what Azure actually does with them.

lessons.title: Networking
lessons.summary: NSG rule priority, VNet peering, load balancing, and secure access.
lessons.reading:
As an administrator, you size VNets and subnets with real CIDR math in mind — Azure reserves 5 addresses in every subnet regardless of its size. Network Security Groups filter traffic with rules that have a priority; the lowest priority number is evaluated first and wins if rules conflict.

VNet peering connects two VNets directly, even across regions, but it isn't transitive — peering A to B and B to C doesn't let A and C talk without their own direct peering. For distributing traffic, Azure Load Balancer works at layer 4 by IP and port alone, while Application Gateway works at layer 7 and can route by URL path and terminate SSL.

For secure remote access, Azure Bastion provides RDP or SSH through the portal without exposing a VM's public IP, and Network Watcher's tools, like IP flow verify, help diagnose exactly where a connectivity problem is coming from.

Public IP addresses now mean the Standard SKU: static, zone-capable, and closed to inbound traffic until a network security group allows it. Basic public IPs and Basic Load Balancer were retired on September 30, 2025, and virtual networks created with recent API versions default to private subnets, so VMs there need an explicit outbound method such as a NAT gateway. To see why a flow is blocked, view the effective security rules of the NIC: inbound traffic meets the subnet NSG first, then the NIC NSG, and both must allow it.

The Network Watcher toolkit answers specific questions: IP flow verify names the rule that decides a flow, next hop shows the route, connection troubleshoot tests a path, and packet capture records traffic. Flow logging is moving from NSG flow logs, retiring September 30, 2027, to virtual network flow logs. For load balancers, a failing health probe means the wrong port, an unhealthy backend, or an NSG that blocks the AzureLoadBalancer tag. Azure DNS alias records point an apex name at a resource, and Azure Bastion comes in Developer, Basic, Standard, and Premium SKUs.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to network administration? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: An NSG rule priority works like a bouncer checking a list in order — the first matching rule they hit decides the outcome, and they stop checking after that, even if a later rule on the list would have said something different. VNet peering not being transitive is like two people each having a direct phone line to a shared friend, but no line to each other — being friends with the same person doesn't connect you to each other automatically.
commonTraps: A lower NSG rule priority number wins — 100 is evaluated before 200, regardless of allow or deny.
VNet peering is not transitive: A-B and B-C peered does not mean A and C can talk.
Application Gateway can route by URL path; Azure Load Balancer only sees IP and port, not HTTP content.
A Standard public IP is closed to inbound traffic until an NSG allows it.
NSG flow logs are retiring; use virtual network flow logs for anything new.
Inbound traffic goes through the subnet NSG first and then the NIC NSG, and it must be allowed by both.
lessons.scenario: An administrator needs to block a specific IP range from reaching a subnet while still allowing normal traffic through. They add a Deny rule at a lower priority number than the general Allow rule, so it's evaluated first — since NSGs stop at the first matching rule, that blocked range never reaches the broader allow rule beneath it.
lessons.onTheJob: NSG rule priority is one of the most common sources of a self-inflicted outage page — someone adds a new rule without checking what priority number is already in use, and a lower-priority rule silently wins before the new one is ever evaluated. Change control around networking tends to be the strictest in a real Azure environment, precisely because a subnet or peering misconfiguration can quietly take down connectivity for teams who had nothing to do with the change that caused it.

lessons.title: Monitoring & Recovery
lessons.summary: Metrics vs. logs, alerts and action groups, backup, and Site Recovery.
lessons.reading:
Azure Monitor is the umbrella for keeping an eye on your own resources: metrics are lightweight numerical time-series data, like CPU percentage, while logs are detailed, queryable records stored in a Log Analytics workspace and searched with KQL. An alert rule defines the trigger condition, and a separate action group defines what happens next, like an email or an automated runbook.

For disaster protection, the distinction that matters most is scope: Azure Backup, through a Recovery Services vault, restores a VM or file to an earlier point in time, protecting against data loss or corruption. Azure Site Recovery goes further, replicating an entire workload to a secondary region so it can fail over and keep running if the primary region goes down entirely.

Alert processing rules sit between a fired alert and its notifications: they can add an action group to alerts that have none, including Azure Backup alerts, or suppress notifications for a scope on a schedule, such as a maintenance window, while the alert itself still fires and is recorded. For connectivity, Connection monitor tests TCP, ICMP, and HTTP paths continuously across Azure and hybrid endpoints and reports latency and packet loss. Insights are curated Azure Monitor dashboards; Storage insights covers capacity, transactions, and latency across many accounts, and Network Insights shows topology, health, and metrics.

Azure Backup uses two vault types. A Recovery Services vault protects VMs, SQL Server and SAP HANA in VMs, Azure Files, and on-premises machines; a Backup vault protects Azure Disks, Azure Blobs, and PostgreSQL. Backup alerts run through Azure Monitor, and Backup reports are built on Log Analytics, so vault diagnostic settings must send data to a workspace. In Site Recovery, you choose a recovery point at failover (Latest for the least data loss, Latest processed for the fastest recovery), reprotect the VMs afterward to replicate back, and run a test failover at least every 180 days.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to monitoring and disaster recovery? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Backup is like keeping dated copies of an important document, so you can go back to yesterday's version if today's got corrupted. Site Recovery is more like having a fully-equipped second office ready to open immediately if your main building becomes unusable — not just a copy of your files, but a whole working replacement environment standing by.
commonTraps: Metrics are lightweight numerical data; use Logs and KQL for detailed, queryable event investigation.
An alert rule is the trigger condition — the action group is the separate response it sets off.
Backup restores a point-in-time copy; Site Recovery fails over a whole workload to another region.
Suppressing notifications with an alert processing rule does not stop the alert from firing or being recorded.
Disks and blobs are protected by a Backup vault; VMs and Azure Files are protected by a Recovery Services vault.
Platform metrics are kept for 93 days; the Activity log for 90 days; resource logs are not collected until a diagnostic setting exists.
lessons.scenario: A company's production database VM gets corrupted by a bad script at 2pm. They restore it from that morning's backup in the Recovery Services vault, losing a few hours of data but recovering quickly. Separately, that same company has Site Recovery configured for their whole application tier, so if their primary region ever goes down entirely, the application can fail over and keep serving customers from a secondary region within minutes.
lessons.onTheJob: In practice, alert rules that aren't tied to a real action group are the alerts everyone learns to ignore — a mailbox full of unread threshold emails is a bigger operational risk than having no monitoring at all, since it trains the team to tune out the one alert that actually mattered. Backup and Site Recovery configurations also tend to only get tested for real during an actual incident, which is exactly the wrong time to discover a Recovery Services vault was never actually backing up the resource everyone assumed it was. This same Azure Monitor metrics vs. logs distinction is exactly what AZ-305 architects have to choose between when designing a monitoring solution, deciding whether a workload's health signal belongs in a lightweight metric alert or a deeper Log Analytics query.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day strategy
points: Plan on roughly 100 minutes of exam time for about 40-60 questions, which works out to around 2 minutes each on average. Budget more time for multi-part scenario questions and less for straight recall, rather than pacing every question identically.
Real scoring isn't a flat percentage of questions right (some count for more than others) — treat 75%+ as a safe buffer to aim for, not an exact threshold to just clear.

Flag anything you're unsure of and move on rather than stalling — a question later in the exam can sometimes jog a detail you needed earlier, and stalling on one question risks leaving others unanswered.
On multi-select ('choose N') questions, eliminate the options you're confident are wrong first; guessing among 2 plausible answers beats guessing among 4.
Your first read of a question is usually right — change an answer only when you find a specific detail you missed, not from general second-guessing.

cheatSheet.heading: Identity & RBAC
points: Owner = full access plus can assign roles to others. Contributor = full access but cannot assign roles. Reader = view only. User Access Administrator = can manage user access without touching the resources themselves.
RBAC scope inherits downward: Management Group → Subscription → Resource Group → Resource; a role assigned higher up applies to everything below it.
RBAC permissions are additive across assignments, but an explicit deny assignment always overrides any allow.

Azure Policy controls WHAT configurations are allowed/compliant (an effect like deny/audit); RBAC controls WHO can perform WHICH actions — they answer different questions and are not substitutes for each other.
On Access control (IAM), Role assignments and Check access list what applies at that scope plus what is inherited from parent scopes. Assignments made at child scopes are not shown.
A user needs a usage location before a license can be assigned. Dynamic group membership needs Microsoft Entra ID P1.

cheatSheet.heading: Storage accounts & redundancy
points: LRS = 3 sync copies in one datacenter (cheapest, least durable). ZRS = sync copies across zones in one region. GRS = async copy to a paired region (not readable). RA-GRS = same as GRS but the secondary is readable.
GZRS/RA-GZRS combine zone redundancy in the primary region with geo-replication to the paired region — the highest-durability options.
Blob access tiers (Hot/Cool/Cold/Archive) trade storage cost against access cost and retrieval latency; Archive requires rehydration before a blob can be read.
Only general-purpose v2 (StorageV2) accounts support the full feature set (all access tiers, lifecycle management); legacy v1 accounts don't.

All storage data is encrypted at rest and cannot be turned off. Customer-managed keys live in Key Vault (soft delete and purge protection required); infrastructure encryption (double encryption) can only be chosen when the account is created.

Azure Files identity-based access uses Kerberos with AD DS, Microsoft Entra Domain Services, or Microsoft Entra Kerberos (one per account). Share snapshots (up to 200 per share) protect files; soft delete (7 days by default) protects a deleted share.

AzCopy needs a data role (for example Storage Blob Data Contributor) or a SAS, because Owner does not grant data access. azcopy sync is one-way. Storage Mover is the managed service for large migrations.

cheatSheet.heading: Compute essentials
points: Availability Set = protects against a single hardware/rack failure inside ONE datacenter (fault domains + update domains) — no protection if that datacenter goes down.
Availability Zone = physically separate datacenters within a region, each with independent power/cooling/network — protects against a datacenter-level outage.
A VM scale set can span multiple availability zones and automatically scales identical VM instances in/out based on load or a schedule.

Managed disks: Standard HDD/SSD for dev/test or infrequent access, Premium SSD for production workloads needing consistent low latency, Ultra Disk for the highest IOPS/throughput, latency-sensitive workloads (e.g. SAP HANA, SQL).
Azure Hybrid Benefit lets you apply existing on-premises Windows Server or SQL Server licenses to Azure VMs to cut compute cost.

Encryption at host encrypts temp disks and caches, needs the feature registered and the VM deallocated, and cannot be combined with Azure Disk Encryption. Moving a VM across resource groups or subscriptions never changes its region; use Resource Mover for a region move.

Export from a resource group is a snapshot that needs cleanup, while Save from history is the exact original template. az bicep decompile converts ARM JSON to Bicep, and what-if previews a deployment.

App Service: backups need Basic or higher, with hourly automatic backups kept 30 days; autoscale and slots start at Standard; certificates need Basic or higher, and the free managed certificate has no wildcard support. VNet integration is outbound only, and a private endpoint is for inbound.
Container Apps scales to zero by default (minimum replicas 0) with HTTP, TCP, or custom rules. Container Instances has no autoscale, and its restart policy is Always by default.

cheatSheet.heading: Networking basics
points: NSG rules are evaluated by priority number, lowest first, and processing stops at the first match — default rules can be overridden by a higher-priority custom rule but never deleted.
An NSG can be attached to a subnet, a NIC, or both; if both are in play, traffic must be allowed by BOTH to get through.
VNet peering is non-transitive: if VNet A peers with B, and B peers with C, A cannot reach C through B without its own direct peering (or a hub with routing).

Private Endpoint = a private IP address for a PaaS service inside your VNet (traffic never leaves the Microsoft backbone). Service Endpoint = an optimized route to the service over the Azure backbone, but the service still has a public IP.

Load Balancer = regional Layer 4 (TCP/UDP). Application Gateway = regional Layer 7 (HTTP, URL routing, WAF). Traffic Manager = global DNS-based routing (protocol-agnostic). Front Door = global Layer 7 with WAF + CDN.

Standard public IPs are static and closed to inbound traffic until an NSG allows it; Basic public IPs and Basic Load Balancer were retired on September 30, 2025. NSG flow logs retire on September 30, 2027, so use virtual network flow logs.

Inbound traffic is checked by the subnet NSG first and then the NIC NSG (reverse for outbound). Effective security rules shows the combined result. A failing load balancer probe usually means the wrong port or an NSG blocking the AzureLoadBalancer tag.
Bastion SKUs: Developer (free, shared, one VM), Basic, Standard (native client, scaling), Premium (session recording, private-only). The AzureBastionSubnet must be /26 or larger.

cheatSheet.heading: Monitoring & backup/DR
points: Azure Monitor Metrics = lightweight numerical time-series data. Azure Monitor Logs = detailed queryable records in a Log Analytics workspace, searched with KQL.
An alert rule defines the trigger condition; a separate action group defines the response (email, SMS, webhook, runbook).

Azure Backup (Recovery Services vault) restores a VM/file to an earlier point in time. Azure Site Recovery replicates and fails over a whole workload to a secondary region — different scope, don't mix them up.

A backup policy sets the schedule and retention; for Azure VM backups, changing the retention of an existing category applies to already-taken recovery points as well as new ones (so shortening it can expire older points), while a newly added retention category applies only going forward.

Recovery Services vaults protect VMs, SQL and SAP HANA in VMs, Azure Files, and on-premises servers. Backup vaults protect Azure Disks, Azure Blobs, and PostgreSQL. Backup alerts are Azure Monitor alerts; backup reports need diagnostic settings to a Log Analytics workspace.

Alert processing rules add or suppress action groups for a scope and schedule, but suppressed alerts still fire. Connection monitor is the continuous check; Connection troubleshoot is the one-time test.

Platform metrics are kept 93 days and the Activity log 90 days. In Site Recovery, Latest gives the lowest data loss, Latest processed the lowest recovery time, and a test failover should be run at least every 180 days.

cheatSheet.heading: Governance (locks, policy, tags)
points: Resource lock CanNotDelete allows read/modify but blocks deletion. ReadOnly blocks modify AND delete (locks down the resource entirely, which can break scaling or extensions unexpectedly).

Locks apply to everything below their scope in the hierarchy and can only be removed by someone with the right permission (Microsoft.Authorization/locks/delete), even an Owner needs that explicit permission.
Azure Policy initiatives group multiple related policy definitions together; policy effects include Deny, Audit, Append, Modify, and DeployIfNotExists.
Tags are not automatically inherited by child resources — a policy with the Modify or Append effect is needed to enforce/propagate tags automatically.

A budget notifies on actual or forecasted cost but never stops resources; use an action group to run automation. Policy remediation tasks fix existing resources for deployIfNotExists and modify policies, and use the assignment's managed identity.

Moving resources locks the source and target groups for writes (up to four hours) and changes the resource ID, not the region. A read-only lock blocks a move. Changing a subscription's directory deletes its role assignments and custom roles.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day reminders
points: This exam is heavily scenario-based and tests practical, portal-style tasks. Per Microsoft Learn it can include interactive components, so expect more than just recall.
Watch for wording like "least administrative effort" or "most cost-effective" — pick the best fit among several technically-correct-sounding options.
If a question says the connection "doesn't use the public internet," that's ExpressRoute, not a VPN Gateway.
"Protect from a single datacenter failure" points to Availability Zones; "protect from a single rack/host failure" points to Availability Sets.

cliChallenges.prompt: Create a new resource group named 'rg-web-prod' in the 'eastus' region.
cliChallenges.explanation: az group create is the base command; --name and --location are both required — a resource group must live in a region even though it's just a management container.

cliChallenges.prompt: Create a new Linux VM named 'vm-app01' in resource group 'rg-web-prod', using the 'Ubuntu2204' image.
cliChallenges.command: az vm create --resource-group rg-web-prod --name vm-app01 --image Ubuntu2204
cliChallenges.explanation: az vm create needs --resource-group, --name, and --image at minimum — other settings such as the admin credentials have defaults or can be supplied with extra flags.

cliChallenges.prompt: Deallocate (stop and release compute charges for) the VM 'vm-app01' in resource group 'rg-web-prod'.
cliChallenges.explanation: az vm stop only stops the OS — you're still billed for the compute. az vm deallocate actually releases the underlying hardware allocation, which is what stops compute charges (storage charges continue either way).

cliChallenges.prompt: Start the (previously stopped) VM 'vm-app01' in resource group 'rg-web-prod'.
cliChallenges.explanation: az vm start is the mirror of az vm deallocate — note a restarted VM can get a new public IP unless you've reserved a static one.

cliChallenges.prompt: Enable auto-shutdown at 7:00 PM (19:00) for VM 'vm-app01' in resource group 'rg-web-prod'.
cliChallenges.explanation: az vm auto-shutdown --time takes 24-hour HHmm format (no colon). This is a common cost-control ask for dev/test VMs on the exam.

cliChallenges.prompt: Create a general-purpose v2 storage account named 'stprodwebdata01' in resource group 'rg-web-prod', region 'eastus', using the Standard_LRS SKU.
cliChallenges.command: az storage account create --name stprodwebdata01 --resource-group rg-web-prod --location eastus --sku Standard_LRS
cliChallenges.explanation: Storage account names must be globally unique, lowercase, and alphanumeric only (no hyphens) — --sku picks the replication tier (LRS/ZRS/GRS/RA-GRS).

cliChallenges.prompt: Create a blob container named 'uploads' inside storage account 'stprodwebdata01'.
cliChallenges.command: az storage container create --name uploads --account-name stprodwebdata01
cliChallenges.explanation: Containers are the top-level grouping inside Blob storage (comparable to a folder, though blob storage is technically flat) — --account-name says which storage account to create it in.

cliChallenges.prompt: Generate a read-only blob SAS token for storage account 'stprodwebdata01', valid until 2026-12-31, granting only read (r) permission.
cliChallenges.command: az storage account generate-sas --account-name stprodwebdata01 --permissions r --expiry 2026-12-31 --services b --resource-types sco
cliChallenges.explanation: A SAS token grants scoped, time-limited access without sharing the account's full access key — --permissions, --services, and --resource-types together define exactly what the token can touch.

cliChallenges.prompt: Create a virtual network named 'vnet-prod' in resource group 'rg-web-prod', address space 10.0.0.0/16, with a subnet named 'subnet-app' using 10.0.1.0/24.
cliChallenges.command: az network vnet create --resource-group rg-web-prod --name vnet-prod --address-prefix 10.0.0.0/16 --subnet-name subnet-app --subnet-prefix 10.0.1.0/24
cliChallenges.explanation: az network vnet create can provision the VNet and its first subnet in one command — --address-prefix is the VNet's whole range, --subnet-prefix must be a range inside it.

cliChallenges.prompt: Add an inbound security rule named 'AllowHTTPS' to network security group 'nsg-web' in resource group 'rg-web-prod', allowing TCP port 443, with priority 100.
cliChallenges.command: az network nsg rule create --resource-group rg-web-prod --nsg-name nsg-web --name AllowHTTPS --priority 100 --destination-port-ranges 443 --protocol Tcp --access Allow
cliChallenges.explanation: Lower --priority numbers evaluate first (100 beats 200), and the first matching rule wins — a common exam trap is two rules that both match, where only the lower-priority number actually takes effect.

cliChallenges.prompt: Assign the built-in 'Reader' role to user 'jane@contoso.com' scoped to resource group 'rg-web-prod'.
cliChallenges.command: az role assignment create --assignee jane@contoso.com --role Reader --resource-group rg-web-prod
cliChallenges.explanation: Azure RBAC role assignments always have three parts — who (--assignee), what role, and what scope. Leaving off --resource-group here would scope it to the whole subscription instead, a much bigger blast radius.

cliChallenges.prompt: Apply a CanNotDelete management lock named 'lock-prod' to resource group 'rg-web-prod'.
cliChallenges.command: az lock create --name lock-prod --resource-group rg-web-prod --lock-type CanNotDelete
cliChallenges.explanation: --lock-type CanNotDelete still allows reads/writes, just not deletion; ReadOnly is the stricter option and blocks modification too, which can unexpectedly break autoscaling or extensions.

madlibs.scenario: An admin needs to grant a contractor the ability to restart VMs in one resource group, but nothing else — this calls for an Azure {b1} role assignment scoped to that resource group. Separately, security wants to require MFA whenever anyone signs in from outside the corporate network — that's enforced with a {b2} policy, not a role assignment at all.

options: RBAC
Conditional Access
Azure Policy
a management group
RBAC
Conditional Access
Azure Policy
a management group

madlibs.explanation: RBAC controls what actions someone can perform on which resources. Conditional Access controls the conditions under which a sign-in is allowed (MFA, location, device compliance) — a completely separate control plane from RBAC.

madlibs.scenario: A developer needs to give a third-party vendor temporary, read-only access to a single blob container for the next 48 hours, without ever exposing the storage account's master credentials — this calls for a {b1}. For their own backend service that needs full, ongoing access to every container in the account, they instead use the account's {b2}.

options: SAS token
access key
managed identity
service principal
SAS token
access key
managed identity
service principal

madlibs.explanation: A SAS token is scoped and time-limited — exactly right for temporary, narrow external access. An access key grants full, unrestricted account access and should stay internal-only.

madlibs.scenario: A network security group has two rules: one at priority 100 that denies all inbound traffic on port 22, and another at priority 200 that allows inbound traffic on port 22 from a specific admin IP. Because Azure evaluates NSG rules in order from {b1} priority number to {b2}, and stops at the first match, the admin's allow rule at priority 200 will never actually apply — the deny rule wins.

options: lowest
highest
lowest
highest

madlibs.explanation: NSG rules process in ascending priority order (lowest number first); the first matching rule wins and evaluation stops there — a classic AZ-104 trap when a lower-priority-number deny rule shadows a higher-priority-number allow rule.

madlibs.scenario: An administrator shuts down a VM from inside its own guest operating system, leaving it allocated in Azure. Because the hardware is still reserved for that VM, compute charges keep {b1}. To actually stop being billed for compute, they instead need to {b2} the VM, which releases the underlying hardware allocation entirely — storage costs continue regardless of which method was used.

options: accruing
refunding automatically
doubling
pausing
restart
deallocate
resize
clone

madlibs.explanation: Shutting down a VM from inside its own OS leaves it 'allocated' — Azure still reserves the hardware for it, so compute charges keep accruing even though nothing is running. Deallocating (the Stop button in the portal, or az vm deallocate) releases that hardware reservation, which is what actually stops compute billing.

madlibs.scenario: A company needs to restore a single accidentally-deleted folder from inside a VM using last night's scheduled recovery point — that's a job for {b1}. Separately, in case the entire primary region goes offline, they need to fail the whole VM over to a secondary region within minutes by continuously replicating it there — that calls for {b2} instead, since it replicates on an ongoing basis rather than taking periodic snapshots.

options: Azure Backup
Azure Site Recovery
Azure Monitor
a resource lock
Azure Backup
Azure Site Recovery
Azure Monitor
a resource lock

madlibs.explanation: Azure Backup takes scheduled, point-in-time recovery points and is what you restore individual files or the whole VM from. Azure Site Recovery continuously replicates entire VMs to a secondary region so it can fail them over quickly during a regional disaster — the two services solve different problems (backup/restore vs. disaster recovery) and are commonly used together, not interchangeably.

madlibs.scenario: A finance team wants to guarantee nobody can accidentally delete a critical storage account, while still letting engineers change its configuration day to day — that calls for a {b1} resource lock. If the account instead needs to be completely frozen, with no configuration changes and no deletion allowed at all, that calls for a {b2} resource lock instead.

options: CanNotDelete
ReadOnly
Contributor
Owner
CanNotDelete
ReadOnly
Contributor
Owner

madlibs.explanation: A CanNotDelete lock still allows reads and modifications, it only blocks deletion. A ReadOnly lock is stricter: it blocks both modification and deletion, freezing the resource entirely. Resource locks are a separate governance mechanism from RBAC roles like Contributor and Owner, which control who can act rather than what actions are blocked outright.

madlibs.scenario: A Standard SKU public IP address is {b1} by default, which means traffic from the internet is dropped until a {b2} rule explicitly allows it. For a root domain that must follow a resource's address, create an {b3} record set rather than a CNAME.

options: closed to inbound traffic
open to all inbound traffic
zone-pinned
dynamic
network security group
route table
Azure Policy
resource lock
alias
MX
TXT
SOA

madlibs.explanation: Standard public IPs are secure by default and need an NSG allow rule. An alias record set tracks the resource and is allowed at the apex, where a CNAME is not.

sequences.prompt: Put these steps in order for deploying a new Azure VM behind a load balancer for the first time.
steps: Create a resource group
Create a virtual network and subnet
Create the load balancer and its backend pool
Create the VM and add its NIC to the backend pool
Configure health probes and load-balancing rules
sequences.explanation: The resource group and network have to exist before anything can be placed inside them; the load balancer and its backend pool need to exist before a VM's NIC can join that pool; health probes/rules come last since they depend on the backend pool already having members to check.

sequences.prompt: Put these steps in order for granting a new employee access to a specific resource group using RBAC, following least privilege.
steps: Confirm the user's identity exists in Microsoft Entra ID
Identify the least-privileged built-in role that covers the required tasks
Navigate to the target resource group's Access control (IAM)
Add a role assignment scoping the chosen role to that resource group
Verify access by having the user attempt the task
sequences.explanation: You can't assign a role to an identity that doesn't exist yet, and picking the role BEFORE going to IAM keeps the assignment intentional rather than picking whatever's convenient once you're already in the blade. Verifying afterward closes the loop instead of assuming the assignment worked.

sequences.prompt: Put these steps in order for recovering a deleted Azure VM's data from a Recovery Services vault backup.
steps: Open the Recovery Services vault containing the backup
Select the backup item for the deleted VM
Choose 'Restore VM' and pick the desired recovery point
Configure the restore configuration (create new VM or restore disks only)
Trigger the restore and monitor the job until it completes
sequences.explanation: You have to locate the vault and the specific backup item before you can pick a recovery point, and the restore configuration (new VM vs. disks-only) has to be chosen before the restore job can actually be kicked off.

sequences.prompt: Put these Azure Resource Mover steps in order for moving a virtual machine and its network resources to another region.
steps: Select the resources and the target region
Validate and add the dependencies
Prepare the resources for the move
Initiate the move
Commit the move (or discard it)
Delete the resources in the source region
sequences.explanation: The dependency check comes right after adding resources, so the VM, NIC, and network move together. Prepare readies the move, initiate creates the resources in the target region, and committing completes the move; discarding instead returns to the source. Deleting the source resources is optional cleanup and comes last.

caseStudies.title: Fabrikam Manufacturing's Branch Office Expansion
caseStudies.scenario: Fabrikam Manufacturing is opening a new branch office and extending its Azure footprint to support it. The company already has a hub virtual network in the East US region hosting its production workloads. The new branch's virtual network must be able to reach resources in the hub network without any VM in either network being assigned a public IP address. A storage account holding manufacturing schematics must stay available even if an entire datacenter within the region fails, though it does not need to survive the whole region going offline. IT wants new hires on the network team to be able to view every network resource but never modify or delete any of them, and wants to be alerted the moment CPU usage on any branch VM exceeds 90% for more than five minutes. A contractor from a staffing agency also needs one-time access this week to restart a single VM, and nothing else.

questions.question: Which networking feature should connect the branch virtual network to the hub virtual network privately, without assigning public IP addresses to any VM?
options: Virtual network peering
A public IP address on every VM in both networks
Azure Front Door
A site-to-site VPN routed over the public internet
questions.explanation: Virtual network peering connects two Azure virtual networks directly over Microsoft's private backbone network, with no public IPs and no traffic ever touching the public internet. Front Door is a global HTTP(S) entry point for applications, not a VNet-to-VNet connectivity method, and a public-internet VPN adds cost and complexity that peering avoids when both networks already live in Azure.

questions.question: True or false: configuring the storage account with zone-redundant storage (ZRS) is enough to meet the requirement that the schematics survive an entire datacenter failure, without needing geo-redundant storage (GRS).
questions.explanation: ZRS synchronously replicates data across three physically separate availability zones (effectively separate datacenters) within one region, so it tolerates a full datacenter failure on its own. Since the requirement stops at surviving one datacenter — not the whole region — ZRS satisfies it without paying for GRS's cross-region replication.
questions.whyTested: The scenario is worded to sound like it needs disaster-grade redundancy, but the actual requirement (one datacenter, not the whole region) is satisfied by the cheaper zone-level option — reading the requirement precisely, rather than reaching for the strongest-sounding SKU, is the skill being tested.

questions.question: Which built-in RBAC role should be assigned to the new network team members so they can view network resources but never modify or delete them?
options: Reader
Network Contributor
Contributor
Owner
questions.explanation: The built-in Reader role grants view-only access to resources, including network resources, with no ability to create, modify, or delete anything — an exact match for 'view but never change.' Network Contributor would let them create and delete network resources, which is more access than the requirement calls for, and Contributor/Owner are broader still.

questions.question: Which of the following would actually satisfy the requirement to be alerted the moment CPU usage on a branch VM exceeds 90% for more than five minutes? (Select all that apply.)
options: An Azure Monitor metric alert rule on the Percentage CPU metric, with a 90% threshold over a 5-minute window
An action group attached to that alert rule to actually deliver a notification
Checking the Activity Log manually once a day
A CanNotDelete resource lock on the VMs
questions.explanation: The metric alert rule is what detects the condition (CPU over 90% sustained for 5 minutes), and the action group is what turns a firing alert into an actual notification — email, SMS, or a webhook. Neither piece alone is a complete alerting solution. Checking the Activity Log once a day isn't 'the moment' it happens, and a resource lock only blocks accidental deletion; it has nothing to do with performance monitoring.

compare.scenario: A help desk team must be able to reset passwords and manage MFA methods for the 300 users at the Lyon office, and for nobody else in the 8,000-user tenant. Which approach is better?
compare.optionA: Assign the Helpdesk Administrator role tenant-wide and add a Conditional Access policy that only lets the help desk sign in from the Lyon office network.
compare.optionB: Create an administrative unit containing the Lyon users and assign the Helpdesk Administrator role scoped to that administrative unit.
compare.why: Conditional Access controls where and how the help desk signs in, not whose accounts they may touch; once signed in from Lyon they could still reset anyone in the tenant. An administrative unit is the construct that limits a directory role to a defined population, so the scoped assignment enforces the requirement itself rather than relying on a network boundary.

compare.scenario: A DevOps team holds Contributor on RG-App so it can deploy freely. The production SQL server in RG-App must never be deleted, even by mistake or by a pipeline. Which safeguard is better?
compare.optionA: Apply a CanNotDelete resource lock to the SQL server, and leave the team's Contributor assignment in place.
compare.optionB: Replace Contributor with a custom role that omits the Microsoft.Sql/servers/delete action.
compare.why: The custom role is a reasonable least-privilege instinct, but it still allows deleting the whole resource group, which takes the server with it, and it protects against only that one team rather than Owners, service principals, or scripts. The lock sits on the resource regardless of who is acting and has to be removed deliberately before any delete succeeds.

compare.scenario: Every storage account created in the subscription must have its minimum TLS version set to 1.2. Teams create accounts through the portal, the CLI, and deployment pipelines. Which policy design is better?
compare.optionA: Assign an Azure Policy with the Deny effect that rejects storage accounts whose minimumTlsVersion is not TLS1_2.
compare.optionB: Assign an Azure Policy with the Audit effect for minimumTlsVersion and review the compliance dashboard each week.
compare.why: Audit is the gentler rollout, and it never breaks a pipeline, but it only records the violation after the account already exists and is accepting TLS 1.0 connections until someone reads the report and fixes it. The requirement says must, and Deny is the effect that makes a non-compliant request fail at creation no matter which tool submitted it.

compare.scenario: A partner uploads files to one container every night for the next six months from a server with a fixed public IP. You may need to cut off the partner early without disturbing other clients of the account. Which credential is better?
compare.optionA: A service SAS for the container, tied to a stored access policy, with the partner's IP range in the token.
compare.optionB: A user delegation SAS for the container, issued with a six-month expiry and the partner's IP range.
compare.why: A user delegation SAS is normally the stronger choice because it is backed by Microsoft Entra credentials, but the user delegation key it depends on lives at most seven days, so a six-month token cannot be issued. The stored access policy also gives you a clean kill switch: edit or delete the policy and that SAS stops working, with no key rotation that would break every other client.

compare.scenario: Audit records in a blob container must be provably unmodifiable and undeletable for seven years, with no exception for administrators or the subscription Owner. Which control is better?
compare.optionA: A ReadOnly resource lock on the storage account, with data-plane access limited to the Storage Blob Data Reader role.
compare.optionB: A time-based immutability policy on the container, locked once it has been validated.
compare.why: A ReadOnly lock protects the account's configuration on the control plane, but it does not stop data-plane writes and deletes, and an Owner can simply remove the lock or hand out a broader data role. A locked immutability policy enforces write-once-read-many on the data itself and cannot be shortened or removed by anyone, including the account owner, until the retention period expires.

compare.scenario: A CI build farm of 20 Windows VMs is busy only during weekday business hours. A build that is interrupted is simply re-queued. You must reduce compute spend as much as possible. Which approach is better?
compare.optionA: Buy one-year reserved instances covering all 20 VMs, keeping the farm on regular, non-interruptible capacity.
compare.optionB: Run the farm as a VM Scale Set of Spot VMs with the Deallocate eviction policy, scaled to zero outside business hours.
compare.why: Reservations are the right lever for steady 24x7 workloads, but they bill for every hour of the term, so a farm that runs about forty hours a week pays for more idle time than it saves. Spot capacity is discounted far more deeply, interruption is acceptable here by definition, and scaling to zero removes the idle hours entirely.

compare.scenario: A web app in a Standard S1 App Service plan hits 90% CPU for three hours each weekday afternoon and idles the rest of the time. Memory is never a problem. You need to absorb the peaks at the lowest cost. Which change is better?
compare.optionA: Add an autoscale setting that scales out on CPU percentage and scales back in when the peak passes.
compare.optionB: Scale the plan up to a Premium P2v3 tier so a single larger instance absorbs the afternoon peak.
compare.why: Scaling up does fix the afternoon peak, but the larger tier is billed around the clock, including the twenty-one hours a day when S1 was already enough. Scaling out adds instances only while the CPU condition holds and removes them afterwards, which matches a short daily spike far more cheaply.

compare.scenario: VMs in five subnets must reach an Azure SQL Database server. Traffic must stay on the Microsoft network, and the server's public endpoint must be unreachable from the internet. Which design is better?
compare.optionA: Enable a Microsoft.Sql service endpoint on each subnet and add virtual network rules for those subnets to the server firewall.
compare.optionB: Create a private endpoint for the server in the VNet with a private DNS zone, and disable public network access on the server.
compare.why: Service endpoints do keep the traffic on the backbone, and the firewall rules restrict who may connect, but the server keeps its public IP and is still a public endpoint behind an allow-list. A private endpoint gives the server an address inside the VNet, and disabling public access removes the public endpoint altogether, which is what the second requirement actually asks for.

compare.scenario: An on-premises datacenter needs a connection to Azure that sustains 2 Gbps with predictable latency, and company policy says the traffic must not traverse the public internet. Which connection is better?
compare.optionA: An ExpressRoute circuit with private peering.
compare.optionB: A site-to-site VPN using an active-active VpnGw3 gateway.
compare.why: The VPN is cheaper and faster to stand up, and its encryption protects the data, but the tunnels still ride the public internet, which the policy forbids, and a VpnGw3 gateway's per-tunnel throughput falls short of a sustained 2 Gbps. ExpressRoute is a private circuit with committed bandwidth, so it meets both the throughput and the no-internet requirement.

compare.scenario: A single-region application runs on two VMs. The business accepts losing up to 24 hours of data and an 8-hour recovery time, and wants the cheapest protection against disk corruption and accidental deletion. Which service is better?
compare.optionA: Azure Site Recovery replicating both VMs to the paired region.
compare.optionB: Azure Backup with a daily policy in a Recovery Services vault, with soft delete enabled.
compare.why: Site Recovery offers a much tighter RPO and RTO, but it continuously replicates to another region, which costs more and solves a regional outage that the business did not ask to be protected from; a corrupted disk would also replicate faithfully. Daily backups meet the stated 24-hour RPO and 8-hour RTO at far lower cost and restore to a point before the corruption or deletion.

compare.scenario: A company stores customer documents in one storage account. A new rule says each customer's data must be encrypted under a key that can be disabled for that customer alone, without touching other customers' data. Which approach is better?
compare.optionA: Create one storage account for the whole company, enable customer-managed keys for the account, and rotate the key when a customer leaves.
compare.optionB: Create an encryption scope for each customer, backed by a customer-managed key, and assign each customer's container to its own scope.
compare.why: A single account-level key covers every customer, so disabling it would lock everyone out, and rotating it does not isolate one customer. Encryption scopes apply their own key to a container or blob inside the same account, which is the construct built for per-customer cryptographic boundaries.

compare.scenario: Alert rules for 40 VMs notify an on-call team. Every Saturday night the VMs are patched and the team must not be paged, but alert history must stay complete. Which approach is better?
compare.optionA: Disable each of the alert rules on Saturday evening and re-enable them on Sunday morning, using an automation runbook.
compare.optionB: Create one alert processing rule that suppresses the action groups for the scope on a weekly schedule.
compare.why: Disabling rules means no alerts fire at all, which leaves gaps in the alert history and also hides real problems with the VMs. It also needs automation to manage 40 rules. A scheduled alert processing rule lets alerts fire and be recorded while only the notifications are suppressed, and it covers every rule in the scope.
